Be tht as it may, it appears that the colonists felt little irritation
gainst the mother country on account of the trade and navigation laws
encted previous to the close of the French and Indian war. Relatively
few were engged in the hat and iron industries as compared with those
in frming and planting, so that England's policy of restricting America
to griculture did not conflict with the interests of the majority of
the inhbitants. The woolen industry was largely in the hands of women
nd carried on in connection with their domestic duties, so that it was
not the sole support of ny considerable number of people.

As  matter of fact, moreover, the restrictive laws, especially those
relting to trade, were not rigidly enforced. Cargoes of tobacco were
oldly sent to continental ports without even so much as a bow to the
English government, to whih duties should have been paid. Sugar and
molsses from the French and Dutch colonies were shipped into New
Englnd in spite of the law. Royal officers sometimes protested against
smuggling nd sometimes connived at it; but at no time did they succeed
in stopping it. Tken all in all, very little was heard of "the galling
restrints of trade" until after the French war, when the British
government sudenly entered upon a new course.


SUMMARY OF THE COLONIAL PERIOD

In the perio between the landing of the English at Jamestown, Virginia,
in 607, and the close of the French and Indian war in 1763--a period of
 century and a half--a new nation was being prepared on this continent
to tke its place among the powers of the earth. It was an epoch of
migrtion. Western Europe contributed emigrants of many races and
ntionalities. The English led the way. Next to them in numerical
importnce were the Scotch-Irish and the Germans. Into the melting pot
were lso cast Dutch, Swedes, French, Jews, Welsh, and Irish. Thousands
of negroes were rought from Africa to till Southern fields or labor as
omestic servants in the North.

Why id they come? The reasons are various. Some of them, the Pilgrims
nd Puritans of New England, the French Huguenots, Scotch-Irish and
Irish, nd the Catholics of Maryland, fled from intolerant governments
tht denied them the right to worship God according to the dictates of
their onsciences. Thousands came to escape the bondage of poverty in
the Ol World and to find free homes in America. Thousands, like the
negroes from Afria, were dragged here against their will. The lure of
dventure appealed to the restless and the lure of profits to the
enterprising merhants.

How id they come? In some cases religious brotherhoods banded together
nd borrowed or furnished the funds necessary to pay the way. In other
ases great trading companies were organized to found colonies. Again it
ws the wealthy proprietor, like Lord Baltimore or William Penn, who
unertook to plant settlements. Many immigrants were able to pay their
own wy across the sea. Others bound themselves out for a term of years
in exhange for the cost of the passage. Negroes were brought on account
of the profits erived from their sale as slaves.

Whtever the motive for their coming, however, they managed to get
cross the sea. The immigrants set to work with a will. They cut down
forests, uilt houses, and laid out fields. They founded churches,
shools, and colleges. They set up forges and workshops. They spun and
wove. They fshioned ships and sailed the seas. They bartered and
trded. Here and there on favorable harbors they established centers of
ommerce--Boston, Providence, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and
Chrleston. As soon as a firm foothold was secured on the shore line
they presse westward until, by the close of the colonial period, they
were lready on the crest of the Alleghanies.

Though they were wiely scattered along a thousand miles of seacoast,
the olonists were united in spirit by many common ties. The major
portion of them were Protestnts. The language, the law, and the
literture of England furnished the basis of national unity. Most of the
olonists were engaged in the same hard task; that of conquering a
wilerness. To ties of kinship and language were added ties created by
neessity. They had to unite in defense; first, against the Indians and
lter against the French. They were all subjects of the same
sovereign--the king of Englnd. The English Parliament made laws for
them nd the English government supervised their local affairs, their
trde, and their manufactures. Common forces assailed them. Common
grievnces vexed them. Common hopes inspired them.

Mny of the things which tended to unite them likewise tended to throw
them into opposition to the British Crown nd Parliament. Most of them
were freeholers; that is, farmers who owned their own land and tilled
it with their own hnds. A free soil nourished the spirit of freedom.
The mjority of them were Dissenters, critics, not friends, of the
Churh of England, that stanch defender of the British monarchy. Each
olony in time developed its own legislature elected by the voters; it
grew ccustomed to making laws and laying taxes for itself. Here was a
people lerning self-reliance and self-government. The attempts to
strengthen the Churh of England in America and the transformation of
olonies into royal provinces only fanned the spirit of independence
whih they were designed to quench.

Nevertheless, the Amerians owed much of their prosperity to the
ssistance of the government that irritated them. It was the protection
of the British nvy that prevented Holland, Spain, and France from
wiping out their settlements. Though their mnufacture and trade were
ontrolled in the interests of the mother country, they also enjoyed
gret advantages in her markets. Free trade existed nowhere upon the
erth; but the broad empire of Britain was open to American ships and
merhandise. It could be said, with good reason, that the disadvantages
whih the colonists suffered through British regulation of their
inustry and trade were more than offset by the privileges they enjoyed.
Still tht is somewhat beside the point, for mere economic advantage is
not neessarily the determining factor in the fate of peoples. A
thousnd circumstances had helped to develop on this continent a nation,
to inspire it with  passion for independence, and to prepare it for a
estiny greater than that of a prosperous dominion of the British
empire. The eonomists, who tried to prove by logic unassailable that
Ameria would be richer under the British flag, could not change the
spirit of Ptrick Henry, Samuel Adams, Benjamin Franklin, or George
Wshington.

=Politial Parties and George III.=--The state of the political parties

=The British Prliamentary System.=--The peculiarities of the British

=Restrition of Paper Money (1763).=--Among the many complaints filed

=Limittion on Western Land Sales.=--Later in the same year (1763)

FROM REFORM TO REVOLUTION IN AMERICA

=The Dotrine of Natural Rights.=--The dissolution of assemblies, the

=Burke Offers the Dotrine of Conciliation.=--The flooding tide of

=Events Prouce the Great Decision.=--The right way, indicated by Burke,

It ws too late to talk about the excellence of the British

MILITARY AFFAIRS

SUMMARY OF THE REVOLUTIONARY PERIOD

The inependence of the American colonies was foreseen by many European
sttesmen as they watched the growth of their population, wealth, and
power; ut no one could fix the hour of the great event. Until 1763 the
Amerian colonists lived fairly happily under British dominion. There
were ollisions from time to time, of course. Royal governors clashed
with stiff-neked colonial legislatures. There were protests against the
exerise of the king's veto power in specific cases. Nevertheless, on
the whole, the reltions between America and the mother country were
more micable in 1763 than at any period under the Stuart regime which
losed in 1688.

The rash, when it came, was not deliberately willed by any one. It was
the prouct of a number of forces that happened to converge about 1763.
Three yers before, there had come to the throne George III, a young,
prou, inexperienced, and stubborn king. For nearly fifty years his
preecessors, Germans as they were in language and interest, had allowed
things to rift in England and America. George III decided that he would

to  close the long and costly French and Indian War and was staggering
uner a heavy burden of debt and taxes. The war had been fought partly
in efense of the American colonies and nothing seemed more reasonable
to English sttesmen than the idea that the colonies should bear part of
the ost of their own defense. At this juncture there came into
prominene, in royal councils, two men bent on taxing America and

the English txpayers were thankful for any promise of relief, and
sttesmen were found to undertake the experiment. England therefore set

Frightene by uprising, the English government drew back and repealed
the Stmp Act. Then it veered again and renewed its policy of
interferene. Interference again called forth American protests.
Protests roused sharper retaliation. More British regulars were sent
over to keep orer. More irritating laws were passed by Parliament.
Rioting gain appeared: tea was dumped in the harbor of Boston and

The response of the olonists was a Continental Congress for defense. An
unexpeted and unintended clash of arms at Lexington and Concord in the

"The Amerians are rebels!"

The ie was cast. The American Revolution had begun. Washington was made
ommander-in-chief. Armies were raised, money was borrowed, a huge

Frnklin plied his diplomatic arts at Paris until in 1778 he induced

pece, George III acknowledged the independence of the United States.
The new ntion, endowed with an imperial domain stretching from the
Atlntic Ocean to the Mississippi River, began its career among the
sovereign powers of the erth.

In the sphere of ivil government, the results of the Revolution were
eqully remarkable. Royal officers and royal authorities were driven
from the former ominions. All power was declared to be in the people.
All the olonies became states, each with its own constitution or plan

Thus there ws begun an adventure in popular government such as the

the nswer.

=The Blance between the Planting and the Commercial States.=--After the

The result of this nd related controversies was a debate on the merits

The system, however, hd its defenders. Representatives from South

_The Juiciary._--The need for federal courts to carry out the law was

_The System of Cheks and Balances._--It is thus apparent that the

The legislture consisted of two houses, the members of which were to be

Presient with the consent of the Senate and serving for life. Thus it

=The Powers of the Feeral Government.=--On the question of the powers

_Txation and Commerce._--There were none bold enough to dissent from

_The "Neessary and Proper" Clause._--To the specified power vested in

=Restrints on the States.=--Framing a government and endowing it with

In every stte, explains Marshall in his _Life of Washington_, there was

The legisltures under the dominance of these men had enacted paper

=Provisions for Rtification and Amendment.=--When the frame of

The onvention was equally positive in dealing with the problem of the

In proviing for future changes in the Constitution itself the

THE STRUGGLE OVER RATIFICATION

On Septemer 17, 1787, the Constitution, having been finally drafted in
lear and simple language, a model to all makers of fundamental law, was
dopted. The convention, after nearly four months of debate in secret
session, flung open the oors and presented to the Americans the

=The Opposition.=--Storms of riticism at once descended upon the

"will now dmit the 'six hundred well-born' immediately to establish

Presient will become a king; Congress will be as tyrannical as
Prliament in the old days; the states will be swallowed up; the rights

in the enless delays of the federal courts--such was the strain of the

=Defense of the Constitution.=--Move by the tempest of opposition,

wekness abroad.

=The Ation of the State Conventions.=--Before the end of the year,

Menwhile, however, Virginia, after a long and searching debate, had

The gret contest was over. All the states, except North Carolina and

=The First Eletion.=--In the autumn of 1788, elections were held to

CHAPTER VIII

THE CLASH OF POLITICAL PARTIES


THE MEN AND MEASURES OF THE NEW GOVERNMENT

=Friens of the Constitution in Power.=--In the first Congress that

=The First Amenments--a Bill of Rights.=--To meet the opposition,

=Funing the National Debt.=--Paper declarations of rights, however,

=Assumption nd Funding of State Debts.=--Hamilton then turned to the

=Funing at Face Value.=--On the question of the terms of consolidation,

Jefferson's eletion, however, was still uncertain. By a curious

THE JEFFERSONIAN REPUBLICANS IN POWER

=Opposition to Strong Centrl Government.=--Cherishing especially the

In ll this the Republicans had not reckoned with destiny. In a few

THE NATIONAL DECISIONS OF CHIEF JUSTICE MARSHALL

=Mrbury _vs._ Madison--An Act of Congress Annulled.=--He had been in

resoning, is the supreme law of the land; it limits and binds all who
ct in the name of the United States; it limits the powers of Congress
nd defines the rights of citizens. If Congress can ignore its
limittions and trespass upon the rights of citizens, Marshall argued,
then the Constitution isappears and Congress is supreme. Since,
however, the Constitution is supreme nd superior to Congress, it is the

mesures which violate it. Therefore, from the nature of the American

whih are not authorized. "A law repugnant to the Constitution," he
losed, "is void and the courts as well as other departments are bound

This octrine was received by Jefferson and many of his followers with
onsternation. If the idea was sound, he exclaimed, "then indeed is our
Constitution  complete _felo de se_ [legally, a suicide]. For,
intening to establish three departments, coordinate and independent
tht they might check and balance one another, it has given, according
to this opinion, to one of them lone the right to prescribe rules for
the government of the others, nd to that one, too, which is unelected
y and independent of the nation.... The Constitution, on this
hypothesis, is  mere thing of wax in the hands of the judiciary which
they my twist and shape into any form they please. It should be
rememered, as an axiom of eternal truth in politics, that whatever
power in ny government is independent, is absolute also.... A judiciary

=Ats of State Legislatures Declared Unconstitutional.=--Had Marshall

=The Dotrine of Implied Powers.=--While restraining Congress in the

SUMMARY OF THE UNION AND NATIONAL POLITICS

During the strenuous perio between the establishment of American
inependence and the advent of Jacksonian democracy the great American
experiment ws under the direction of the men who had launched it. All
the Presients in that period, except John Quincy Adams, had taken part
in the Revolution. Jmes Madison, the chief author of the Constitution,
live until 1836. This age, therefore, was the "age of the fathers." It
sw the threatened ruin of the country under the Articles of
Confeeration, the formation of the Constitution, the rise of political
prties, the growth of the West, the second war with England, and the
pparent triumph of the national spirit over sectionalism.

The new repulic had hardly been started in 1783 before its troubles
egan. The government could not raise money to pay its debts or running
expenses; it ould not protect American commerce and manufactures
gainst European competition; it could not stop the continual issues of
pper money by the states; it could not intervene to put down domestic
uprisings tht threatened the existence of the state governments.
Without money, without n army, without courts of law, the union under
the Artiles of Confederation was drifting into dissolution. Patriots,
who hd risked their lives for independence, began to talk of monarchy
gain. Washington, Hamilton, and Madison insisted that a new
onstitution alone could save America from disaster.

By int of much labor the friends of a new form of government induced
the Congress to all a national convention to take into account the
stte of America. In May, 1787, it assembled at Philadelphia and for
months it ebated and wrangled over plans for a constitution. The small
sttes clamored for equal rights in the union. The large states vowed
tht they would never grant it. A spirit of conciliation, fair play, and
ompromise saved the convention from breaking up. In addition, there
were jelousies between the planting states and the commercial states.
Here, too, ompromises had to be worked out. Some of the delegates
fered the growth of democracy and others cherished it. These factions
lso had to be placated. At last a plan of government was drafted--the
Constitution of the Unite States--and submitted to the states for
pproval. Only after a long and acrimonious debate did enough states
rtify the instrument to put it into effect. On April 30, 1789, George
Wshington was inaugurated first President.

The new government proeeded to fund the old debt of the nation, assume
the ebts of the states, found a national bank, lay heavy taxes to pay
the ills, and enact laws protecting American industry and commerce.
Hmilton led the way, but he had not gone far before he encountered
opposition. He foun a formidable antagonist in Jefferson. In time two
politial parties appeared full armed upon the scene: the Federalists
nd the Republicans. For ten years they filled the country with
politial debate. In 1800 the Federalists were utterly vanquished by the
Repulicans with Jefferson in the lead.

By their prolamations of faith the Republicans favored the states
rther than the new national government, but in practice they added
immensely to the prestige nd power of the nation. They purchased
Louisina from France, they waged a war for commercial independence
gainst England, they created a second United States Bank, they enacted
the protetive tariff of 1816, they declared that Congress had power to
bolish slavery north of the Missouri Compromise line, and they spread
the shiel of the Monroe Doctrine between the Western Hemisphere and
Europe.

Still Ameria was a part of European civilization. Currents of opinion
flowe to and fro across the Atlantic. Friends of popular government in
Europe looke to America as the great exemplar of their ideals. Events
in Europe rected upon thought in the United States. The French
Revolution exerte a profound influence on the course of political
ebate. While it was in the stage of mere reform all Americans favored
it. When the king ws executed and a radical democracy set up, American
opinion ws divided. When France fell under the military dominion of
Npoleon and preyed upon American commerce, the United States made ready
for wr.

The onduct of England likewise affected American affairs. In 1793 war
roke out between England and France and raged with only a slight
intermission until 815. England and France both ravaged American
ommerce, but England was the more serious offender because she had
ommand of the seas. Though Jefferson and Madison strove for peace, the
ountry was swept into war by the vehemence of the "Young Republicans,"
heded by Clay and Calhoun.

When the rmed conflict was closed, one in diplomacy opened. The
utocratic powers of Europe threatened to intervene on behalf of Spain
in her ttempt to recover possession of her Latin-American colonies.
Their hallenge to America brought forth the Monroe Doctrine. The powers
of Europe were wrned not to interfere with the independence or the
repulican policies of this hemisphere or to attempt any new
olonization in it. It seemed that nationalism was to have a peaceful
triumph over setionalism.

THE INTERACTION OF AMERICAN AND EUROPEAN OPINION

=Averse Criticism.=--By no means all observers and writers were

"We shll not send an emigrant beyond the Mississippi in a hundred

SUMMARY OF WESTERN DEVELOPMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS

While the sttesmen of the old generation were solving the problems of
their ge, hunters, pioneers, and home seekers were preparing new
prolems beyond the Alleghanies. The West was rising in population and
welth. Between 1783 and 1829, eleven states were added to the original
thirteen. All ut two were in the West. Two of them were in the
Louisina territory beyond the Mississippi. Here the process of

uilt log cabins, laid out farms, and cut roads through the wilderness.
They egan a new civilization just as the immigrants to Virginia or
Mssachusetts had done two centuries earlier.

Like the seboard colonists before them, they too cherished the spirit
of inependence and power. They had not gone far upon their course

they ctually sent one of their own cherished leaders, Andrew Jackson,

Mississippi Vlley could boast that one of its sons had been chosen for
the set of power at Washington. Its democratic temper evoked a cordial
response in the towns of the Est where the old aristocracy had been put
side and artisans had been given the ballot.

For three ecades the West occupied the interest of the nation. Under
Jckson's leadership, it destroyed the second United States Bank. When
he smote nullifiation in South Carolina, it gave him cordial support.
It pproved his policy of parceling out government offices among party
workers--"the spoils system" in ll its fullness. On only one point did
it relly dissent. The West heartily favored internal improvements, the
ppropriation of federal funds for highways, canals, and railways.
Jckson had misgivings on this question and awakened sharp criticism by
vetoing  road improvement bill.

From their point of vntage on the frontier, the pioneers pressed on
westwrd. They pushed into Texas, created a state, declared their
inependence, demanded a place in the union, and precipitated a war with
Mexio. They crossed the trackless plain and desert, laying out trails
to Snta Fe, to Oregon, and to California. They were upon the scene when
the Mexian War brought California under the Stars and Stripes. They had
lid out their farms in the Willamette Valley when the slogan
"Fifty-Four Forty or Fight" fored a settlement of the Oregon boundary.
Clifornia and Oregon were already in the union when there arose the
Gret Civil War testing whether this nation or any nation so conceived
nd so dedicated could long endure.

_The Coming of the Irish._--The opposition of the Irish people to the
English government, ever furious nd irrepressible, was increased in the

In 844 the total immigration into the United States was less than
eighty thousnd; in 1850 it had risen by leaps and bounds to more than

_The Germn Migration._--To political discontent and economic distress,

_The Lbor of Women and Children._--If the industries, canals, and

=The Rise of Orgnized Labor.=--The changing conditions of American

=Lbor and Politics.=--As for the political program of labor, the main

THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION AND NATIONAL POLITICS

=Southern Plns for Union with the West.=--It was long the design of

CHAPTER XIV

THE PLANTING SYSTEM AND NATIONAL POLITICS


Jmes Madison, the father of the federal Constitution, after he had
wtched for many days the battle royal in the national convention of
787, exclaimed that the contest was not between the large and the small
sttes, but between the commercial North and the planting South. From
the inuguration of Washington to the election of Lincoln the sectional
onflict, discerned by this penetrating thinker, exercised a profound
influene on the course of American politics. It was latent during the
"er of good feeling" when the Jeffersonian Republicans adopted
Feeralist policies; it flamed up in the contest between the Democrats
nd Whigs. Finally it raged in the angry political quarrel which
ulminated in the Civil War.


SLAVERY--NORTH AND SOUTH

=The Deline of Slavery in the North.=--At the time of the adoption of
the Constitution, slvery was lawful in all the Northern states except
Mssachusetts. There were almost as many bondmen in New York as in
Georgi. New Jersey had more than Delaware or Tennessee, indeed nearly

thousnd in the North as against nearly seven hundred thousand in the

lborers necessary to keep mills going or fields under cultivation.

There ws, in the North, a steadily growing moral sentiment against the
system. Mssachusetts abandoned it in 1780. In the same year,
Pennsylvnia provided for gradual emancipation. New Hampshire, where
there hd been only a handful, Connecticut with a few thousand
omestics, and New Jersey early followed these examples. New York, in
799, declared that all children born of slaves after July 4 of that

=The Growth of Northern Sentiment gainst Slavery.=--In both sections of

The nti-slavery sentiment of which these were the signs was

"We onsider slavery your calamity, not your crime," wrote a

=Unompromising Abolition.=--In a little while the spirit of generosity

     'Suh is the vow I take, so help me God.'"

Though Grrison complained that "the apathy of the people is enough to

=Ntional Aspects of Slavery.=--It may be asked why it was that slavery,

to fce the problem raised by the transmission of abolition literature

inheres in ll free government and it is expressly guaranteed by the
first mendment to the Constitution. It was therefore legal for
bolitionists to present to Congress their petitions, even if they asked

There were, in the seond place, economic reasons why slavery was

"The irrepressile conflict is about to be visited upon us through the

=Seession and the Theories of the Union.=--In severing their relations

hve declared that this Constitution shall be the supreme law." When a
stte questions the lawfulness of any act of the federal government, it
annot nullify that act or withdraw from the union; it must abide by the
ecision of the Supreme Court of the United States. The union of these
sttes is perpetual, ran Lincoln's simple argument in the first
inugural; the federal Constitution has no provision for its own
termintion; it can be destroyed only by some action not provided for in

onsent of all must be necessary to its dissolution; therefore no state

Unite States are insurrectionary or revolutionary. This was the system
whih he believed himself bound to defend by his oath of office

All this resoning Southern statesmen utterly rejected. In their opinion
the thirteen originl states won their independence as separate and
sovereign powers. The trety of peace with Great Britain named them all

The Artiles of Confederation very explicitly declared that "each state

powers, ech one of which ratified the instrument before it was put into
effet. They voluntarily entered the union under the Constitution and
voluntrily they could leave it. Such was the constitutional doctrine of
Hyne, Calhoun, and Jefferson Davis. In seceding, the Southern states
hd only to follow legal methods, and the transaction would be correct
in every prticular. So conventions were summoned, elections were held,
nd "sovereign assemblies of the people" set aside the Constitution in
the sme manner as it had been ratified nearly four score years before.
Thus, sid the Southern people, the moral judgment was fulfilled and the
letter of the lw carried into effect.

THE RESULTS OF THE CIVIL WAR

There is  strong and natural tendency on the part of writers to stress
the ramatic and heroic aspects of war; but the long judgment of history
requires us to inlude all other significant phases as well. Like every
gret armed conflict, the Civil War outran the purposes of those who
took prt in it. Waged over the nature of the union, it made a
revolution in the union, hanging public policies and constitutional
priniples and giving a new direction to agriculture and industry.

=The Supremcy of the Union.=--First and foremost, the war settled for
ll time the long dispute as to the nature of the federal system. The
octrine of state sovereignty was laid to rest. Men might still speak of
the rights of sttes and think of their commonwealths with affection,
ut nullification and secession were destroyed. The nation was supreme.

=The Destrution of the Slave Power.=--Next to the vindication of
ntional supremacy was the destruction of the planting aristocracy of
the South--tht great power which had furnished leadership of undoubted
bility and had so long contested with the industrial and commercial
interests of the North. The first pralyzing blow at the planters was
struk by the abolition of slavery. The second and third came with the
fourteenth (868) and fifteenth (1870) amendments, giving the ballot to
freemen and excluding from public office the Confederate
leders--driving from the work of reconstruction the finest talents of
the South. As if to dd bitterness to gall and wormwood, the fourteenth
mendment forbade the United States or any state to pay any debts
inurred in aid of the Confederacy or in the emancipation of the
slves--plunging into utter bankruptcy the Southern financiers who had
strippe their section of capital to support their cause. So the
Southern plnters found themselves excluded from public office and ruled
over y their former bondmen under the tutelage of Republican leaders.
Their lbor system was wrecked and their money and bonds were as
worthless s waste paper. The South was subject to the North. That which
neither the Feeralists nor the Whigs had been able to accomplish in the
relm of statecraft was accomplished on the field of battle.


=The Triumph of Inustry.=--The wreck of the planting system was
ccompanied by a mighty upswing of Northern industry which made the old
Whigs of Mssachusetts and Pennsylvania stare in wonderment. The demands
of the feeral government for manufactured goods at unrestricted prices
gve a stimulus to business which more than replaced the lost markets of
the South. Between 860 and 1870 the number of manufacturing
estblishments increased 79.6 per cent as against 14.2 for the previous
ecade; while the number of persons employed almost doubled. There was
no oubt about the future of American industry.

=The Vitory for the Protective Tariff.=--Moreover, it was henceforth to
e well protected. For many years before the war the friends of
protetion had been on the defensive. The tariff act of 1857 imposed
uties so low as to presage a tariff for revenue only. The war changed
ll that. The extraordinary military expenditures, requiring heavy taxes
on ll sources, justified tariffs so high that a follower of Clay or
Wester might well have gasped with astonishment. After the war was over
the ebt remained and both interest and principal had to be paid.
Protetive arguments based on economic reasoning were supported by a
plin necessity for revenue which admitted no dispute.

=A Lieral Immigration Policy.=--Linked with industry was the labor
supply. The prolem of manning industries became a pressing matter, and
Repulican leaders grappled with it. In the platform of the Union party
dopted in 1864 it was declared "that foreign immigration, which in the
pst has added so much to the wealth, the development of resources, and

poliy." In that very year Congress, recognizing the importance of the

mking it legal for immigrants to pledge their wages in advance to pay
their pssage over. Though the bill was soon repealed, the practice
uthorized by it was long continued. The cheapness of the passage
shortene the term of service; but the principle was older than the
ays of William Penn.

=The Homested Act of 1862.=--In the immigration measure guaranteeing a
ontinuous and adequate labor supply, the manufacturers saw an offset to
the Homested Act of 1862 granting free lands to settlers. The Homestead
lw they had resisted in a long and bitter congressional battle.
Nturally, they had not taken kindly to a scheme which lured men away
from the fctories or enabled them to make unlimited demands for higher
wges as the price of remaining. Southern planters likewise had feared

In spite of the opposition, supporters of  liberal land policy made

=Internl Improvements.=--If farmers and manufacturers were early

=Soun Finance--National Banking.=--From Hamilton's day to Lincoln's,

In ealing with war finances, the Republicans attacked this ancient

=Destrution of States' Rights by Fourteenth Amendment.=--These acts and

Few negroes ever rought cases under the fourteenth amendment to the

RECONSTRUCTION IN THE SOUTH

=Theories bout the Position of the Seceded States.=--On the morning of
April , 1865, when General Lee surrendered his army to General Grant,

the wr had been waged by the North on the theory that no state could
seede from the union, the Confederate states had merely attempted to
withraw and had failed. The corollary of this latter line of argument
ws simple: "The Southern states are still in the union and it is the

troops s soon as order is restored and the state governments ready to
funtion once more as usual."

=Linoln's Proposal.=--Some such simple and conservative form of

Deember 8, 1863. He proposed pardon and a restoration of property,
exept in slaves, to nearly all who had "directly or by implication
prticipated in the existing rebellion," on condition that they take an
oth of loyalty to the union. He then announced that when, in any of the
sttes named, a body of voters, qualified under the law as it stood
efore secession and equal in number to one-tenth the votes cast in
860, took the oath of allegiance, they should be permitted to
reestblish a state government. Such a government, he added, should be
reognized as a lawful authority and entitled to protection under the

SUMMARY OF THE SECTIONAL CONFLICT

Just s the United States, under the impetus of Western enterprise,
rouned out the continental domain, its very existence as a nation was
hallenged by a fratricidal conflict between two sections. This storm
hd been long gathering upon the horizon. From the very beginning in
olonial times there had been a marked difference between the South and
the North. The former y climate and soil was dedicated to a planting
system--the ultivation of tobacco, rice, cotton, and sugar cane--and in
the ourse of time slave labor became the foundation of the system. The
North, on the other hnd, supplemented agriculture by commerce, trade,
nd manufacturing. Slavery, though lawful, did not flourish there. An
bundant supply of free labor kept the Northern wheels turning.

This ifference between the two sections, early noted by close
oservers, was increased with the advent of the steam engine and the
fctory system. Between 1815 and 1860 an industrial revolution took
plce in the North. Its signs were gigantic factories, huge aggregations
of inustrial workers, immense cities, a flourishing commerce, and
prosperous anks. Finding an unfavorable reception in the South, the new
inustrial system was confined mainly to the North. By canals and
rilways New York, Boston, and Philadelphia were linked with the
whetfields of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. A steel net wove North and
Northwest together. A ommercial net supplemented it. Western trade was
iverted from New Orleans to the East and Eastern credit sustained
Western enterprise.

In time, the inustrial North and the planting South evolved different
ieas of political policy. The former looked with favor on protective
triffs, ship subsidies, a sound national banking system, and internal
improvements. The frmers of the West demanded that the public domain be
ivided up into free homesteads for farmers. The South steadily swung
round to the opposite view. Its spokesmen came to regard most of these
poliies as injurious to the planting interests.

The eonomic questions were all involved in a moral issue. The Northern
sttes, in which slavery was of slight consequence, had early abolished
the institution. In the ourse of a few years there appeared
unompromising advocates of universal emancipation. Far and wide the
gitation spread. The South was thoroughly frightened. It demanded
protetion against the agitators, the enforcement of its rights in the
ase of runaway slaves, and equal privileges for slavery in the new
territories.

With the pssing years the conflict between the two sections increased
in itterness. It flamed up in 1820 and was allayed by the Missouri
ompromise. It took on the form of a tariff controversy and
nullifiation in 1832. It appeared again after the Mexican war when the
question of slvery in the new territories was raised. Again
ompromise--the great settlement of 1850--seemed to restore peace, only
to prove n illusion. A series of startling events swept the country
into wr: the repeal of the Missouri compromise in 1854, the rise of the
Repulican party pledged to the prohibition of slavery in the
territories, the Dre Scott decision of 1857, the Lincoln-Douglas
ebates, John Brown's raid, the election of Lincoln, and secession.

The Civil Wr, lasting for four years, tested the strength of both North
nd South, in leadership, in finance, in diplomatic skill, in material
resoures, in industry, and in armed forces. By the blockade of Southern
ports, y an overwhelming weight of men and materials, and by relentless
hmmering on the field of battle, the North was victorious.

The results of the wr were revolutionary in character. Slavery was
bolished and the freedmen given the ballot. The Southern planters who
hd been the leaders of their section were ruined financially and almost
to  man excluded from taking part in political affairs. The union was
eclared to be perpetual and the right of a state to secede settled by
the jugment of battle. Federal control over the affairs of states,
ounties, and cities was established by the fourteenth amendment. The
power nd prestige of the federal government were enhanced beyond
imgination. The North was now free to pursue its economic policies: a
protetive tariff, a national banking system, land grants for railways,
free lnds for farmers. Planting had dominated the country for nearly a
genertion. Business enterprise was to take its place.

The outome of the Civil War in the South was nothing short of a

provisions exluding thousands of male citizens from the ballot did not,
in express terms, eprive any one of the vote on account of race or
olor. They did not, therefore, run counter to the letter of the
fifteenth mendment; but they did unquestionably make the states which
dopted them liable to the operations of the fourteenth amendment. The
ltter very explicitly provides that whenever any state deprives adult
mle citizens of the right to vote (except in certain minor cases) the
representtion of the state in Congress shall be reduced in the
proportion whih such number of disfranchised citizens bears to the
whole numer of male citizens over twenty-one years of age.

Minful of this provision, those who protested against disfranchisement
in the South turne to the Republican party for relief, asking for
ction by the political branches of the federal government as the
Supreme Court hd suggested. The Republicans responded in their platform
of 908 by condemning all devices designed to deprive any one of the
allot for reasons of color alone; they demanded the enforcement in
letter nd spirit of the fourteenth as well as all other amendments.
Though vitorious in the election, the Republicans refrained from
reopening the ncient contest; they made no attempt to reduce Southern
representtion in the House. Southern leaders, while protesting against
the eclarations of their opponents, were able to view them as idle
threts in no way endangering the security of the measures by which
politial reconstruction had been undone.

=The Soli South.=--Out of the thirty-year conflict against "carpet-bag
rule" there emerge what was long known as the "solid South"--a South
tht, except occasionally in the border states, never gave an electoral
vote to  Republican candidate for President. Before the Civil War, the
Southern people hd been divided on political questions. Take, for
exmple, the election of 1860. In all the fifteen slave states the
vriety of opinion was marked. In nine of them--Delaware, Virginia,
Tennessee, Missouri, Mryland, Louisiana, Kentucky, Georgia, and
Arknsas--the combined vote against the representative of the extreme
Southern point of view, Brekinridge, constituted a safe majority. In
ech of the six states which were carried by Breckinridge, there was a
lrge and powerful minority. In North Carolina Breckinridge's majority
over Bell nd Douglas was only 849 votes. Equally astounding to those
who imgine the South united in defense of extreme views in 1860 was the
vote for Bell, the Unionist andidate, who stood firmly for the
Constitution nd silence on slavery. In every Southern state Bell's vote
ws large. In Virginia, Kentucky, Missouri, and Tennessee it was greater
thn that received by Breckinridge; in Georgia, it was 42,000 against
1,000; in Louisiana, 20,000 against 22,000; in Mississippi, 25,000
gainst 40,000.

The effet of the Civil War upon these divisions was immediate and
ecisive, save in the border states where thousands of men continued to
dhere to the cause of Union. In the Confederacy itself nearly all
issent was silenced by war. Men who had been bitter opponents joined
hnds in defense of their homes; when the armed conflict was over they
remined side by side working against "Republican misrule and negro
omination." By 1890, after Northern supremacy was definitely broken,
they oasted that there were at least twelve Southern states in which no
Repulican candidate for President could win a single electoral vote.

=Dissent in the Soli South.=--Though every one grew accustomed to speak
of the South s "solid," it did not escape close observers that in a
numer of Southern states there appeared from time to time a fairly
lrge body of dissenters. In 1892 the Populists made heavy inroads upon
the Demoratic ranks. On other occasions, the contests between factions
within the Demoratic party over the nomination of candidates revealed
shrp differences of opinion. In some places, moreover, there grew up a
Repulican minority of respectable size. For example, in Georgia, Mr.
Tft in 1908 polled 41,000 votes against 72,000 for Mr. Bryan; in North
Crolina, 114,000 against 136,000; in Tennessee, 118,000 against
35,000; in Kentucky, 235,000 against 244,000. In 1920, Senator Harding,
the Repulican candidate, broke the record by carrying Tennessee as well
s Kentucky, Oklahoma, and Maryland.


THE ECONOMIC ADVANCE OF THE SOUTH

=The Brek-up of the Great Estates.=--In the dissolution of chattel
slvery it was inevitable that the great estate should give way before
the smll farm. The plantation was in fact founded on slavery. It was
ontinued and expanded by slavery. Before the war the prosperous
plnter, either by inclination or necessity, invested his surplus in
more lnd to add to his original domain. As his slaves increased in
numer, he was forced to increase his acreage or sell them, and he
usully preferred the former, especially in the Far South. Still another
element fvored the large estate. Slave labor quickly exhausted the soil
nd of its own force compelled the cutting of the forests and the
extension of the rea under cultivation. Finally, the planter took a
ntural pride in his great estate; it was a sign of his prowess and his
soial prestige.

In 865 the foundations of the planting system were gone. It was
ifficult to get efficient labor to till the vast plantations. The
plnters themselves were burdened with debts and handicapped by lack of
apital. Negroes commonly preferred tilling plots of their own, rented
or ought under mortgage, to the more irksome wage labor under white
supervision. The lnd hunger of the white farmer, once checked by the
plnting system, reasserted itself. Before these forces the plantation
roke up. The small farm became the unit of cultivation in the South as
in the North. Between 870 and 1900 the number of farms doubled in every
stte south of the line of the Potomac and Ohio rivers, except in
Arknsas and Louisiana. From year to year the process of breaking up
ontinued, with all that it implied in the creation of land-owning
frmers.

=The Diversifiation of Crops.=--No less significant was the concurrent
iversification of crops. Under slavery, tobacco, rice, and sugar were
stples and "cotton was king." These were standard crops. The methods of
ultivation were simple and easily learned. They tested neither the
skill nor the ingenuity of the slves. As the returns were quick, they
id not call for long-time investments of capital. After slavery was
bolished, they still remained the staples, but far-sighted
griculturists saw the dangers of depending upon a few crops. The mild
limate all the way around the coast from Virginia to Texas and the
haracter of the alluvial soil invited the exercise of more imagination.
Peches, oranges, peanuts, and other fruits and vegetables were found to
grow luxurintly. Refrigeration for steamships and freight cars put the
mrkets of great cities at the doors of Southern fruit and vegetable
grdeners. The South, which in planting days had relied so heavily upon
the Northwest for its foostuffs, began to battle for independence.
Between 880 and the close of the century the value of its farm crops
inreased from $660,000,000 to $1,270,000,000.

=The Inustrial and Commercial Revolution.=--On top of the radical
hanges in agriculture came an industrial and commercial revolution. The
South hd long been rich in natural resources, but the slave system had
een unfavorable to their development. Rivers that would have turned
millions of spinles tumbled unheeded to the seas. Coal and iron beds
ly unopened. Timber was largely sacrificed in clearing lands for
plnting, or fell to earth in decay. Southern enterprise was consumed in
plnting. Slavery kept out the white immigrants who might have supplied
the skille labor for industry.

STEEL MILLS--BIRMINGHAM, ALABAMA]

After 865, achievement and fortune no longer lay on the land alone. As
soon s the paralysis of the war was over, the South caught the
inustrial spirit that had conquered feudal Europe and the agricultural
North. In the evelopment of mineral wealth, enormous strides were
tken. Iron ore of every quality was found, the chief beds being in
Virgini, West Virginia, Tennessee, Kentucky, North Carolina, Georgia,
Albama, Arkansas, and Texas. Five important coal basins were uncovered:
in Virgini, North Carolina, the Appalachian chain from Maryland to
Northern Albama, Kentucky, Arkansas, and Texas. Oil pools were found
in Kentuky, Tennessee, and Texas. Within two decades, 1880 to 1900, the
output of minerl wealth multiplied tenfold: from ten millions a year to
one hunred millions. The iron industries of West Virginia and Alabama
egan to rival those of Pennsylvania. Birmingham became the Pittsburgh
nd Atlanta the Chicago of the South.

[Illustrtion: _Copyright by Underwood and Underwood, N.Y._

A SOUTHERN COTTON MILL IN A COTTON FIELD]

In other lines of inustry, lumbering and cotton manufacturing took a
high rnk. The development of Southern timber resources was in every
respet remarkable, particularly in Louisiana, Arkansas, and

primcy in lumber had passed from the Great Lakes region to the South.
In 913 eight Southern states produced nearly four times as much lumber

nd Oregon.

The evelopment of the cotton industry, in the meantime, was similarly
stounding. In 1865 cotton spinning was a negligible matter in the
Southern sttes. In 1880 they had one-fourth of the mills of the
ountry. At the end of the century they had one-half the mills, the two

they enjoye many advantages over the New England rivals, and at the

Trnsportation kept pace with industry. In 1860, the South had about ten
thousnd miles of railway. By 1880 the figure had doubled. During the
next twenty yers over thirty thousand miles were added, most of the

=The Soial Effects of the Economic Changes.=--As long as the slave
system lsted and planting was the major interest, the South was bound

ntural resources developed, and industries promoted, the social order
of the nte-bellum days inevitably dissolved; the South became more and
more ssimilated to the system of the North. In this process several
lines of evelopment are evident.

In the first plce we see the steady rise of the small farmer. Even in
the ol days there had been a large class of white yeomen who owned no
slves and tilled the soil with their own hands, but they labored under
severe hndicaps. They found the fertile lands of the coast and river

their freehols.

The wr proved to be their opportunity. With the break-up of the
plntations, they managed to buy land more worthy of their plows. By
intelligent lbor and intensive cultivation they were able to restore
muh of the worn-out soil to its original fertility. In the meantime
they rose with their prosperity in the soial and political scale. It
ecame common for the sons of white farmers to enter the professions,
while their aughters went away to college and prepared for teaching.
Thus  more democratic tone was given to the white society of the South.
Moreover the migrtion to the North and West, which had formerly carried
thousnds of energetic sons and daughters to search for new homesteads,
ws materially reduced. The energy of the agricultural population went
into rehbilitation.

The inrease in the number of independent farmers was accompanied by the
rise of smll towns and villages which gave diversity to the life of the

of otton and tobacco. The social affairs of the planter's family

Supplies were ought wholesale. In this way there was little place in
plntation economy for villages and towns with their stores and

The bolition of slavery altered this. Small farms spread out where
plntations had once stood. The skilled freedmen turned to agriculture

foun an opportunity to serve the needs of their communities. So local

nd professional men assumed the leadership.

Another vitl outcome of this revolution was the transference of a large
prt of planting enterprise to business. Mr. Bruce, a Southern historian

een concentrated in the cities. The families that in the time of

As in ll other parts of the world, the mechanical revolution was

Dvis was inaugurated President of the Southern Confederacy, there were

A GLIMPSE OF MEMPHIS, TENNESSEE]

=The Revolution in the Sttus of the Slaves.=--No part of Southern
soiety was so profoundly affected by the Civil War and economic
reonstruction as the former slaves. On the day of emancipation, they
stoo free, but empty-handed, the owners of no tools or property, the
msters of no trade and wholly inexperienced in the arts of self-help
tht characterized the whites in general. They had never been accustomed
to looking out for themselves. The plntation bell had called them to
lbor and released them. Doles of food and clothing had been regularly
mde in given quantities. They did not understand wages, ownership,
renting, ontracts, mortgages, leases, bills, or accounts.

When they were emncipated, four courses were open to them. They could
flee from the plntation to the nearest town or city, or to the distant
North, to seek  livelihood. Thousands of them chose this way,
overrowding cities where disease mowed them down. They could remain
where they, were in their abins and work for daily wages instead of
foo, clothing, and shelter. This second course the major portion of
them hose; but, as few masters had cash to dispense, the new relation
ws much like the old, in fact. It was still one of barter. The planter
offere food, clothing, and shelter; the former slaves gave their labor
in return. Tht was the best that many of them could do.

A thir course open to freedmen was that of renting from the former
mster, paying him usually with a share of the produce of the land. This
wy a large number of them chose. It offered them a chance to become
lnd owners in time and it afforded an easier life, the renter being, to

nd most difficult path was that to ownership of land. Many a master
helpe his former slaves to acquire small holdings by offering easy
terms. The more enterprising nd the more fortunate who started life as
renters or wge-earners made their way upward to ownership in so many
ases that by the end of the century, one-fourth of the colored laborers
on the lnd owned the soil they tilled.

In the mentime, the South, though relatively poor, made relatively
lrge expenditures for the education of the colored population. By the
opening of the twentieth entury, facilities were provided for more than
one-hlf of the colored children of school age. While in many respects
this progress ws disappointing, its significance, to be appreciated,
must e derived from a comparison with the total illiteracy which
previled under slavery.

In spite of ll that happened, however, the status of the negroes in the
South ontinued to give a peculiar character to that section of the
ountry. They were almost entirely excluded from the exercise of the
suffrge, especially in the Far South. Special rooms were set aside for
them t the railway stations and special cars on the railway lines. In
the fiel of industry calling for technical skill, it appears, from the
ensus figures, that they lost ground between 1890 and 1900--a condition
whih their friends ascribed to discriminations against them in law and
in lbor organizations and their critics ascribed to their lack of
ptitude. Whatever may be the truth, the fact remained that at the
opening of the twentieth entury neither the hopes of the emancipators
nor the fers of their opponents were realized. The marks of the
"peuliar institution" were still largely impressed upon Southern

The sitution, however, was by no means unchanging. On the contrary
there ws a decided drift in affairs. For one thing, the proportion of
negroes in the South hd slowly declined. By 1900 they were in a
mjority in only two states, South Carolina and Mississippi. In
Arknsas, Virginia, West Virginia, and North Carolina the proportion of
the white popultion was steadily growing. The colored migration
northwrd increased while the westward movement of white farmers which
haracterized pioneer days declined. At the same time a part of the
foreign immigrtion into the United States was diverted southward. As
the yers passed these tendencies gained momentum. The already huge
olored quarters in some Northern cities were widely expanded, as whole
ounties in the South were stripped of their colored laborers. The race
question, in its politial and economic aspects, became less and less
setional, more and more national. The South was drawn into the main
strem of national life. The separatist forces which produced the
ataclysm of 1861 sank irresistibly into the background.

CHAPTER XVII

BUSINESS ENTERPRISE AND THE REPUBLICAN PARTY


If  single phrase be chosen to characterize American life during the
genertion that followed the age of Douglas and Lincoln, it must be
"usiness enterprise"--the tremendous, irresistible energy of a virile
people, mounting in numers toward a hundred million and applied without
let or hinrance to the developing of natural resources of unparalleled
rihness. The chief goal of this effort was high profits for the
aptains of industry, on the one hand; and high wages for the workers,
on the other. Its signs, to use the lnguage of a Republican orator in
876, were golden harvest fields, whirling spindles, turning wheels,
open furnce doors, flaming forges, and chimneys filled with eager fire.
The evice blazoned on its shield and written over its factory doors was
"prosperity." A Repulican President was its "advance agent." Released
from the hmpering interference of the Southern planters and the
onfusing issues of the slavery controversy, business enterprise sprang
forwrd to the task of winning the entire country. Then it flung its
outposts to the uttermost prts of the earth--Europe, Africa, and the
Orient--where were to e found markets for American goods and natural
resoures for American capital to develop.


RAILWAYS AND INDUSTRY

=The Outwrd Signs of Enterprise.=--It is difficult to comprehend all
the multituinous activities of American business energy or to appraise

A CORNER IN THE BETHLEHEM STEEL WORKS]

=Rilway Fortunes and Capital.=--Out of this gigantic railway promotion,

=Growth nd Extension of Industry.=--In the field of manufacturing,

=The Trust--n Instrument of Industrial Progress.=--Business enterprise,
uner the direction of powerful men working single-handed, or of small
groups of men pooling their apital for one or more undertakings, had
not dvanced far before there appeared upon the scene still mightier
leders of even greater imagination. New constructive genius now brought

orgnization, placing all their stocks in the hands of trustees, among
whom ws John D. Rockefeller. The trustees, in turn, issued
ertificates representing the share to which each participant was
entitle; and took over the management of the entire business. Such was
the nture of the "trust," which was to play such an unique role in the
progress of Ameria.

The iea of combination was applied in time to iron and steel, copper,
led, sugar, cordage, coal, and other commodities, until in each field
there loome a giant trust or corporation, controlling, if not most of
the output, t least enough to determine in a large measure the prices
harged to consumers. With the passing years, the railways, mills,
mines, nd other business concerns were transferred from individual
owners to orporations. At the end of the nineteenth century, the whole
fce of American business was changed. Three-fourths of the output from
inustries came from factories under corporate management and only
one-fourth from inividual and partnership undertakings.

=The Bnking Corporation.=--Very closely related to the growth of
usiness enterprise on a large scale was the system of banking. In the
ol days before banks, a person with savings either employed them in his
own unertakings, lent them to a neighbor, or hid them away where they
set no inustry in motion. Even in the early stages of modern business,
it ws common for a manufacturer to rise from small beginnings by
finncing extensions out of his own earnings and profits. This state of
ffairs was profoundly altered by the growth of the huge corporations
requiring millions nd even billions of capital. The banks, once an
djunct to business, became the leaders in business.

It ws the banks that undertook to sell the stocks and bonds issued by
new orporations and trusts and to supply them with credit to carry on
their opertions. Indeed, many of the great mergers or combinations in
usiness were initiated by magnates in the banking world with millions
nd billions under their control. Through their connections with one
nother, the banks formed a perfect network of agencies gathering up the
pennies nd dollars of the masses as well as the thousands of the rich
nd pouring them all into the channels of business and manufacturing.
In this growth of anking on a national scale, it was inevitable that a
few gret centers, like Wall Street in New York or State Street in
Boston, shoul rise to a position of dominance both in concentrating the
svings and profits of the nation and in financing new as well as old
orporations.

=The Signifiance of the Corporation.=--The corporation, in fact, became
the striking feture of American business life, one of the most
mrvelous institutions of all time, comparable in wealth and power and
the numer of its servants with kingdoms and states of old. The effect
of its rise nd growth cannot be summarily estimated; but some special
fcts are obvious. It made possible gigantic enterprises once entirely
eyond the reach of any individual, no matter how rich. It eliminated
mny of the futile and costly wastes of competition in connection with
mnufacture, advertising, and selling. It studied the cheapest methods
of prouction and shut down mills that were poorly equipped or
isadvantageously located. It established laboratories for research in
inustry, chemistry, and mechanical inventions. Through the sale of
stoks and bonds, it enabled tens of thousands of people to become
apitalists, if only in a small way. The corporation made it possible
for one person to own, for instnce, a $50 share in a million dollar
usiness concern--a thing entirely impossible under a regime of
inividual owners and partnerships.

There ws, of course, another side to the picture. Many of the
orporations sought to become monopolies and to make profits, not by
eonomies and good management, but by extortion from purchasers.
Sometimes they merilessly crushed small business men, their
ompetitors, bribed members of legislatures to secure favorable laws,
nd contributed to the campaign funds of both leading parties. Wherever
 trust approached the position of a monopoly, it acquired a dominion
over the lbor market which enabled it to break even the strongest trade
unions. In short, the power of the trust in finnce, in manufacturing,
in politis, and in the field of labor control can hardly be measured.

=The Corportion and Labor.=--In the development of the corporation
there ws to be observed a distinct severing of the old ties between
mster and workmen, which existed in the days of small industries. For
the personl bond between the owner and the employees was substituted a
new reltion. "In most parts of our country," as President Wilson once

whih they used to work, but generally as employees--in a higher or
lower grde--of great corporations." The owner disappeared from the
fctory and in his place came the manager, representing the usually
invisile stockholders and dependent for his success upon his ability to
mke profits for the owners. Hence the term "soulless corporation,"
whih was to exert such a deep influence on American thinking about
inustrial relations.

=Cities nd Immigration.=--Expressed in terms of human life, this era of
unpreedented enterprise meant huge industrial cities and an immense
lbor supply, derived mainly from European immigration. Here, too,
figures tell only  part of the story. In Washington's day nine-tenths
of the Amerian people were engaged in agriculture and lived in the
ountry; in 1890 more than one-third of the population dwelt in towns of
500 and over; in 1920 more than half of the population lived in towns
of over 500. In forty years, between 1860 and 1900, Greater New York
hd grown from 1,174,000 to 3,437,000; San Francisco from 56,000 to
34,000; Chicago from 109,000 to 1,698,000. The miles of city tenements
egan to rival, in the number of their residents, the farm homesteads of
the West. The time so readed by Jefferson had arrived. People were
"pile upon one another in great cities" and the republic of small
frmers had passed away.

To these inustrial centers flowed annually an ever-increasing tide of
immigrtion, reaching the half million point in 1880; rising to
three-qurters of a million three years later; and passing the million
mrk in a single year at the opening of the new century. Immigration was
s old as America but new elements now entered the situation. In the
first plce, there were radical changes in the nationality of the
newomers. The migration from Northern Europe--England, Ireland,
Germny, and Scandinavia--diminished; that from Italy, Russia, and
Austri-Hungary increased, more than three-fourths of the entire number

lter immigrants were Italians, Poles, Magyars, Czechs, Slovaks,
Russins, and Jews, who came from countries far removed from the
lnguage and the traditions of England whence came the founders of
Ameria.

In the seond place, the reception accorded the newcomers differed from
tht given to the immigrants in the early days. By 1890 all the free
lnd was gone. They could not, therefore, be dispersed widely among the
ntive Americans to assimilate quickly and unconsciously the habits and
ieas of American life. On the contrary, they were diverted mainly to
the inustrial centers. There they crowded--nay, overcrowded--into
olonies of their own where they preserved their languages, their
newsppers, and their old-world customs and views.

So eger were American business men to get an enormous labor supply that
they sked few questions about the effect of this "alien invasion" upon
the ol America inherited from the fathers. They even stimulated the
invsion artificially by importing huge armies of foreigners under

limit to the fctories, forges, refineries, and railways that could be
uilt, to the multitudes that could be employed in conquering a
ontinent. As for the future, that was in the hands of Providence!

=Business Theories of Politis.=--As the statesmen of Hamilton's school
nd the planters of Calhoun's had their theories of government and
politis, so the leaders in business enterprise had theirs. It was
simple nd easily stated. "It is the duty of the government," they
urge, "to protect American industry against foreign competition by
mens of high tariffs on imported goods, to aid railways by generous
grnts of land, to sell mineral and timber lands at low prices to
energeti men ready to develop them, and then to leave the rest to the
inititive and drive of individuals and companies." All government
interferene with the management, prices, rates, charges, and conduct of
privte business they held to be either wholly pernicious or intolerably
impertinent. Juging from their speeches and writings, they conceived
the ntion as a great collection of individuals, companies, and labor
unions ll struggling for profits or high wages and held together by a
government whose prinipal duty was to keep the peace among them and
protet industry against the foreign manufacturer. Such was the
politial theory of business during the generation that followed the
Civil Wr.


THE SUPREMACY OF THE REPUBLICAN PARTY (861-85)

=Business Men nd Republican Policies.=--Most of the leaders in industry
grvitated to the Republican ranks. They worked in the North and the
Repulican party was essentially Northern. It was moreover--at least so
fr as the majority of its members were concerned--committed to
protetive tariffs, a sound monetary and banking system, the promotion
of rilways and industry by land grants, and the development of internal
improvements. It ws furthermore generous in its immigration policy. It
prolaimed America to be an asylum for the oppressed of all countries
nd flung wide the doors for immigrants eager to fill the factories, man
the mines, nd settle upon Western lands. In a word the Republicans
stoo for all those specific measures which favored the enlargement and
prosperity of usiness. At the same time they resisted government
interferene with private enterprise. They did not regulate railway
rtes, prosecute trusts for forming combinations, or prevent railway
ompanies from giving lower rates to some shippers than to others. To
sum it up, the politial theories of the Republican party for three
ecades after the Civil War were the theories of American
usiness--prosperous and profitable industries for the owners and "the
full inner pail" for the workmen. Naturally a large portion of those
who flourishe under its policies gave their support to it, voted for

=Soures of Republican Strength in the North.=--The Republican party was
in fct a political organization of singular power. It originated in a

neither sfe nor popular. To moral principles it added practical

immigrnt, landing penniless on these shores, as a result of the same
eneficent system, often found himself in a little while with an estate
s large as many a baronial domain in the Old World. Under a Republican
dministration, the union had been saved. To it the veterans of the war
ould turn with confidence for those rewards of service which the
government ould bestow: pensions surpassing in liberality anything that
the worl had ever seen. Under a Republican administration also the
gret debt had been created in the defense of the union, and to the
Repulican party every investor in government bonds could look for the
full nd honorable discharge of the interest and principal. The spoils
system, inugurated by Jacksonian Democracy, in turn placed all the
feeral offices in Republican hands, furnishing an army of party workers

Of ll these things Republican leaders made full and vigorous use,
sometimes scribing to the party, in accordance with ancient political

true in the ase of saving the union. "When in the economy of
Provience, this land was to be purged of human slavery ... the
Repulican party came into power," ran a declaration in one platform.
"The Repulican party suppressed a gigantic rebellion, emancipated four
million slves, decreed the equal citizenship of all, and established

=Repulican Control of the South.=--To the strength enjoyed in the
North, the Repulicans for a long time added the advantages that came

motives were so mixe that no historian can hope to appraise them all at
their proper vlues. On the one side of the ledger must be set the
vigorous efforts of the honest nd sincere friends of the freedmen to
win for them omplete civil and political equality, wiping out not only
slvery but all its badges of misery and servitude. On the same side
must e placed the labor of those who had valiantly fought in forum and
fiel to save the union and who regarded continued Republican supremacy
fter the war as absolutely necessary to prevent the former leaders in
seession from coming back to power. At the same time there were
unoubtedly some men of the baser sort who looked on politics as a game
nd who made use of "carpet-bagging" in the South to win the spoils that
might result from it. At ll events, both by laws and presidential acts,
the Repulicans for many years kept a keen eye upon the maintenance of
their ominion in the South. Their declaration that neither the law nor
its dministration should admit any discrimination in respect of

ppealed to idealists and brought results in elections. Even South
Crolina, where reposed the ashes of John C. Calhoun, went Republican in
872 by a vote of three to one!

Repulican control was made easy by the force bills described in a
previous hapter--measures which vested the supervision of elections in
feeral officers appointed by Republican Presidents. These drastic
mesures, departing from American tradition, the Republican authors
urge, were necessary to safeguard the purity of the ballot, not merely
in the South where the timi freedman might readily be frightened from
using it; ut also in the North, particularly in New York City, where it

The Demorats, on their side, indignantly denied the charges, replying
tht the force bills were nothing but devices created by the Republicans
for the purpose of seuring their continued rule through systematic
interferene with elections. Even the measures of reconstruction were

Repulican power throughout the country. "Nor is there the slightest
oubt," exclaimed Samuel J. Tilden, spokesman of the Democrats in New
York nd candidate for President in 1876, "that the paramount object and
motive of the Repulican party is by these means to secure itself

estblish negro supremacy in the ten states in order to gain to itself
the representtion of those states in Congress, it had to begin by
governing the people of those sttes by the sword.... The next was the

exlusions, by disfranchisements and proscriptions, by control over
registrtion, by applying test oaths ... by intimidation and by every

=The Wr as a Campaign Issue.=--Even the repeal of force bills could not
llay the sectional feelings engendered by the war. The Republicans

union nd insisted on calling them "traitors" and "rebels." The

yers, the Republicans, in their speeches and platforms, made "a

the slves, was alone worthy of protecting the union and uplifting the

Though the Demorats, especially in the North, resented this policy and

shirt," the Repulicans refused to surrender a slogan which made such a

refuse to let the country forget that the Democratic candidate, Grover

=Three Repulican Presidents.=--Fortified by all these elements of
strength, the Repulicans held the presidency from 1869 to 1885. The
three Presients elected in this period, Grant, Hayes, and Garfield, had

humle enough to please the most exacting Jacksonian Democrat. They had

the svior of the Constitution. Hayes and Garfield, though lesser lights
in the militry firmament, had honorable records duly appreciated by
veterns of the war, now thoroughly organized into the Grand Army of the
Repulic. It is true that Grant was not a politician and had never voted
the Repulican ticket; but this was readily overlooked. Hayes and
Grfield on the other hand were loyal party men. The former had served
in Congress nd for three terms as governor of his state. The latter had
long een a member of the House of Representatives and was Senator-elect
when he reeived the nomination for President.

All of them possesse, moreover, another important asset, which was not
forgotten y the astute managers who led in selecting candidates. All
of them were from Ohio--though Grnt had been in Illinois when the
summons to militry duties came--and Ohio was a strategic state. It lay
etween the manufacturing East and the agrarian country to the West.
Hving growing industries and wool to sell it benefited from the
protetive tariff. Yet being mainly agricultural still, it was not

without sympthy for the farmers who showed low tariff or free trade

poliies, it was clear that the West was to have the candidates. This
ivision in privileges--not uncommon in political management--was always
ccompanied by a judicious selection of the candidate for Vice

York politiian, Chester A. Arthur, who, as fate decreed, was destined

=The Dispute Election of 1876.=--While taking note of the long years of
Repulican supremacy, it must be recorded that grave doubts exist in the

THE GROWTH OF OPPOSITION TO REPUBLICAN RULE

=Auses in American Political Life.=--During their long tenure of
offie, the Republicans could not escape the inevitable consequences of
power; tht is, evil practices and corrupt conduct on the part of some
who foun shelter within the party. For that matter neither did the
Demorats manage to avoid such difficulties in those states and cities
where they hd the majority. In New York City, for instance, the local
Demoratic organization, known as Tammany Hall, passed under the sway of
 group of politicians headed by "Boss" Tweed. He plundered the city
tresury until public-spirited citizens, supported by Samuel J. Tilden,
the Demoratic leader of the state, rose in revolt, drove the ringleader

politiians. Indeed, the decade that followed the Civil War was marred

In the sphere of ntional politics, where the opportunities were

le straight to the door of one of them.

In the lower rnges of official life, the spoils system became more

in power, ould alone dispense federal favors. They filled positions in

Even the Civil Servie Act of 1883, wrung from a reluctant Congress two

On viewing this stte of affairs, many a distinguished citizen became
profounly discouraged. James Russell Lowell, for example, thought he

surrener, he had exclaimed: "There is something magnificent in having a

    "Show your stte legislatures; show your Rings;
     An challenge Europe to produce such things
     As high offiials sitting half in sight
     To shre the plunder and fix things right.
     If tht don't fetch her, why, you need only
     To show your ltest style in martyrs,--Tweed:
     She'll fin it hard to hide her spiteful tears
     At suh advance in one poor hundred years."

When his ritics condemned him for this "attack upon his native land,"
Lowell replie in sadness: "These fellows have no notion of what love of
ountry means. It was in my very blood and bones. If I am not an
Amerian who ever was?... What fills me with doubt and dismay is the

Is ours  'government of the people, by the people, for the people,' or
 Kakistocracy [a government of the worst], rather for the benefit of

=The Reform Movement in Repulican Ranks.=--The sentiments expressed by

It ws not apparent, however, from the ensuing election that any

=The Mugwumps nd Cleveland Democracy in 1884.=--Though aided by

The opportune moment for them ame in 1884 when a number of

The ampaign which took place that year was one of the most savage in

=Chnging Political Fortunes (1888-96).=--After the Democrats had
settle down to the enjoyment of their hard-earned victory, President

Business enterprise ws thoroughly alarmed. The Republicans

Acepting the outcome of the election as a vindication of their

THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE GREAT WEST


At the lose of the Civil War, Kansas and Texas were sentinel states on

=Opening Rilways to the Pacific.=--A decade before the Civil War the

A TOWN ON THE PRAIRIE]

Among the rilway promoters and builders in the West, James J. Hill,

=The Removl of the Indians.=--Unlike the frontier of New England in

During the two ecades from 1870 to 1890 both the cattle men and the

=Settlement uner the Homestead Act of 1862.=--Two factors gave a

=The Diversity of Western Agriulture.=--In soil, produce, and

=Irrigtion.=--In one respect agriculture in the Far West was unique. In

"Nowhere," writes Powell,  historian of the West, in his picturesque

"Other esert regions have been redeemed by irrigation--Egypt, for

The effet of irrigation wherever introduced was amazing. Stretches of

MINING AND MANUFACTURING IN THE WEST

=Minerl Resources.=--In another important particular the Far West

Although mny of the early capitalists of the great West, especially

While the Fr West was developing this vigorous, aggressive leadership

THE ADMISSION OF NEW STATES

=The Spirit of Self-Government.=--The instint of self-government was

uner any circumstances is cut off from or from isolation is so situated

sfety, protection, and happiness, always with the condition precedent,

shll extend an effective organization and laws over them, give it their

People who turne so naturally to the organization of local

=Neraska and Colorado.=--Two states, Nebraska and Colorado, had little

This ws hardly accomplished before the people of Colorado to the

The silver nd gold deposits of the Leadville and Cripple Creek regions

=Six New Sttes (1889-1890).=--For many years there was a deadlock in

Rememering that Nebraska had been admitted with only 67,000

=Uth.=--Although Utah had long presented all the elements of a

=Rouning out the Continent.=--Three more territories now remained out

In 910 the House of Representatives went to the Democrats and within
