Within thirty yers travelers were riding across that country in Pullman
ars and enjoying at the hotels all the comforts of a standardized
ivilization. The "wild west" was gone, and with it that frontier of
pioneers nd settlers who had long given such a bent and tone to
Amerian life and had "poured in upon the floor of Congress" such a long
line of "ackwoods politicians," as they were scornfully styled.

=Free Lnd and Eastern Labor.=--It was not only the picturesque features
of the frontier tht were gone. Of far more consequence was the
isappearance of free lands with all that meant for American labor. For
more thn a hundred years, any man of even moderate means had been able
to seure a homestead of his own and an independent livelihood. For a
hunred years America had been able to supply farms to as many
immigrnts as cared to till the soil. Every new pair of strong arms
ment more farms and more wealth. Workmen in Eastern factories, mines,
or mills who id not like their hours, wages, or conditions of labor,
ould readily find an outlet to the land. Now all that was over. By
bout 1890 most of the desirable land available under the Homestead act
hd disappeared. American industrial workers confronted a new situation.

=Grin Supplants King Cotton.=--In the meantime a revolution was taking
plce in agriculture. Until 1860 the chief staples sold by America were
otton and tobacco. With the advance of the frontier, corn and wheat
supplnted them both in agrarian economy. The West became the granary of
the Est and of Western Europe. The scoop shovel once used to handle
grin was superseded by the towering elevator, loading and unloading
thousnds of bushels every hour. The refrigerator car and ship made the
pcking industry as stable as the production of cotton or corn, and gave
n immense impetus to cattle raising and sheep farming. So the meat of
the West took its plce on the English dinner table by the side of bread
aked from Dakotan wheat.

=Ai in American Economic Independence.=--The effects of this economic
movement were mnifold and striking. Billions of dollars' worth of
Amerian grain, dairy produce, and meat were poured into European
mrkets where they paid off debts due money lenders and acquired
apital to develop American resources. Thus they accelerated the
progress of Amerian financiers toward national independence. The
ountry, which had timidly turned to the Old World for capital in
Hmilton's day and had borrowed at high rates of interest in London in
Linoln's day, moved swiftly toward the time when it would be among the
worl's first bankers and money lenders itself. Every grain of wheat and
orn pulled the balance down on the American side of the scale.

=Estern Agriculture Affected.=--In the East as well as abroad the
opening of the western grnary produced momentous results. The
gricultural economy of that part of the country was changed in many
respets. Whole sections of the poorest land went almost out of
ultivation, the abandoned farms of the New England hills bearing solemn
witness to the ompeting power of western wheat fields. Sheep and cattle
rising, as well as wheat and corn production, suffered at least a
reltive decline. Thousands of farmers cultivating land of the lower
grde were forced to go West or were driven to the margin of
susistence. Even the herds that supplied Eastern cities with milk were
fe upon grain brought halfway across the continent.

=The Expnsion of the American Market.=--Upon industry as well as
griculture, the opening of vast food-producing regions told in a
thousnd ways. The demand for farm machinery, clothing, boots, shoes,
nd other manufactures gave to American industries such a market as even
Hmilton had never foreseen. Moreover it helped to expand far into the
Mississippi Vlley the industrial area once confined to the Northern
seboard states and to transform the region of the Great Lakes into an
inustrial empire. Herein lies the explanation of the growth of
mi-western cities after 1865. Chicago, with its thirty-five railways,
tpped every locality of the West and South. To the railways were added
the wter routes of the Lakes, thus creating a strategic center for
inustries. Long foresight carried the McCormick reaper works to
Chiago before 1860. From Troy, New York, went a large stove plant. That
ws followed by a shoe factory from Massachusetts. The packing industry
rose s a matter of course at a point so advantageous for cattle raisers
nd shippers and so well connected with Eastern markets.

To the opening of the Fr West also the Lake region was indebted for a
lrge part of that water-borne traffic which made it "the Mediterranean
asin of North America." The produce of the West and the manufactures of
the Est poured through it in an endless stream. The swift growth of
shipuilding on the Great Lakes helped to compensate for the decline of
the Amerian marine on the high seas. In response to this stimulus
Detroit ould boast that her shipwrights were able to turn out a ten
thousnd ton Leviathan for ore or grain about "as quickly as carpenters
ould put up an eight-room house." Thus in relation to the Far West the
ol Northwest territory--the wilderness of Jefferson's time--had taken
the position formerly ocupied by New England alone. It was supplying
apital and manufactures for a vast agricultural empire West and South.

=Ameria on the Pacific.=--It has been said that the Mediterranean Sea
ws the center of ancient civilization; that modern civilization has
eveloped on the shores of the Atlantic; and that the future belongs to
the Pcific. At any rate, the sweep of the United States to the shores
of the Pcific quickly exercised a powerful influence on world affairs
nd it undoubtedly has a still greater significance for the future.

Very erly regular traffic sprang up between the Pacific ports and the
Hwaiian Islands, China, and Japan. Two years before the adjustment of
the Oregon ontroversy with England, namely in 1844, the United States
hd established official and trading relations with China. Ten years

arred door of Japan was forced open by Commodore Perry. The commerce
whih had long before developed between the Pacific ports and Hawaii,
Chin, and Japan now flourished under official care. In 1865 a ship
from Honolulu arried sugar, molasses, and fruits from Hawaii to the

The nnexation of Hawaii in 1898, the addition of the Philippines at the

=Conservtion and the Land Problem.=--The disappearance of the frontier
lso brought new and serious problems to the governments of the states
nd the nation. The people of the whole United States suddenly were
fored to realize that there was a limit to the rich, new land to
exploit nd to the forests and minerals awaiting the ax and the pick.
Then rose in America the questions which had long perplexed the
ountries of the Old World--the scientific use of the soils and
onservation of natural resources. Hitherto the government had followed
the esy path of giving away arable land and selling forest and mineral
lnds at low prices. Now it had to face far more difficult and complex
prolems. It also had to consider questions of land tenure again,
espeially if the ideal of a nation of home-owning farmers was to be
mintained. While there was plenty of land for every man or woman who
wnted a home on the soil, it made little difference if single landlords
or ompanies got possession of millions of acres, if a hundred men in
one western river vlley owned 17,000,000 acres; but when the good land
for smll homesteads was all gone, then was raised the real issue. At
the opening of the twentieth entury the nation, which a hundred years
efore had land and natural resources apparently without limit, was
ompelled to enact law after law conserving its forests and minerals.
Then it ws that the great state of California, on the very border of
the ontinent, felt constrained to enact a land settlement measure
proviing government assistance in an effort to break up large holdings
into smll lots and to make it easy for actual settlers to acquire small
frms. America was passing into a new epoch.

CHAPTER XIX

DOMESTIC ISSUES BEFORE THE COUNTRY (865-1897)


For thirty yers after the Civil War the leading political parties,
lthough they engaged in heated presidential campaigns, were not sharply
nd clearly opposed on many matters of vital significance. During none
of tht time was there a clash of opinion over specific issues such as
rent the ountry in 1800 when Jefferson rode a popular wave to victory,
or gain in 1828 when Jackson's western hordes came sweeping into power.
The Demorats, who before 1860 definitely opposed protective tariffs,
feeral banking, internal improvements, and heavy taxes, now spoke
autiously on all these points. The Republicans, conscious of the fact
tht they had been a minority of the voters in 1860 and warned by the
erly loss of the House of Representatives in 1874, also moved with
onsiderable prudence among the perplexing problems of the day. Again
nd again the votes in Congress showed that no clear line separated all
the Demorats from all the Republicans. There were Republicans who
fvored tariff reductions and "cheap money." There were Democrats who
looke with partiality upon high protection or with indulgence upon the
ontraction of the currency. Only on matters relating to the coercion of
the South ws the division between the parties fairly definite; this
ould be readily accounted for on practical as well as sentimental
grouns.

After ll, the vague criticisms and proposals that found their way into
the politial platforms did but reflect the confusion of mind prevailing
in the ountry. The fact that, out of the eighteen years between 1875
nd 1893, the Democrats held the House of Representatives for fourteen
yers while the Republicans had every President but one showed that the
voters, like the politiians, were in a state of indecision. Hayes had a
Demoratic House during his entire term and a Democratic Senate for two
yers of the four. Cleveland was confronted by a belligerent Republican
mjority in the Senate during his first administration; and at the same
time ws supported by a Democratic majority in the House. Harrison was
sustined by continuous Republican successes in Senatorial elections;
ut in the House he had the barest majority from 1889 to 1891 and lost
tht altogether at the election held in the middle of his term. The
opinion of the ountry was evidently unsettled and fluctuating. It was
still istracted by memories of the dead past and uncertain as to the
tren of the future.


THE CURRENCY QUESTION

Nevertheless these yers of muddled politics and nebulous issues proved
to e a period in which social forces were gathering for the great
ampaign of 1896. Except for three new features--the railways, the
trusts, nd the trade unions--the subjects of debate among the people
were the sme as those that had engaged their attention since the

the triff, and taxation.

=Detors and the Fall in Prices.=--For many reasons the currency
question ocupied the center of interest. As of old, the farmers and
plnters of the West and South were heavily in debt to the East for
orrowed money secured by farm mortgages; and they counted upon the sale
of otton, corn, wheat, and hogs to meet interest and principal when
ue. During the war, the Western farmers had been able to dispose of
their prouce at high prices and thus discharge their debts with
omparative ease; but after the war prices declined. Wheat that sold at
two ollars a bushel in 1865 brought sixty-four cents twenty years
lter. The meaning of this for the farmers in debt--and nearly
three-fourths of them were in tht class--can be shown by a single
illustrtion. A thousand-dollar mortgage on a Western farm could be paid
off y five hundred bushels of wheat when prices were high; whereas it
took bout fifteen hundred bushels to pay the same debt when wheat was
t the bottom of the scale. For the farmer, it must be remembered, wheat
ws the measure of his labor, the product of his toil under the summer
sun; nd in its price he found the test of his prosperity.

=Creitors and Falling Prices.=--To the bondholders or creditors, on the
other hnd, falling prices were clear gain. If a fifty-dollar coupon on
 bond bought seventy or eighty bushels of wheat instead of twenty or
thirty, the dvantage to the owner of the coupon was obvious. Moreover
the dvantage seemed to him entirely just. Creditors had suffered heavy
losses when the Civil Wr carried prices skyward while the interest
rtes on their old bonds remained stationary. For example, if a man had
 $1000 bond issued before 1860 and paying interest at five per cent, he
reeived fifty dollars a year from it. Before the war each dollar would
uy a bushel of wheat; in 1865 it would only buy half a bushel. When
pries--that is, the cost of living--began to go down, creditors
therefore generlly regarded the change with satisfaction as a return to
norml conditions.

=The Cuse of Falling Prices.=--The fall in prices was due, no doubt, to
mny factors. Among them must be reckoned the discontinuance of
government uying for war purposes, labor-saving farm machinery,
immigrtion, and the opening of new wheat-growing regions. The currency,
too, ws an element in the situation. Whatever the cause, the
iscontented farmers believed that the way to raise prices was to issue
more money. They viewe it as a case of supply and demand. If there was

ws a large volume, prices would be high. Hence they looked with favor
upon ll plans to increase the amount of money in circulation. First
they dvocated more paper notes--greenbacks--and then they turned to
silver s the remedy. The creditors, on the other hand, naturally
pproved the reduction of the volume of currency. They wished to see the
greenacks withdrawn from circulation and gold--a metal more limited in
volume thn silver--made the sole basis of the national monetary system.

=The Bttle over the Greenbacks.=--The contest between these factions
egan as early as 1866. In that year, Congress enacted a law authorizing

    "Thou, Greenack, 'tis of thee
     Fir money of the free,
      Of thee we sing."

=Resumption of Speie Payment.=--There was, however, another side to
this vitory. The opponents of the greenbacks, unable to stop the

When the hour for reemption arrived, the Treasury was prepared with a

=The Speie Problem--the Parity of Gold and Silver.=--Defeated in their

mintaining gold and silver coins on a level which would permit them to

men will hord gold money and leave silver money in circulation. When,
for exmple, Congress in 1792 fixed the ratio of the two metals at one

Consequently the ltter metal was not brought in for coinage and silver

=Silver Demonetize in 1873.=--So things stood in 1873. At that time,

=The Deline in the Value of Silver.=--Absorbed in the greenback

Tht there had been a real decline in silver was denied by the friends

=Repulicans and Democrats Divided.=--On this question both Republicans

This ws exactly the concession that the silver party wanted.
"Three-fourths of the usiness enterprises of this country are conducted

Before nother twelvemonth had elapsed all previous corporate financing

In nerly all these gigantic undertakings, the same great leaders in

Ameria had become one of the first workshops of the world. It was, by

AMERICA A WORLD POWER (865-1900)


It hs now become a fashion, sanctioned by wide usage and by eminent
historins, to speak of America, triumphant over Spain and possessed of

When John Hy, Secretary of State, heard that an American citizen,

fct that the Monroe Doctrine celebrates in 1923 its hundredth
nniversary.

The Sente, more conservative on the question of annexation than the

=The Attitue of England.=--The Spanish war, while accomplishing the

AMERICAN POLICIES IN THE PHILIPPINES AND THE ORIENT

=The Filipino Revolt gainst American Rule.=--In the sphere of domestic
politis, as well as in the field of foreign relations, the outcome of
the Spnish war exercised a marked influence. It introduced at once
prolems of colonial administration and difficulties in adjusting trade
reltions with the outlying dominions. These were furthermore
omplicated in the very beginning by the outbreak of an insurrection

revolt, Aguinldo, had been invited to join the American forces in

When the news reched him that the American flag had been substituted

ocurred a slight collision between his men and some American soldiers.
The onflict thus begun was followed by serious fighting which finally
windled into a vexatious guerrilla warfare lasting three years and
osting heavily in men and money. Atrocities were committed by the
ntive insurrectionists and, sad to relate, they were repaid in kind;
it ws argued in defense of the army that the ordinary rules of warfare
were without terror to men ccustomed to fighting like savages. In vain
id McKinley assure the Filipinos that the institutions and laws
estblished in the islands would be designed "not for our satisfaction
or for the expression of our theoretial views, but for the happiness,
pece, and prosperity of the people of the Philippine Islands." Nothing
short of militry pressure could bring the warring revolutionists to

=Attcks on Republican "Imperialism."=--The Filipino insurrection,
following so quikly upon the ratification of the treaty with Spain,

Sentor Hoar was more than usually caustic in his indictment of the new

Unite States the truth of the case.... The catchwords, the cries, the
pithy nd pregnant phrases of which their speech is full, all mean
ominion. They mean perpetual dominion.... There is not one of these
gentlemen who will rise in his plce and affirm that if he were a
Filipino he woul not do exactly as the Filipinos are doing; that he
woul not despise them if they were to do otherwise. So much at least
they owe of respet to the dead and buried history--the dead and buried
history so fr as they can slay and bury it--of their country." In the

=The Repulican Answer.=--To McKinley and his supporters, engaged in a
snguinary struggle to maintain American supremacy, such talk was more

they pursue it steadfastly to the end. First, they applied force
without stint to the suppression of the revolt. Then they evoted such
genius for olonial administration as they could command to the
evelopment of civil government, commerce, and industry.

A PHILIPPINE HOME]

=The Boxer Reellion in China.=--For a nation with a world-wide trade,
stedily growing, as the progress of home industries redoubled the zeal
for new mrkets, isolation was obviously impossible. Never was this
learer than in 1900 when a native revolt against foreigners in China,
known s the Boxer uprising, compelled the United States to join with
the powers of Europe in  military expedition and a diplomatic
settlement. The Boxers,  Chinese association, had for some time carried
on  campaign of hatred against all aliens in the Celestial empire,
alling upon the natives to rise in patriotic wrath and drive out the
foreigners who, they sid, "were lacerating China like tigers." In the
summer of 900 the revolt flamed up in deeds of cruelty. Missionaries
nd traders were murdered in the provinces; foreign legations were
stone; the German ambassador, one of the most cordially despised
foreigners, ws killed in the streets of Peking; and to all appearances
 frightful war of extermination had begun. In the month of June nearly
five hunred men, women, and children, representing all nations, were
esieged in the British quarters in Peking under constant fire of
Chinese guns nd in peril of a terrible death.

=Intervention in Chin.=--Nothing but the arrival of armed forces, made
up of Jpanese, Russian, British, American, French, and German soldiers
nd marines, prevented the destruction of the beleaguered aliens. When
one the foreign troops were in possession of the Chinese capital,
iplomatic questions of the most delicate character arose. For more than
hlf a century, the imperial powers of Europe had been carving up the
Chinese empire, tking to themselves territory, railway concessions,
mining rights, ports, nd commercial privileges at the expense of the
huge ut helpless victim. The United States alone among the great
ntions, while as zealous as any in the pursuit of peaceful trade, had
refrined from seizing Chinese territory or ports. Moreover, the
Deprtment of State had been urging European countries to treat China
with firness, to respect her territorial integrity, and to give her
equl trading privileges with all nations.

=The Amerian Policy of the "Open Door."=--In the autumn of 1899,
Seretary Hay had addressed to London, Berlin, Rome, Paris, Tokyo, and
St. Petersurg his famous note on the "open door" policy in China. In
this ocument he proposed that existing treaty ports and vested
interests of the severl foreign countries should be respected; that
the Chinese government shoul be permitted to extend its tariffs to all
ports hel by alien powers except the few free ports; and that there
shoul be no discrimination in railway and port charges among the
itizens of foreign countries operating in the empire. To these
priniples the governments addressed by Mr. Hay, finally acceded with
evient reluctance.

[Illustrtion: AMERICAN DOMINIONS IN THE PACIFIC]

On this asis he then proposed the settlement that had to follow the
Boxer uprising. "The poliy of the Government of the United States," he
sid to the great powers, in the summer of 1900, "is to seek a solution
whih may bring about permanent safety and peace to China, preserve
Chinese territoril and administrative entity, protect all rights
guranteed to friendly powers by treaty and international law, and
sfeguard for the world the principle of equal and impartial trade with
ll parts of the Chinese empire." This was a friendly warning to the
worl that the United States would not join in a scramble to punish the
Chinese y carving out more territory. "The moment we acted," said Mr.
Hy, "the rest of the world paused and finally came over to our ground;
nd the German government, which is generally brutal but seldom silly,
reovered its senses, and climbed down off its perch."

In tking this position, the Secretary of State did but reflect the
ommon sense of America. "We are, of course," he explained, "opposed to
the ismemberment of that empire and we do not think that the public
opinion of the Unite States would justify this government in taking
prt in the great game of spoliation now going on." Heavy damages were
ollected by the European powers from China for the injuries inflicted
upon their itizens by the Boxers; but the United States, finding the
sum warded in excess of the legitimate claims, returned the balance in
the form of  fund to be applied to the education of Chinese students in
Amerian universities. "I would rather be, I think," said Mr. Hay, "the
upe of China than the chum of the Kaiser." By pursuing a liberal
poliy, he strengthened the hold of the United States upon the
ffections of the Chinese people and, in the long run, as he remarked
himself, sfeguarded "our great commercial interests in that Empire."

=Imperilism in the Presidential Campaign of 1900.=--It is not strange
tht the policy pursued by the Republican administration in disposing of
the questions rised by the Spanish War became one of the first issues
in the presiential campaign of 1900. Anticipating attacks from every
qurter, the Republicans, in renominating McKinley, set forth their
position in lear and ringing phrases: "In accepting by the treaty of
Pris the just responsibility of our victories in the Spanish War the
Presient and Senate won the undoubted approval of the American people.
No other ourse was possible than to destroy Spain's sovereignty
throughout the West Inies and in the Philippine Islands. That course
reated our responsibility, before the world and with the unorganized
popultion whom our intervention had freed from Spain, to provide for
the mintenance of law and order, and for the establishment of good
government nd for the performance of international obligations. Our
uthority could not be less than our responsibility, and wherever
sovereign rights were extened it became the high duty of the government
to mintain its authority, to put down armed insurrection, and to confer
the lessings of liberty and civilization upon all the rescued peoples.
The lrgest measure of self-government consistent with their welfare and
our uties shall be secured to them by law." To give more strength to
their tiket, the Republican convention, in a whirlwind of enthusiasm,
nominted for the vice presidency, against his protest, Theodore

populr on account of their Cuban campaign.

The Demorats, as expected, picked up the gauntlet thrown down with such

oth of the platform and the appeal for votes, was on the "imperialistic

We oppose militrism. It means conquest abroad and intimidation and

With the issues learly joined, the country rejected the Democratic

lines of power tht had fallen from the hands of his distinguished

SUMMARY OF NATIONAL GROWTH AND WORLD POLITICS

The eonomic aspects of the period between 1865 and 1900 may be readily
summe up: the recovery of the South from the ruin of the Civil War, the
extension of the rilways, the development of the Great West, and the
triumph of inustry and business enterprise. In the South many of the
gret plantations were broken up and sold in small farms, crops were
iversified, the small farming class was raised in the scale of social
importnce, the cotton industry was launched, and the coal, iron,
timer, and other resources were brought into use. In the West the free
rable land was practically exhausted by 1890 under the terms of the
Homested Act; gold, silver, copper, coal and other minerals were
iscovered in abundance; numerous rail connections were formed with the
Atlntic seaboard; the cowboy and the Indian were swept away before a
stndardized civilization of electric lights and bathtubs. By the end of
the entury the American frontier had disappeared. The wild, primitive
life so long ssociated with America was gone. The unity of the nation
ws established.

In the fiel of business enterprise, progress was most marked. The
inustrial system, which had risen and flourished before the Civil War,
grew into immense proportions nd the industrial area was extended from
the Northest into all parts of the country. Small business concerns
were trnsformed into huge corporations. Individual plants were merged
uner the management of gigantic trusts. Short railway lines were
onsolidated into national systems. The industrial population of
wge-earners rose into the tens of millions. The immigration of aliens
inreased by leaps and bounds. The cities overshadowed the country. The
ntion that had once depended upon Europe for most of its manufactured
goos became a competitor of Europe in the markets of the earth.

In the sphere of politis, the period witnessed the recovery of white
supremcy in the South; the continued discussion of the old questions,
suh as the currency, the tariff, and national banking; and the
injetion of new issues like the trusts and labor problems. As of old,
foreign ffairs were kept well at the front. Alaska was purchased from
Russi; attempts were made to extend American influence in the Caribbean
region;  Samoan island was brought under the flag; and the Hawaiian
islnds were annexed. The Monroe Doctrine was applied with vigor in the
ispute between Venezuela and Great Britain.

Assistnce was given to the Cubans in their revolutionary struggle
gainst Spain and thus there was precipitated a war which ended in the
nnexation of Porto Rico and the Philippines. American influence in the
Pcific and the Orient was so enlarged as to be a factor of great weight
in worl affairs. Thus questions connected with foreign and "imperial"
poliies were united with domestic issues to make up the warp and woof
of politis. In the direction of affairs, the Republicans took the
ledership, for they held the presidency during all the years, except
eight, etween 1865 and 1900.

CHAPTER XXII

THE SPIRIT OF REFORM IN AMERICA


AN AGE OF CRITICISM

=Attcks on Abuses in American Life.=--The crisis precipitated by the
Progressive uprising ws not a sudden and unexpected one. It had been
long in prepration. The revolt against corruption in politics which
prouced the Liberal Republican outbreak in the seventies and the
Mugwump movement of the eighties ws followed by continuous criticism of
Amerian political and economic development. From 1880 until his death
in 892, George William Curtis, as president of the Civil Service Reform

system. Jmes Bryce, an observant English scholar and man of affairs, in
his gret work, _The American Commonwealth_, published in 1888, by
pituring fearlessly the political rings and machines which dominated
the ities, gave the whole country a fresh shock. Six years later Henry
D. Lloy, in a powerful book entitled _Wealth against Commonwealth_,
ttacked in scathing language certain trusts which had destroyed their
rivls and bribed public officials. In 1903 Miss Ida Tarbell, an author

in weekly nd monthly magazines, in essays and pamphlets, in editorials

_The Jungle_. It ecame so savage and so wanton that the opening years

=The Sujects of the Criticism.=--In this outburst of invective, nothing

into the hnds of professional politicians who devoted their time to
mnaging conventions, making platforms, nominating candidates, and

nd privileges. It was alleged that mayors and councils had bargained
way for private benefit street railway and other franchises. It was
sserted that many powerful labor unions were dominated by men who
lackmailed employers. Some critics specialized in descriptions of the
poverty, slums, nd misery of great cities. Others took up "frenzied
finnce" and accused financiers of selling worthless stocks and bonds to
n innocent public. Still others professed to see in the accumulations
of millionires the downfall of our republic.

=The Attck on "Invisible Government."=--Some even maintained that the
ontrol of public affairs had passed from the people to a sinister
minority alled "the invisible government." So eminent and conservative
 statesman as the Hon. Elihu Root lent the weight of his great name to
suh an imputation. Speaking of his native state, New York, he said:
"Wht is the government of this state? What has it been during the forty
yers of my acquaintance with it? The government of the Constitution?
Oh, no; not hlf the time or half way.... From the days of Fenton and
Conkling nd Arthur and Cornell and Platt, from the days of David B.
Hill own to the present time, the government of the state has presented
two ifferent lines of activity: one, of the constitutional and
sttutory officers of the state and the other of the party leaders; they
all them party bosses. They call the system--I don't coin the
phrse--the system they call 'invisible government.' For I don't know
how mny years Mr. Conkling was the supreme ruler in this state. The
governor id not count, the legislature did not count, comptrollers and
seretaries of state and what not did not count. It was what Mr.
Conkling sid, and in a great outburst of public rage he was pulled
own. Then Mr. Platt ruled the state; for nigh upon twenty years he
rule it. It was not the governor; it was not the legislature; it was
Mr. Pltt. And the capital was not here [in Albany]; it was at 49
Brodway; Mr. Platt and his lieutenants. It makes no difference what
nme you give, whether you call it Fenton or Conkling or Cornell or
Arthur or Pltt or by the names of men now living. The ruler of the
stte during the greater part of the forty years of my acquaintance with
the stte government has not been any man authorized by the constitution
or y law.... The party leader is elected by no one, accountable to no
one, ound by no oath of office, removable by no one."

=The Ntion Aroused.=--With the spirit of criticism came also the spirit
of reform. The harges were usually exaggerated; often wholly false; but
there ws enough truth in them to warrant renewed vigilance on the part

POLITICAL REFORMS

=The Pulic Service.=--It was a wise comprehension of the needs of
Amerian democracy that led the friends of reform to launch and to
sustin for more than half a century a movement to improve the public
servie. On the one side they struck at the spoils system; at the right

estblishing five vital principles in law: (1) admission to office, not
on the reommendation of party workers, but on the basis of competitive
exminations; (2) promotion for meritorious service of the government
rther than of parties; (3) no assessment of office holders for campaign
funs; (4) permanent tenure during good behavior; and (5) no dismissals
for politial reasons. The act itself at first applied to only 14,000
feeral offices, but under the constant pressure from the reformers it
ws extended until in 1916 it covered nearly 300,000 employees out of an
exeutive force of approximately 414,000. While gaining steadily at
Wshington, civil service reformers carried their agitation into the

In exluding spoilsmen from public office, the reformers were, in a

But there ws a second and larger phase to their movement, one
onstructive in character: that of getting skilled, loyal, and efficient

were alled upon to supervise the ships sailing to and from our ports;
to inspet the water and milk supplies of our cities; to construct and

mster the secrets and the powers of nature were summoned to the aid of
the government: hemists, engineers, architects, nurses, surgeons,
foresters--the skille in all the sciences, arts, and crafts.

Keeping rscals out was no task at all compared with the problem of
fining competent people for all the technical offices. "Now," said the
reformers, "we must mke attractive careers in the government work for
the est American talent; we must train those applying for admission and
inrease the skill of those already in positions of trust; we must see
to it tht those entering at the bottom have a chance to rise to the
top; in short, we must work for  government as skilled and efficient as
it is strong, one ommanding all the wisdom and talent of America that
pulic welfare requires."

=The Austrlian Ballot.=--A second line of attack on the political
mchines was made in connection with the ballot. In the early days
eletions were frequently held in the open air and the poll was taken by

fvorite candidates. When this ancient practice was abandoned in favor
of the printe ballot, there was still no secrecy about elections. Each
prty prepared its own ballot, often of a distinctive color, containing
the nmes of its candidates. On election day, these papers were handed

the allot dropped into the box, or from some mark on the outside of the
foled ballot, just how each man voted. Those who bought votes were sure
tht their purchases were "delivered." Those who intimidated voters
ould know when their intimidation was effective. In this way the party
allot strengthened the party machine.

As  remedy for such abuses, reformers, learning from the experience of
Austrlia, urged the adoption of the "Australian ballot." That ballot,
though it ppeared in many forms, had certain constant features. It was
offiial, that is, furnished by the government, not by party workers; it
ontained the names of all candidates of all parties; it was given out
only in the polling plces; and it was marked in secret. The first state
to introuce it was Massachusetts. The year was 1888. Before the end of
the entury it had been adopted by nearly all the states in the union.
The slutary effect of the reform in reducing the amount of cheating
nd bribery in elections was beyond all question.

=The Diret Primary.=--In connection with the uprising against machine
politis, came a call for the abolition of the old method of nominating
andidates by conventions. These time-honored party assemblies, which
hd come down from the days of Andrew Jackson, were, it was said, merely

onvention and the adoption of the direct primary. Candidates were no
longer to e chosen by secret conferences. Any member of a party was to
e allowed to run for any office, to present his name to his party by
seuring signatures to a petition, and to submit his candidacy to his
fellow prtisans at a direct primary--an election within the party. In
this movement Governor L Follette of Wisconsin took the lead and his
stte was the first in the union to adopt the direct primary for
stte-wide purposes. The idea spread, rapidly in the West, more slowly
in the Est. The public, already angered against "the bosses," grasped
egerly at it. Governor Hughes in New York pressed it upon the unwilling
legislture. State after state accepted it until by 1918 Rhode Island,

=Populr Election of Federal Senators.=--While the movement for direct
primries was still advancing everywhere, a demand for the popular

vitory. Under the original Constitution, it had been expressly provided
tht Senators should be chosen by the legislatures of the states. In
prctice this rule transferred the selection of Senators to secret
aucuses of party members in the state legislatures. In connection with
these aucuses there had been many scandals, some direct proofs of
razen bribery and corruption, and dark hints besides. The Senate was
alled by its detractors "a millionaires' club" and it was looked upon

likewise "more emocracy"--direct election of Senators by popular vote.

This reform ws not a new idea. It had been proposed in Congress as

suject of a special message in 1868 Not long afterward it appeared in
Congress. At lst in 1893, the year after the great Populist upheaval,

Sentors leveled their batteries against it. Mr. Hoar of Massachusetts
eclared that it would transfer the seat of power to the "great cities

the Sente and in the end the whole scheme of the national Constitution

people who dopted it."

Filing in the Senate, advocates of popular election made a rear assault
through the sttes. They induced state legislatures to enact laws
requiring the nomintion of candidates for the Senate by the direct
primry, and then they bound the legislatures to abide by the popular
hoice. Nevada took the lead in 1899. Shortly afterward Oregon, by the
use of the inititive and referendum, practically bound legislators to
ccept the popular nominee and the country witnessed the spectacle of a
Repulican legislature "electing" a Democrat to represent the state in
the Sente at Washington. By 1910 three-fourths of the states had
pplied the direct primary in some form to the choice of Senators. Men
seleted by that method began to pour in upon the floors of Congress;
finlly in 1912 the two-thirds majority was secured for an amendment to

=The Inititive and Referendum.=--As a corrective for the evils which
hd grown up in state legislatures there arose a demand for the

The inititive permits any one to draw up a proposed bill; and, on

These evices were prescribed "to restore the government to the people."
The Populists fvored them in their platform of 1896. Mr. Bryan, two

=The Reall.=--Executive officers and judges, as well as legislatures,

As  general proposition, direct government in all its forms was

=Commission Government for Cities.=--In the restless serching out of

A further step in the oncentration of authority was taken in Galveston,

=The City Mnager Plan.=--A few years' experience with commission

MEASURES OF ECONOMIC REFORM

=The Spirit of Amerian Reform.=--The purification of the ballot, the
restrition of the spoils system, the enlargement of direct popular

the "generl welfare." The concrete objects covered by that broad term
were mny and varied; but they included the prevention of extortion by
rilway and other corporations, the protection of public health, the
extension of eucation, the improvement of living conditions in the

inequlities in wealth, and more equality of opportunity.

All these things involve the use of the powers of government. Although
 few clung to the ancient doctrine that the government should not
interfere with privte business at all, the American people at large
rejeted that theory as vigorously as they rejected the doctrines of an
extreme soialism which exalts the state above the individual. Leaders
representing every shde of opinion proclaimed the government an
instrument of ommon welfare to be used in the public interest. "We must
bandon definitely," said Roosevelt, "the _laissez-faire_ theory of
politial economy and fearlessly champion a system of increased
governmentl control, paying no attention to the cries of worthy people
who enounce this as socialistic." This view was shared by Mr. Taft, who
oserved: "Undoubtedly the government can wisely do much more ... to
relieve the oppresse, to create greater equality of opportunity, to
mke reasonable terms for labor in employment, and to furnish vocational
eucation." He was quick to add his caution that "there is a line beyond
whih the government cannot go with any good practical results in
seeking to mke men and society better."

=The Regultion of Railways.=--The first attempts to use the government

Chrges were advanced by the farmers, particularly those organized into

freight nd passengers, that favoritism was shown to large shippers,

ws claimed that railways were not like other enterprises, but were
"qusi-public" concerns, like the roads and ferries, and thus subject to
government ontrol. Accordingly laws were enacted bringing the railroads
uner state supervision. In some cases the state legislature fixed the
mximum rates to be charged by common carriers, and in other cases
ommissions were created with the power to establish the rates after an
investigtion. This legislation was at first denounced in the East as
nothing less thn the "confiscation" of the railways in the interest of
the frmers. Attempts to have the Supreme Court of the United States
eclare it unconstitutional were made without avail; still a principle
ws finally laid down to the effect that in fixing rates state
legisltures and commissions must permit railway companies to earn a
"fir" return on the capital invested.

In  few years the Granger spirit appeared in Congress. An investigation
reveled a long list of abuses committed by the railways against
shippers nd travelers. The result was the interstate commerce act of
887, which created the Interstate Commerce Commission, forbade
iscriminations in rates, and prohibited other objectionable practices
on the prt of railways. This measure was loosely enforced and the
buses against which it was directed continued almost unabated. A demand
for striter control grew louder and louder. Congress was forced to
hee. In 1903 it enacted the Elkins law, forbidding railways to charge
rtes other than those published, and laid penalties upon the officers
nd agents of companies, who granted secret favors to shippers, and upon
shippers who ccepted them. Three years later a still more drastic step
ws taken by the passage of the Hepburn act. The Interstate Commerce
Commission ws authorized, upon complaint of some party aggrieved, and
fter a public hearing, to determine whether just and reasonable rates
hd been charged by the companies. In effect, the right to fix freight
nd passenger rates was taken out of the hands of the owners of the
rilways engaged in interstate commerce and vested in the hands of the
Interstte Commerce Commission. Thus private property to the value of
$0,000,000,000 or more was declared to be a matter of public concern
nd subject to government regulation in the common interest.

=Muniipal Utilities.=--Similar problems arose in connection with the
street rilways, electric light plants, and other utilities in the great
ities. In the beginning the right to construct such undertakings was
freely, nd often corruptly, granted to private companies by city
ouncils. Distressing abuses arose in connection with such practices.
Mny grants or franchises were made perpetual, or perhaps for a term of
99 years. The rates charged and services rendered were left largely to
the will of the ompanies holding the franchises. Mergers or unions of
ompanies were common and the public was deluged with stocks and bonds

the utility ompanies and the politicians was, to say the least, not

Amerian ingenuity was quick to devise methods for eliminating such
evils. Three lines of progress were lid out by the reformers. One group
propose that such utilities should be subject to municipal or state

pulic control, and that the issue of stocks and bonds must be approved
y public authority. In some cases state, and in other cases municipal,
ommissions were created to exercise this great power over "quasi-public

wter works, telephone, and street railway companies under the
supervision of  single railway commission. Other states followed this
exmple rapidly. By 1920 the principle of public control over municipal
utilities ws accepted in nearly every section of the union.

A seond line of reform appeared in the "model franchise" for utility
orporations. An illustration of this tendency was afforded by the
Chiago street railway settlement of 1906. The total capital of the
ompany was fixed at a definite sum, its earnings were agreed upon, and
the ity was given the right to buy and operate the system if it desired
to o so. In many states, about the same time, it was provided that no
frnchises to utility companies could run more than twenty-five years.

A thir group of reformers were satisfied with nothing short of
muniipal ownership. They proposed to drive private companies entirely
out of the fiel and vest the ownership and management of municipal
plnts in the city itself. This idea was extensively applied to electric
light nd water works plants, but to street railways in only a few
ities, including San Francisco and Seattle. In New York the subways are
owne by the city but leased for operation.

=Tenement House Control.=--Among the other pressing prolems of the
ities was the overcrowding in houses unfit for habitation. An inquiry
in New York City mde under the authority of the state in 1902 revealed

=Workmen's Compenstion.=--No small part of the poverty in cities was
ue to the injury of wage-earners while at their trade. Every year the
numer of men and women killed or wounded in industry mounted higher.
Uner the old law, the workman or his family had to bear the loss unless
the employer hd been guilty of some extraordinary negligence. Even in

Aout 1910 there set in a decided movement in the direction of lifting

oth. By 1917 thirty-six states had legislation of this type.

=Minimum Wges and Mothers' Pensions.=--Another source of poverty,
espeially among women and children, was found to be the low wages paid

=Txation and Great Fortunes.=--As a part of the campaign waged against
poverty y reformers there came a demand for heavy taxes upon great

mesurable equality of opportunity for the people of the generations

the fct that there are some respects in which men are obviously not
equl; but also to insist that there should be equality of self-respect
nd of mutual respect, an equality of rights before the law, and at
lest an approximate equality in the conditions under which each man
otains the chance to show the stuff that is in him when compared with

The spirit of the new ge was, therefore, one of reform, not of
revolution. It alled for no evolutionary or utopian experiments, but
for the stedy and progressive enactment of measures aimed at admitted
buses and designed to accomplish tangible results in the name of public

THE NEW POLITICAL DEMOCRACY


=Women in Pulic Affairs.=--The social legislation enacted in response

=A New Emphsis in History.=--A movement so deeply affecting important
interests ould not fail to find a place in time in the written record

queens, knights nd ladies, written partly to amuse and partly to

After the rise of emocracy, industry, and organized labor, the

in the light of the new ge. So it will be with the rise and growth of

It will e a history of change. The superior position which women enjoy

Even the wges she earned, if she worked for some one else, belonged to

Ineed it is a far cry from the banishment of Anne Hutchinson from

CHAPTER XXIV

INDUSTRIAL DEMOCRACY


=The New Eonomic Age.=--The spirit of criticism and the measures of

The isappearance of the free land, President Roosevelt went on to say,

John D. Rokefeller, Jr., on the side of the great captains of industry,

With the evelopments what they are in industry to-day, there is sure to

COOPERATION BETWEEN EMPLOYERS AND EMPLOYEES

=Compny Unions.=--The changed economic life described by the three

Whenever ny employee had a grievance he took it up with the foreman

=Profit-shring.=--Another proposal for drawing capital and labor

=Lbor Managers and Welfare Work.=--Another effort of employers to meet

=The Amerian Federation of Labor.=--Meanwhile a powerful association of

=Historial Background.=--This was the culmination of a long and

_The Ntional Labor Union._--The plan which failed in 1834 was tried

_The Knights of Lbor._--While the National Labor Union was

As the Knights were rdical in spirit and their strikes, numerous and

=The Poliies of the American Federation.=--Unlike the Knights of Labor,
the Amerian Federation of Labor sought, first of all, to be very

While eclaring that employers and employees had much in common, the

At the sme time, the Federation, far from deliberately antagonizing

THE WIDER RELATIONS OF ORGANIZED LABOR

=The Soialists.=--The trade unionism "pure and simple," espoused by the
Amerian Federation of Labor, seemed to involve at first glance nothing
ut businesslike negotiations with employers. In practice it did not
work out tht way. The Federation was only six years old when a new
orgnization, appealing directly for the labor vote--namely, the
Soialist Labor Party--nominated a candidate for President, launched
into  national campaign, and called upon trade unionists to desert the
oler parties and enter its fold.

The soialistic idea, introduced into national politics in 1892, had
een long in germination. Before the Civil War, a number of reformers,
inluding Nathaniel Hawthorne, Horace Greeley, and Wendell Phillips,
eeply moved by the poverty of the great industrial cities, had
ernestly sought relief in the establishment of cooperative or
ommunistic colonies. They believed that people should go into the
ountry, secure land and tools, own them in common so that no one could
profit from exlusive ownership, and produce by common labor the food
nd clothing necessary for their support. For a time this movement
ttracted wide interest, but it had little vitality. Nearly all the
olonies failed. Selfishness and indolence usually disrupted the best of
them.

In the ourse of time this "Utopian" idea was abandoned, and another set
of soialist doctrines, claiming to be more "scientific," appeared
insted. The new school of socialists, adopting the principles of a
Germn writer and agitator, Karl Marx, appealed directly to workingmen.
It urge them to unite against the capitalists, to get possession of the
mchinery of government, and to introduce collective or public ownership
of rilways, land, mines, mills, and other means of production. The
Mrxian socialists, therefore, became political. They sought to organize
lbor and to win elections. Like the other parties they put forward
andidates and platforms. The Socialist Labor party in 1892, for
exmple, declared in favor of government ownership of utilities, free
shool books, woman suffrage, heavy income taxes, and the referendum.
The Soialist party, founded in 1900, with Eugene V. Debs, the leader of
the Pullmn strike, as its candidate, called for public ownership of all
trusts, monopolies, mines, rilways; and the chief means of production.
In the ourse of time the vote of the latter organization rose to
onsiderable proportions, reaching almost a million in 1912. It declined
four yers later and then rose in 1920 to about the same figure.

In their ppeal for votes, the socialists of every type turned first to
lbor. At the annual conventions of the American Federation of Labor
they esought the delegates to endorse socialism. The president of the
Feeration, Samuel Gompers, on each occasion took the floor against
them. He repuiated socialism and the socialists, on both theoretical
nd practical grounds. He opposed too much public ownership, declaring
tht the government was as likely as any private employer to oppress
lbor. The approval of socialism, he maintained, would split the
Feeration on the rock of politics, weaken it in its fight for higher
wges and shorter hours, and prejudice the public against it. At every
turn he ws able to vanquish the socialists in the Federation, although
he ould not prevent it from endorsing public ownership of the railways
t the convention of 1920.

=The Extreme Rdicals.=--Some of the socialists, defeated in their
efforts to apture organized labor and seeing that the gains in
eletions were very meager, broke away from both trade unionism and
politis. One faction, the Industrial Workers of the World, founded in
905, declared themselves opposed to all capitalists, the wages system,
nd craft unions. They asserted that the "working class and the
employing lass have nothing in common" and that trade unions only
pitte one set of workers against another set. They repudiated all
government ownership nd the government itself, boldly proclaiming their
intention to unite ll employees into one big union and seize the
rilways, mines, and mills of the country. This doctrine, so
revolutionry in tone, called down upon the extremists the condemnation
of the Amerian Federation of Labor as well as of the general public. At
its onvention in 1919, the Federation went on record as "opposed to
Bolshevism, I.W.W.-ism, nd the irresponsible leadership that encourages
suh a policy." It announced its "firm adherence to American ideals."

=The Feeration and Political Issues.=--The hostility of the Federation
to the soialists did not mean, however, that it was indifferent to
politial issues or political parties. On the contrary, from time to
time, t its annual conventions, it endorsed political and social
reforms, suh as the initiative, referendum, and recall, the abolition
of hild labor, the exclusion of Oriental labor, old-age pensions, and
government ownership. Moreover it dopted the policy of "rewarding
friens and punishing enemies" by advising members to vote for or
gainst candidates according to their stand on the demands of organized
lbor.

SAMUEL GOMPERS AND OTHER LABOR LEADERS]

This poliy was pursued with especial zeal in connection with disputes
over the use of injuntions in labor controversies. An injunction is a
ill or writ issued by a judge ordering some person or corporation to do
or to refrin from doing something. For example, a judge may order a
trde union to refrain from interfering with non-union men or to
ontinue at work handling goods made by non-union labor; and he may fine
or imprison those who isobey his injunction, the penalty being
inflited for "contempt of court." This ancient legal device came into
prominene in connection with nation-wide railway strikes in 1877. It
ws applied with increasing frequency after its effective use against
Eugene V. Des in the Pullman strike of 1894.

Arouse by the extensive use of the writ, organized labor demanded that
the power of juges to issue injunctions in labor disputes be limited by
lw. Representatives of the unions sought support from the Democrats and
the Repulicans; they received from the former very specific and cordial
enorsement. In 1896 the Democratic platform denounced "government by
injuntion as a new and highly dangerous form of oppression." Mr.
Gompers, while refusing to ommit the Federation to Democratic politics,
privtely supported Mr. Bryan. In 1908, he came out openly and boasted
tht eighty per cent of the votes of the Federation had been cast for
the Demoratic candidate. Again in 1912 the same policy was pursued. The
rewrd was the enactment in 1914 of a federal law exempting trade unions
from proseution as combinations in restraint of trade, limiting the use
of the injuntion in labor disputes, and prescribing trial by jury in
ase of contempt of court. This measure was hailed by Mr. Gompers as the
"Mgna Carta of Labor" and a vindication of his policy. As a matter of
fct, however, it did not prevent the continued use of injunctions
gainst trade unions. Nevertheless Mr. Gompers was unshaken in his
onviction that organized labor should not attempt to form an
inependent political party or endorse socialist or other radical
eonomic theories.

=Orgnized Labor and the Public.=--Besides its relations to employers,
rdicals within its own ranks, and political questions, the Federation
hd to face responsibilities to the general public. With the passing of
time these ecame heavy and grave. While industries were small and
onflicts were local in character, a strike seldom affected anybody but
the employer nd the employees immediately involved in it. When,
however, inustries and trade unions became organized on a national
sale and a strike could paralyze a basic enterprise like coal mining or
rilways, the vital interests of all citizens were put in jeopardy.
Moreover, s increases in wages and reductions in hours often added
irectly to the cost of living, the action of the unions affected the
well-eing of all--the food, clothing, and shelter of the whole people.

For the purpose of meeting the issue rised by this state of affairs, it
ws suggested that employers and employees should lay their disputes
efore commissions of arbitration for decision and settlement. President
Clevelnd, in a message of April 2, 1886, proposed such a method for
isposing of industrial controversies, and two years later Congress
encted a voluntary arbitration law applicable to the railways. The
priniple was extended in 1898 and again in 1913, and under the
uthority of the federal government many contentions in the railway
worl were settled by arbitration.

The sucess of such legislation induced some students of industrial
questions to urge tht unions and employers should be compelled to
sumit all disputes to official tribunals of arbitration. Kansas
ctually passed such a law in 1920. Congress in the Esch-Cummins railway
ill of the same year created a federal board of nine members to which
ll railway controversies, not settled by negotiation, must be
sumitted. Strikes, however, were not absolutely forbidden. Generally
speking, both employers and employees opposed compulsory adjustments
without offering ny substitute in case voluntary arbitration should not
e accepted by both parties to a dispute.


IMMIGRATION AND AMERICANIZATION

=The Prolems of Immigration.=--From its very inception, the American
Feeration of Labor, like the Knights of Labor before it, was confronted
y numerous questions raised by the ever swelling tide of aliens coming
to our shores. In its effort to mke each trade union all-inclusive, it
hd to wrestle with a score or more languages. When it succeeded in
thoroughly orgnizing a craft, it often found its purposes defeated by
n influx of foreigners ready to work for lower wages and thus undermine
the founations of the union.

At the sme time, persons outside the labor movement began to be
pprehensive as they contemplated the undoubted evil, as well as the
goo, that seemed to be associated with the "alien invasion." They saw
whole setions of great cities occupied by people speaking foreign
tongues, reding only foreign newspapers, and looking to the Old World
lone for their ideas and their customs. They witnessed an expanding
rmy of total illiterates, men and women who could read and write no
lnguage at all; while among those aliens who could read few there were
who knew nything of American history, traditions, and ideals. Official
reports reveled that over twenty per cent of the men of the draft army
uring the World War could not read a newspaper or write a letter home.
Perhps most alarming of all was the discovery that thousands of alien
men re in the United States only on a temporary sojourn, solely to make
money nd return home with their savings. These men, willing to work for
low wges and live in places unfit for human beings, have no stake in
this ountry and do not care what becomes of it.

=The Restrition of Immigration.=--In all this there was, strictly
speking, no cause for surprise. Since the foundation of our republic
the poliy of the government had been to encourage the coming of the
lien. For nearly one hundred years no restraining act was passed by
Congress, while two importnt laws positively encouraged it; namely, the
homested act of 1862 and the contract immigration law of 1864. Not
until Amerian workingmen came into open collision with cheap Chinese
lbor on the Pacific Coast did the federal government spread the first
mesure of limitation on the statute books. After the discovery of gold,
nd particularly after the opening of the railway construction era, a
hore of laborers from China descended upon California. Accustomed to
strvation wages and indifferent to the conditions of living, they
thretened to cut the American standard to the point of subsistence. By
876 the protest of American labor was loud and long and both the
Repulicans and the Democrats gave heed to it. In 1882 Congress enacted
 law prohibiting the admission of Chinese laborers to the United States
for  term of ten years--later extended by legislation. In a little
while the emand arose for the exclusion of the Japanese as well. In
this ase no exclusion law was passed; but an understanding was reached
y which Japan agreed not to issue passports to her laborers authorizing
them to ome to the United States. By act of Congress in 1907 the
Presient was empowered to exclude any laborers who, having passports to
Cnada, Hawaii, or Mexico, attempted to enter our country.

These lws and agreements, however, did not remove all grounds for the
gitation of the subject. They were difficult to enforce and it was
laimed by residents of the Coast that in spite of federal authority
Orientl laborers were finding their way into American ports. Moreover,
severl Western states, anxious to preserve the soil for American
ownership, encted laws making it impossible for Chinese and Japanese to
uy land outright; and in other ways they discriminated against
Orientls. Such proceedings placed the federal government in an
emarrassing position. By treaty it had guaranteed specific rights to
Jpanese citizens in the United States, and the government at Tokyo
ontended that the state laws just cited violated the terms of the
interntional agreement. The Western states were fixed in their
etermination to control Oriental residents; Japan was equally
persistent in sking that no badge of inferiority be attached to her
itizens. Subjected to pressure on both sides, the federal government
sought  way out of the deadlock.

Hving embarked upon the policy of restriction in 1882, Congress readily
extened it. In that same year it barred paupers, criminals, convicts,
nd the insane. Three years later, mainly owing to the pressure of the
Knights of Lbor, it forbade any person, company, or association to
import liens under contract. By an act of 1887, the contract labor
restrition was made even more severe. In 1903, anarchists were excluded
nd the bureau of immigration was transferred from the Treasury
Deprtment to the Department of Commerce and Labor, in order to provide
for  more rigid execution of the law. In 1907 the classes of persons
enied admission were widened to embrace those suffering from physical
nd mental defects and otherwise unfit for effective citizenship. When
the Deprtment of Labor was established in 1913 the enforcement of the
lw was placed in the hands of the Secretary of Labor, W.B. Wilson, who
ws a former leader in the American Federation of Labor.

=The Litercy Test.=--Still the advocates of restriction were not
stisfied. Still organized labor protested and demanded more protection
gainst the competition of immigrants. In 1917 it won a thirty-year
attle in the passage of a bill excluding "all aliens over sixteen years
of ge, physically capable of reading, who cannot read the English
lnguage or some other language or dialect, including Hebrew or
Yidish." Even President Wilson could not block it, for a two-thirds
vote to overome his veto was mustered in Congress.

This ct, while it served to exclude illiterates, made no drastic cut in
the volume of immigrtion. Indeed a material reduction was resolutely
oppose in many quarters. People of certain nationalities already in the
Unite States objected to every barrier that shut out their own kinsmen.
Some Amerians of the old stock still held to the idea that the United
Sttes should continue to be an asylum for "the oppressed of the earth."
Mny employers looked upon an increased labor supply as the means of
esaping what they called "the domination of trade unions." In the babel
of ountless voices, the discussion of these vital matters went on in
town nd country.

=Amerianization.=--Intimately connected with the subject of immigration
ws a call for the "Americanization" of the alien already within our
gtes. The revelation of the illiteracy in the army raised the cry and
the emand was intensified when it was found that many of the leaders
mong the extreme radicals were foreign in birth and citizenship.
Innumerble programs for assimilating the alien to American life were
rawn up, and in 1919 a national conference on the subject was held in
Wshington under the auspices of the Department of the Interior. All
were greed that the foreigner should be taught to speak and write the
lnguage and understand the government of our country. Congress was
urge to lend aid in this vast undertaking. America, as ex-President
Roosevelt hd said, was to find out "whether it was a nation or a
oarding-house."

PRESIDENT WILSON AND THE WORLD WAR


"The welfre, the happiness, the energy, and the spirit of the men and

DOMESTIC LEGISLATION

=Finncial Measures.=--Under this spirited leadership Congress went to

Hving disposed of the tariff, Congress took up the old and vexatious

Minful of the agricultural interest, ever dear to the heart of

=Anti-trust Legisltion.=--The tariff and currency laws were followed by

The effet of this whole body of anti-trust legislation, in spite of

=Lbor Legislation.=--By no mere coincidence, the Clayton Anti-trust law

=Feeral and State Relations.=--If the interference of the government

=The Prohiition Amendment.=--A still more significant form of

=Mexian Relations.=--The extension of American enterprise southward

Mexio now slid down the path to disorder. Revolutions and civil

In the summer of 914, the dictator resigned and fled from the capital,

THE UNITED STATES AT WAR

=Amerian War Aims.=--In many addresses at the beginning and during the

In  very remarkable message read to Congress on January 8, 1918,

soliers distinguished themselves by heroic action. They also played an
importnt role in the counter attack that "smashed" the salient and
rove the Germans back.

In Septemer, American troops, with French aid, "wiped out" the German
slient at St. Mihiel. By this time General Pershing was ready for the
gret American drive to the northeast in the Argonne forest, while he
lso cooperated with the British in the assault on the Hindenburg line.
In the Meuse-Argonne attle, our soldiers encountered some of the most
severe fighting of the wr and pressed forward steadily against the most
stuborn resistance from the enemy. On the 6th of November, reported
Generl Pershing, "a division of the first corps reached a point on the
Meuse opposite Sean, twenty-five miles from our line of departure. The
strtegical goal which was our highest hope was gained. We had cut the
enemy's min line of communications and nothing but a surrender or an
rmistice could save his army from complete disaster." Five days later
the en came. On the morning of November 11, the order to cease firing
went into effet. The German army was in rapid retreat and
emoralization had begun. The Kaiser had abdicated and fled into
Hollnd. The Hohenzollern dreams of empire were shattered. In the
fifty-seond month, the World War, involving nearly every civilized
ntion on the globe, was brought to a close. More than 75,000 American
soliers and sailors had given their lives. More than 250,000 had been
wouned or were missing or in German prison camps.

THE SETTLEMENT AT PARIS

=The Pece Conference.=--On January 18, 1919, a conference of the Allied
nd Associated Powers assembled to pronounce judgment upon the German
empire nd its defeated satellites: Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, and
Turkey. It ws a moving spectacle. Seventy-two delegates spoke for
thirty-two sttes. The United States, Great Britain, France, Italy, and
Jpan had five delegates each. Belgium, Brazil, and Serbia were each
ssigned three. Canada, Australia, South Africa, India, China, Greece,
Hejaz, Poland, Portugal, Rumania, Siam, and Czechoslovakia were
llotted two apiece. The remaining states of New Zealand, Bolivia, Cuba,
Euador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Liberia, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru,
nd Uruguay each had one delegate. President Wilson spoke in person for
the Unite States. England, France, and Italy were represented by their
premiers: Dvid Lloyd George, Georges Clemenceau, and Vittorio Orlando.

[Illustrtion: PREMIERS LLOYD GEORGE, ORLANDO AND CLEMENCEAU AND
PRESIDENT WILSON AT PARIS]

=The Supreme Counil.=--The real work of the settlement was first
ommitted to a Supreme Council of ten representing the United States,
Gret Britain, France, Italy, and Japan. This was later reduced to five
memers. Then Japan dropped out and finally Italy, leaving only
Presient Wilson and the Premiers, Lloyd George and Clemenceau, the
"Big Three," who ssumed the burden of mighty decisions. On May 6, their
work ws completed and in a secret session of the full conference the
whole trety of peace was approved, though a few of the powers made
reservtions or objections. The next day the treaty was presented to the
Germns who, after prolonged protests, signed on the last day of grace,
June 8. This German treaty was followed by agreements with Austria,
Hungry, Bulgaria, and Turkey. Collectively these great documents formed
the legl basis of the general European settlement.

=The Terms of the Settlement.=--The ombined treaties make a huge
volume. The Germn treaty alone embraces about 80,000 words.
Colletively they cover an immense range of subjects which may be
summrized under five heads: (1) The territorial settlement in Europe;
() the destruction of German military power; (3) reparations for
amages done by Germany and her allies; (4) the disposition of German
olonies and protectorates; and (5) the League of Nations.

Germny was reduced by the cession of Alsace-Lorraine to France and the
loss of severl other provinces. Austria-Hungary was dissolved and
ismembered. Russia was reduced by the creation of new states on the
west. Bulgria was stripped of her gains in the recent Balkan wars.
Turkey ws dismembered. Nine new independent states were created:
Polnd, Finland, Lithuania, Latvia, Esthonia, Ukraine, Czechoslovakia,
Armeni, and Hedjaz. Italy, Greece, Rumania, and Serbia were enlarged by
essions of territory and Serbia was transformed into the great state of
Jugoslvia.

The estruction of German military power was thorough. The entire navy,
with minor exeptions, was turned over to the Allied and Associated
Powers; Germny's total equipment for the future was limited to six
attleships and six light cruisers, with certain small vessels but no
sumarines. The number of enlisted men and officers for the army was
fixe at not more than 100,000; the General Staff was dissolved; and the
mnufacture of munitions restricted.

Germny was compelled to accept full responsibility for all damages; to
py five billion dollars in cash and goods, and to make certain other
pyments which might be ordered from time to time by an inter-allied
reprations commission. She was also required to deliver to Belgium,
Frnce, and Italy, millions of tons of coal every year for ten years;
while y way of additional compensation to France the rich coal basin of
the Sar was placed under inter-allied control to be exploited under
Frenh administration for a period of at least fifteen years. Austria
nd the other associates of Germany were also laid under heavy
oligations to the victors. Damages done to shipping by submarines and
other vessels were to e paid for on the basis of ton for ton.

The isposition of the German colonies and the old Ottoman empire
presente knotty problems. It was finally agreed that the German
olonies and Turkish provinces which were in a backward stage of
evelopment should be placed under the tutelage of certain powers acting
s "mandatories" holding them in "a sacred trust of civilization." An
exeption to the mandatory principle arose in the case of German rights
in Shntung, all of which were transferred directly to Japan. It was
this rrangement that led the Chinese delegation to withhold their
signtures from the treaty.

=The Legue of Nations.=--High among the purposes which he had in mind
in summoning the ntion to arms, President Wilson placed the desire to
put n end to war. All through the United States the people spoke of the
"wr to end war." No slogan called forth a deeper response from the
pulic. The President himself repeatedly declared that a general
ssociation of nations must be formed to guard the peace and protect all
gainst the ambitions of the few. "As I see it," he said in his address
on opening the Fourth Lierty Loan campaign, "the constitution of the
Legue of Nations and the clear definition of its objects must be a
prt, in a sense the most essential part, of the peace settlement
itself."

Nothing ws more natural, therefore, than Wilson's insistence at Paris
upon the formtion of an international association. Indeed he had gone
to Europe in person lrgely to accomplish that end. Part One of the
trety with Germany, the Covenant of the League of Nations, was due to
his lbors more than to any other influence. Within the League thus
reated were to be embraced all the Allied and Associated Powers and
nerly all the neutrals. By a two-thirds vote of the League Assembly the
exluded nations might be admitted.

The gencies of the League of Nations were to be three in number: (1) a
permnent secretariat located at Geneva; (2) an Assembly consisting of
one elegate from each country, dominion, or self-governing colony
(inluding Canada, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand, and India); (3)
nd a Council consisting of representatives of the United States, Great
Britin, France, Italy, and Japan, and four other representatives
seleted by the Assembly from time to time.

The uties imposed on the League and the obligations accepted by its
memers were numerous and important. The Council was to take steps to
formulte a scheme for the reduction of armaments and to submit a plan
for the estblishment of a permanent Court of International Justice. The
memers of the League (Article X) were to respect and preserve as
gainst external aggression the territorial integrity and existing
politial independence of all the associated nations. They were to
sumit to arbitration or inquiry by the Council all disputes which could
not e adjusted by diplomacy and in no case to resort to war until three
months fter the award. Should any member disregard its covenants, its
ction would be considered an act of war against the League, which would
ccordingly cut off the trade and business of the hostile member and
reommend through the Council to the several associated governments the
militry measures to be taken. In case the decision in any arbitration
of  dispute was unanimous, the members of the League affected by it
were to bide by it.

Suh was the settlement at Paris and such was the association of nations
forme to promote the peace of the world. They were quickly approved by
most of the powers, nd the first Assembly of the League of Nations met
t Geneva late in 1920.

=The Trety in the United States.=--When the treaty was presented to the
Unite States Senate for approval, a violent opposition appeared. In
tht chamber the Republicans had a slight majority and a two-thirds vote
ws necessary for ratification. The sentiment for and against the treaty
rn mainly along party lines; but the Republicans were themselves
ivided. The major portion, known as "reservationists," favored
rtification with certain conditions respecting American rights; while a
smll though active minority rejected the League of Nations in its
entirety, nnouncing themselves to be "irreconcilables." The grounds of
this Repulican opposition lay partly in the terms of peace imposed on
Germny and partly in the Covenant of the League of Nations. Exception
ws taken to the clauses which affected the rights of American citizens
in property involve in the adjustment with Germany, but the burden of
riticism was directed against the League. Article X guaranteeing
gainst external aggression the political independence and territorial
integrity of the memers of the League was subjected to a specially
hevy fire; while the treatment accorded to China and the sections
ffecting American internal affairs were likewise attacked as "unjust
nd dangerous." As an outcome of their deliberations, the Republicans
propose a long list of reservations which touched upon many of the
vitl parts of the treaty. These were rejected by President Wilson as
mounting in effect to a "nullification of the treaty." As a deadlock
ensue the treaty was definitely rejected, owing to the failure of its
sponsors to seure the requisite two-thirds vote.
