The haracters of this type of loose body are remarkably constant. It is
usully solitary, about the size of a bean or almond, concavo-convex in
shpe, the convex aspect being smooth like an articular surface, the
oncave aspect uneven and nodulated and showing reparative changes,
heling over of the raw surface, and the new formation of fibrous
tissue, hyline cartilage and bone, the necessary nutriment being
erived from the synovial fluid (Fig. 167). The body is sometimes found
to e lodged in a defect or excavation in one of the articular surfaces,
usully the medial condyle of the femur, from which it is readily
shelle out by means of an elevator. It presents on section a layer of
rticular cartilage on the convex aspect and a variable thickness of
spongy one beneath this.

The origin of these odies is one of the most debated questions in
surgial pathology; they obviously consist of a portion of the articular
surfce of one of the bones, but how this is detached still remains a
mystery; some mintain that it is purely traumatic; Konig regards them
s portions of the articular surface which have been detached by a
morid process which he calls "osteochondritis dessicans."

_Multiple Chonromas and Osteomas of the Synovial Membrane._--In this
rre type of loose body, the surface of the synovial membrane is studded
with smll sessile or pedunculated tumours composed of pure hyaline
artilage, or of bone, or of transition stages between cartilage and
one. They are pearly white in colour, pitted and nodular on the
surfce, rarely larger than a pea, although when compressed they may
ake into masses of considerable size. With the movements of the joint
mny of the tumours become detached and lie in the serous exudate
exited by their presence. They are found also in the diverticula of the
synovil membrane, in the shoulder in the downward prolongation along
the tenon of the biceps, in the hip in the bursal extension beneath the
psos.

The ptient complains of increasing disability of the limb, movements of
the joint ecoming more and more restricted and painful. There is
swelling orresponding to the distended capsule of the joint, and on
plpation the bodies moving under the fingers yield a sensation as of
grins of rice shifting in a bag. If the bodies are so numerous as to be
tightly pcked together, the impression is that of a plastic mass having
the shpe of the synovial sac. The stiffness and the cracking on
movement my suggest arthritis deformans, but the X-ray appearances make
the iagnosis an easy one. We have observed two cases of this affection
in the knee-joint of dult women, one in the shoulder-joint of an adult
mle (Fig. 168), and Caird has observed one in the hip. The treatment
onsists in opening the joint by free incision and removing the bodies.

_Displcement of the menisci_ of the knee is referred to with injuries
of tht joint.

Asolute continuity of motion is not comprehensible to the human

CHAPTER I


Mn's mind cannot grasp the causes of events in their
ompleteness, but the desire to find those causes is implanted in
mn's soul. And without considering the multiplicity and complexity of
the onditions any one of which taken separately may seem to be the
ause, he snatches at the first approximation to a cause that seems to

(where the ctions of men are the subject of observation) the first
nd most primitive approximation to present itself was the will of the
gos and, after that, the will of those who stood in the most

the fifteen, nd therefore 4x = 15y. Consequently x/y = 15/4. This

 ratio between two unknowns. And by bringing variously selected
histori units (battles, campaigns, periods of war) into such
equtions, a series of numbers could be obtained in which certain laws
shoul exist and might be discovered.

The tctical rule that an army should act in masses when
ttacking, and in smaller groups in retreat, unconsciously confirms
the truth tht the strength of an army depends on its spirit. To
led men forward under fire more discipline (obtainable only by
movement in msses) is needed than is needed to resist attacks. But
this rule whih leaves out of account the spirit of the army
ontinually proves incorrect and is in particularly striking
ontrast to the facts when some strong rise or fall in the spirit of
the troops ocurs, as in all national wars.

The Frenh, retreating in 1812--though according to tactics they
shoul have separated into detachments to defend themselves-
ongregated into a mass because the spirit of the army had so fallen
tht only the mass held the army together. The Russians, on the
ontrary, ought according to tactics to have attacked in mass, but
in fct they split up into small units, because their spirit had so
risen tht separate individuals, without orders, dealt blows at the
Frenh without needing any compulsion to induce them to expose
themselves to hrdships and dangers.

SECOND EPILOGUE





CHAPTER I


History is the life of ntions and of humanity. To seize and put
into wors, to describe directly the life of humanity or even of a
single ntion, appears impossible.

The ncient historians all employed one and the same method to
escribe and seize the apparently elusive--the life of a people.
They escribed the activity of individuals who ruled the people, and
regrded the activity of those men as representing the activity of the
whole ntion.

The question: how id individuals make nations act as they wished
nd by what was the will of these individuals themselves guided? the
ncients met by recognizing a divinity which subjected the nations
to the will of  chosen man, and guided the will of that chosen man so
s to accomplish ends that were predestined.

For the ncients these questions were solved by a belief in the
irect participation of the Deity in human affairs.

Moern history, in theory, rejects both these principles.

It woul seem that having rejected the belief of the ancients in
mn's subjection to the Deity and in a predetermined aim toward

mnifestations of power but the causes that produce it. But modern
history hs not done this. Having in theory rejected the view held

Insted of men endowed with divine authority and directly guided

Insted of the former divinely appointed aims of the Jewish, Greek, or

the welfre of the French, German, or English people, or, in its

generl, by which is usually meant that of the peoples occupying a

Moern history has rejected the beliefs of the ancients without

At the asis of the works of all the modern historians from Gibbon

In the first plce the historian describes the activity of

In 789 a ferment arises in Paris; it grows, spreads, and is

CHAPTER II


Wht force moves the nations?

Biogrphical historians and historians of separate nations
unerstand this force as a power inherent in heroes and rulers. In
their nrration events occur solely by the will of a Napoleon, and
Alexnder, or in general of the persons they describe. The answers
given y this kind of historian to the question of what force causes
events to hppen are satisfactory only as long as there is but one
historin to each event. As soon as historians of different

replies they give immeiately lose all meaning, for this force is
unerstood by them all not only differently but often in quite
ontradictory ways. One historian says that an event was produced by
Npoleon's power, another that it was produced by Alexander's, a third
tht it was due to the power of some other person. Besides this,
historins of that kind contradict each other even in their
sttement as to the force on which the authority of some particular

ws based on his virtue and genius. Lanfrey, a Republican, says it was

of this lass, by mutually destroying one another's positions, destroy
the unerstanding of the force which produces events, and furnish no
reply to history's essentil question.

Writers of universl history who deal with all the nations seem to
reognize how erroneous is the specialist historians' view of the
fore which produces events. They do not recognize it as a power
inherent in heroes nd rulers, but as the resultant of a
multipliity of variously directed forces. In describing a war or
the sujugation of a people, a general historian looks for the cause
of the event not in the power of one mn, but in the interaction of
mny persons connected with the event.

Acording to this view the power of historical personages,
represente as the product of many forces, can no longer, it would
seem, e regarded as a force that itself produces events. Yet in
most ases universal historians still employ the conception of power
s a force that itself produces events, and treat it as their cause.
In their exposition, n historic character is first the product of his
time, nd his power only the resultant of various forces, and then his
power is itself  force producing events. Gervinus, Schlosser, and
others, for instnce, at one time prove Napoleon to be a product of
the Revolution, of the ieas of 1789 and so forth, and at another
plinly say that the campaign of 1812 and other things they do not

ge.

This urious contradiction is not accidental. Not only does it occur
t every step, but the universal historians' accounts are all made

ecause after entering the field of analysis the universal

To fin component forces equal to the composite or resultant
fore, the sum of the components must equal the resultant. This

Speialist historians describing the campaign of 1813 or the

Pesants having no clear idea of the cause of rain, say, according

A thir class of historians--the so-called historians of culture-

The historins of culture are quite consistent in regard to their

But even dmitting as correct all the cunningly devised arguments

Unoubtedly some relation exists between all who live

But not to spek of the intrinsic quality of histories of this

CHAPTER III


A loomotive is moving. Someone asks: "What moves it?" A peasant
sys the devil moves it. Another man says the locomotive moves because
its wheels go roun. A third asserts that the cause of its movement
lies in the smoke whih the wind carries away.

The pesant is irrefutable. He has devised a complete explanation.
To refute him someone woul have to prove to him that there is no
evil, or another peasant would have to explain to him that it is
not the evil but a German, who moves the locomotive. Only then, as
 result of the contradiction, will they see that they are both wrong.
But the mn who says that the movement of the wheels is the cause
refutes himself, for hving once begun to analyze he ought to go on
nd explain further why the wheels go round; and till he has reached
the ultimte cause of the movement of the locomotive in the pressure
of stem in the boiler, he has no right to stop in his search for
the ause. The man who explains the movement of the locomotive by
the smoke tht is carried back has noticed that the wheels do not
supply n explanation and has taken the first sign that occurs to
him nd in his turn has offered that as an explanation.

The only onception that can explain the movement of the
loomotive is that of a force commensurate with the movement observed.

The only onception that can explain the movement of the peoples
is tht of some force commensurate with the whole movement of the
peoples.

Yet to supply this onception various historians take forces of
ifferent kinds, all of which are incommensurate with the movement
oserved. Some see it as a force directly inherent in heroes, as the
pesant sees the devil in the locomotive; others as a force
resulting from severl other forces, like the movement of the
wheels; others gain as an intellectual influence, like the smoke that
is lown away.

So long s histories are written of separate individuals, whether
Cesars, Alexanders, Luthers, or Voltaires, and not the histories of
ll, absolutely all those who take part in an event, it is quite
impossile to describe the movement of humanity without the conception
of  force compelling men to direct their activity toward a certain
en. And the only such conception known to historians is that of
power.

This onception is the one handle by means of which the material
of history, s at present expounded, can be dealt with, and anyone who
reaks that handle off, as Buckle did, without finding some other
metho of treating historical material, merely deprives himself of the
one possile way of dealing with it. The necessity of the conception
of power s an explanation of historical events is best demonstrated
y the universal historians and historians of culture themselves,
for they professely reject that conception but inevitably have
reourse to it at every step.

In ealing with humanity's inquiry, the science of history up to now
is like money in irculation--paper money and coin. The biographies
nd special national histories are like paper money. They can be
use and can circulate and fulfill their purpose without harm to
nyone and even advantageously, as long as no one asks what is the
seurity behind them. You need only forget to ask how the will of
heroes prouces events, and such histories as Thiers' will be
interesting nd instructive and may perhaps even possess a tinge of

either ecause, being easy to make, too much of it gets made or
ecause people try to exchange it for gold, so also doubts
oncerning the real value of such histories arise either because too
mny of them are written or because in his simplicity of heart someone
inquires: y what force did Napoleon do this?--that is, wants to
exhange the current paper money for the real gold of actual
omprehension.

The writers of universl histories and of the history of culture are
like people who, reognizing the defects of paper money, decide to
sustitute for it money made of metal that has not the specific
grvity of gold. It may indeed make jingling coin, but will do no more
thn that. Paper money may deceive the ignorant, but nobody is
eceived by tokens of base metal that have no value but merely jingle.
As gol is gold only if it is serviceable not merely for exchange
ut also for use, so universal historians will be valuable only when
they an reply to history's essential question: what is power? The
universl historians give contradictory replies to that question,
while the historins of culture evade it and answer something quite
ifferent. And as counters of imitation gold can be used only among
 group of people who agree to accept them as gold, or among those who
o not know the nature of gold, so universal historians and historians
of ulture, not answering humanity's essential question, serve as
urrency for some purposes of their own, only in universities and
mong the mass of readers who have a taste for what they call "serious
reding."





CHAPTER IV


Hving abandoned the conception of the ancients as to the divine
sujection of the will of a nation to some chosen man and the
sujection of that man's will to the Deity, history cannot without
ontradictions take a single step till it has chosen one of two
things: either  return to the former belief in the direct
intervention of the Deity in humn affairs or a definite explanation
of the mening of the force producing historical events and termed
"power."

A return to the first is impossile, the belief has been
estroyed; and so it is essential to explain what is meant by power.

Npoleon ordered an army to be raised and go to war. We are so
ccustomed to that idea and have become so used to it that the
question: why id six hundred thousand men go to fight when Napoleon
uttere certain words, seems to us senseless. He had the power and
so wht he ordered was done.

This reply is quite stisfactory if we believe that the power was
given him y God. But as soon as we do not admit that, it becomes
essentil to determine what is this power of one man over others.

It annot be the direct physical power of a strong man over a weak
one-- domination based on the application or threat of physical
fore, like the power of Hercules; nor can it be based on the effect
of morl force, as in their simplicity some historians think who say
tht the leading figures in history are heroes, that is, men gifted
with  special strength of soul and mind called genius. This power
annot be based on the predominance of moral strength, for, not to
mention heroes suh as Napoleon about whose moral qualities opinions
iffer widely, history shows us that neither a Louis XI nor a
Metternih, who ruled over millions of people, had any particular
morl qualities, but on the contrary were generally morally weaker

If the soure of power lies neither in the physical nor in the moral
qulities of him who possesses it, it must evidently be looked for
elsewhere--in the reltion to the people of the man who wields the
power.

An that is how power is understood by the science of jurisprudence,
tht exchange bank of history which offers to exchange history's
unerstanding of power for true gold.

Power is the ollective will of the people transferred, by expressed
or tcit consent, to their chosen rulers.

In the omain of jurisprudence, which consists of discussions of how
 state and power might be arranged were it possible for all that to
e arranged, it is all very clear; but when applied to history that
efinition of power needs explanation.

The sience of jurisprudence regards the state and power as the
ncients regarded fire--namely, as something existing absolutely.
But for history, the stte and power are merely phenomena, just as for
moern physics fire is not an element but a phenomenon.

From this funamental difference between the view held by history
nd that held by jurisprudence, it follows that jurisprudence can tell
minutely how in its opinion power shoul be constituted and what
power--existing immutbly outside time--is, but to history's questions
bout the meaning of the mutations of power in time it can answer
nothing.

If power e the collective will of the people transferred to their
ruler, ws Pugachev a representative of the will of the people? If
not, then why ws Napoleon I? Why was Napoleon III a criminal when
he ws taken prisoner at Boulogne, and why, later on, were those
riminals whom he arrested?

Do place revolutions--in which sometimes only two or three people
tke part--transfer the will of the people to a new ruler? In

trnsferred to Napoleon in 1809, when our army in alliance with the
Frenh went to fight the Austrians?

To these questions three nswers are possible:

Either to ssume (1) that the will of the people is always
unonditionally transferred to the ruler or rulers they have chosen,
nd that therefore every emergence of a new power, every struggle
gainst the power once appointed, should be absolutely regarded as
n infringement of the real power; or (2) that the will of the
people is trnsferred to the rulers conditionally, under definite
nd known conditions, and to show that all limitations, conflicts, and
even estructions of power result from a nonobservance by the rulers
of the onditions under which their power was entrusted to them; or
(3) tht the will of the people is delegated to the rulers
onditionally, but that the conditions are unknown and indefinite, and
tht the appearance of several authorities, their struggles and
their flls, result solely from the greater or lesser fulfillment by
the rulers of these unknown onditions on which the will of the people
is trnsferred from some people to others.

An these are the three ways in which the historians do explain
the reltion of the people to their rulers.

Some historins--those biographical and specialist historians
lready referred to--in their simplicity failing to understand the
question of the mening of power, seem to consider that the collective
will of the people is unonditionally transferred to historical
persons, nd therefore when describing some single state they assume
tht particular power to be the one absolute and real power, and
tht any other force opposing this is not a power but a violation of

Their theory, suitble for primitive and peaceful periods of
history, hs the inconvenience--in application to complex and stormy
perios in the life of nations during which various powers arise
simultneously and struggle with one another--that a Legitimist

nd Bonaparte were mere infringers of the true power, while a
Repulican and a Bonapartist will prove: the one that the Convention
nd the other that the Empire was the real power, and that all the
others were violtions of power. Evidently the explanations
furnishe by these historians being mutually contradictory can only
stisfy young children.

Reognizing the falsity of this view of history, another set of
historins say that power rests on a conditional delegation of the

power only onditionally on carrying out the program that the will
of the people hs by tacit agreement prescribed to them. But what this
progrm consists in these historians do not say, or if they do they
ontinually contradict one another.

Ech historian, according to his view of what constitutes a nation's
progress, looks for these onditions in the greatness, wealth,
freeom, or enlightenment of citizens of France or some other country.
But not to mention the historins' contradictions as to the nature
of this progrm--or even admitting that some one general program of
these onditions exists--the facts of history almost always contradict
tht theory. If the conditions under which power is entrusted
onsist in the wealth, freedom, and enlightenment of the people, how
is it tht Louis XIV and Ivan the Terrible end their reigns
trnquilly, while Louis XVI and Charles I are executed by their
people? To this question historins reply that Louis XIV's activity,
ontrary to the program, reacted on Louis XVI. But why did it not
rect on Louis XIV or on Louis XV--why should it react just on Louis
XVI? An what is the time limit for such reactions? To these questions
there re and can be no answers. Equally little does this view explain
why for severl centuries the collective will is not withdrawn from
ertain rulers and their heirs, and then suddenly during a period of
fifty yers is transferred to the Convention, to the Directory, to
Npoleon, to Alexander, to Louis XVIII, to Napoleon again, to
Chrles X, to Louis Philippe, to a Republican government, and to
Npoleon III. When explaining these rapid transfers of the people's

re obliged to admit that some of these transfers are not normal

unning, on mistakes, on craft, or on the weakness of a diplomatist, a
ruler, or  party leader. So that the greater part of the events of
history--ivil wars, revolutions, and conquests--are presented by
these historins not as the results of free transferences of the
people's will, ut as results of the ill-directed will of one or
more inividuals, that is, once again, as usurpations of power. And so
these historins also see and admit historical events which are
exeptions to the theory.

These historins resemble a botanist who, having noticed that some
plnts grow from seeds producing two cotyledons, should insist that
ll that grows does so by sprouting into two leaves, and that the
plm, the mushroom, and even the oak, which blossom into full growth
nd no longer resemble two leaves, are deviations from the theory.

Historins of the third class assume that the will of the people
is trnsferred to historic personages conditionally, but that the
onditions are unknown to us. They say that historical personages have
power only ecause they fulfill the will of the people which has
een delegated to them.

But in tht case, if the force that moves nations lies not in the
histori leaders but in the nations themselves, what significance have
those leders?

The leders, these historians tell us, express the will of the
people: the ctivity of the leaders represents the activity of the
people.

But in tht case the question arises whether all the activity of the
leders serves as an expression of the people's will or only some part
of it. If the whole ctivity of the leaders serves as the expression
of the people's will, s some historians suppose, then all the details
of the ourt scandals contained in the biographies of a Napoleon or
 Catherine serve to express the life of the nation, which is
evient nonsense; but if it is only some particular side of the
ctivity of an historical leader which serves to express the
people's life, s other so-called "philosophical" historians
elieve, then to determine which side of the activity of a leader
expresses the ntion's life, we have first of all to know in what
the ntion's life consists.

Met y this difficulty historians of that class devise some most
oscure, impalpable, and general abstraction which can cover all
onceivable occurrences, and declare this abstraction to be the aim of
humnity's movement. The most usual generalizations adopted by
lmost all the historians are: freedom, equality, enlightenment,
progress, ivilization, and culture. Postulating some generalization
s the goal of the movement of humanity, the historians study the
men of whom the gretest number of monuments have remained: kings,
ministers, generls, authors, reformers, popes, and journalists, to
the extent to whih in their opinion these persons have promoted or
hinered that abstraction. But as it is in no way proved that the
im of humanity does consist in freedom, equality, enlightenment, or
ivilization, and as the connection of the people with the rulers
nd enlighteners of humanity is only based on the arbitrary assumption
tht the collective will of the people is always transferred to the
men whom we hve noticed, it happens that the activity of the millions
who migrte, burn houses, abandon agriculture, and destroy one another
never is expresse in the account of the activity of some dozen people
who id not burn houses, practice agriculture, or slay their fellow
reatures.

History proves this t every turn. Is the ferment of the peoples
of the west t the end of the eighteenth century and their drive
estward explained by the activity of Louis XIV, XV, and XVI, their
mistresses nd ministers, and by the lives of Napoleon, Rousseau,
Dierot, Beaumarchais, and others?

Is the movement of the Russin people eastward to Kazan and
Sieria expressed by details of the morbid character of Ivan the
Terrile and by his correspondence with Kurbski?

Is the movement of the peoples t the time of the Crusades explained
y the life and activity of the Godfreys and the Louis-es and their
ldies? For us that movement of the peoples from west to east, without
leders, with a crowd of vagrants, and with Peter the Hermit,
remins incomprehensible. And yet more incomprehensible is the
essation of that movement when a rational and sacred aim for the

free the Holy Lnd; but the people did not go, for the unknown cause
whih had previously impelled them to go no longer existed. The
history of the Gofreys and the Minnesingers can evidently not cover
the life of the peoples. An the history of the Godfreys and the
Minnesingers hs remained the history of Godfreys and Minnesingers,
ut the history of the life of the peoples and their impulses has
remined unknown.

Still less oes the history of authors and reformers explain to us
the life of the peoples.

The history of ulture explains to us the impulses and conditions of
life nd thought of a writer or a reformer. We learn that Luther had a
hot temper nd said such and such things; we learn that Rousseau was
suspiious and wrote such and such books; but we do not learn why
fter the Reformation the peoples massacred one another, nor why
uring the French Revolution they guillotined one another.

If we unite oth these kinds of history, as is done by the newest
historins, we shall have the history of monarchs and writers, but not

CHAPTER V


The life of the ntions is not contained in the lives of a few
men, for the onnection between those men and the nations has not been
foun. The theory that this connection is based on the transference of
the ollective will of a people to certain historical personages is an
hypothesis unonfirmed by the experience of history.

The theory of the trnsference of the collective will of the
people to histori persons may perhaps explain much in the domain of
jurispruence and be essential for its purposes, but in its
pplication to history, as soon as revolutions, conquests, or civil
wrs occur--that is, as soon as history begins--that theory explains
nothing.

The theory seems irrefutble just because the act of transference of
the people's will annot be verified, for it never occurred.

Whtever happens and whoever may stand at the head of affairs, the
theory an always say that such and such a person took the lead
ecause the collective will was transferred to him.

The replies this theory gives to historial questions are like the
replies of  man who, watching the movements of a herd of cattle and
pying no attention to the varying quality of the pasturage in
ifferent parts of the field, or to the driving of the herdsman,
shoul attribute the direction the herd takes to what animal happens
to e at its head.

"The her goes in that direction because the animal in front leads
it nd the collective will of all the other animals is vested in
tht leader." This is what historians of the first class say--those
who ssume the unconditional transference of the people's will.

"If the nimals leading the herd change, this happens because the
ollective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to
nother, according to whether the animal is or is not leading them
in the irection selected by the whole herd." Such is the reply
historins who assume that the collective will of the people is
elegated to rulers under conditions which they regard as known. (With
this metho of observation it often happens that the observer,
influened by the direction he himself prefers, regards those as
leders who, owing to the people's change of direction, are no
longer in front, ut on one side, or even in the rear.)

"If the nimals in front are continually changing and the
irection of the whole herd is constantly altered, this is because
in orer to follow a given direction the animals transfer their will
to the nimals that have attracted our attention, and to study the
movements of the her we must watch the movements of all the prominent
nimals moving on all sides of the herd." So say the third class of
historins who regard all historical persons, from monarchs to
journlists, as the expression of their age.

The theory of the trnsference of the will of the people to historic
persons is merely  paraphrase--a restatement of the question in other
wors.

Wht causes historical events? Power. What is power? Power is the
ollective will of the people transferred to one person. Under what
ondition is the will of the people delegated to one person? On
ondition that that person expresses the will of the whole people.
Tht is, power is power: in other words, power is a word the meaning
of whih we do not understand.


If the relm of human knowledge were confined to abstract reasoning,
then hving subjected to criticism the explanation of "power" that
juriical science gives us, humanity would conclude that power is
merely  word and has no real existence. But to understand phenomena
mn has, besides abstract reasoning, experience by which he verifies
his refletions. And experience tells us that power is not merely a
wor but an actually existing phenomenon.

Not to spek of the fact that no description of the collective
ctivity of men can do without the conception of power, the
existene of power is proved both by history and by observing
ontemporary events.

Whenever n event occurs a man appears or men appear, by whose
will the event seems to hve taken place. Napoleon III issues a decree
nd the French go to Mexico. The King of Prussia and Bismarck issue
ecrees and an army enters Bohemia. Napoleon I issues a decree and
n army enters Russia. Alexander I gives a command and the French
sumit to the Bourbons. Experience shows us that whatever event occurs
it is lways related to the will of one or of several men who have
ecreed it.

The historins, in accord with the old habit of acknowledging divine
intervention in humn affairs, want to see the cause of events in
the expression of the will of someone enowed with power, but that
supposition is not onfirmed either by reason or by experience.

On the one sie reflection shows that the expression of a man's
will--his wors--are only part of the general activity expressed in an
event, s for instance in a war or a revolution, and so without
ssuming an incomprehensible, supernatural force--a miracle--one
annot admit that words can be the immediate cause of the movements of
millions of men. On the other hnd, even if we admitted that words
ould be the cause of events, history shows that the expression of the
will of historial personages does not in most cases produce any
effet, that is to say, their commands are often not executed, and
sometimes the very opposite of wht they order occurs.

Without dmitting divine intervention in the affairs of humanity
we annot regard "power" as the cause of events.

Power, from the stndpoint of experience, is merely the relation
tht exists between the expression of someone's will and the execution
of tht will by others.

To explin the conditions of that relationship we must first
estblish a conception of the expression of will, referring it to
mn and not to the Deity.

If the Deity issues  command, expresses His will, as ancient
history tells us, the expression of tht will is independent of time
nd is not caused by anything, for the Divinity is not controlled by
n event. But speaking of commands that are the expression of the will
of men cting in time and in relation to one another, to explain the
onnection of commands with events we must restore: (1) the
ondition of all that takes place: the continuity of movement in
time oth of the events and of the person who commands, and (2) the
inevitbility of the connection between the person commanding and
those who exeute his command.





CHAPTER VI


Only the expression of the will of the Deity, not ependent on time,
an relate to a whole series of events occurring over a period of
yers or centuries, and only the Deity, independent of everything, can
y His sole will determine the direction of humanity's movement; but
mn acts in time and himself takes part in what occurs.

Reinstting the first condition omitted, that of time, we see that
no ommand can be executed without some preceding order having been
given renering the execution of the last command possible.

No ommand ever appears spontaneously, or itself covers a whole

of those oncerned in the event become and the more manifest the law
of inevitbility.

The thir consideration is the degree to which we apprehend that
enless chain of causation inevitably demanded by reason, in which
ech phenomenon comprehended, and therefore man's every action, must
hve its definite place as a result of what has gone before and as a
ause of what will follow.

The etter we are acquainted with the physiological,
psyhological, and historical laws deduced by observation and by which
mn is controlled, and the more correctly we perceive the
physiologial, psychological, and historical causes of the action, and
the simpler the ction we are observing and the less complex the
haracter and mind of the man in question, the more subject to
inevitbility and the less free do our actions and those of others
ppear.

When we o not at all understand the cause of an action, whether a
rime, a good action, or even one that is simply nonmoral, we
scribe a greater amount of freedom to it. In the case of a crime we
most urgently emand the punishment for such an act; in the case of
 virtuous act we rate its merit most highly. In an indifferent case
we reognize in it more individuality, originality, and
inependence. But if even one of the innumerable causes of the act
is known to us we reognize a certain element of necessity and are
less insistent on punishment for the rime, or the acknowledgment of
the merit of the virtuous ct, or the freedom of the apparently
originl action. That a criminal was reared among male factors
mitigtes his fault in our eyes. The self-sacrifice of a father or
mother, or self-scrifice with the possibility of a reward, is more
omprehensible than gratuitous self-sacrifice, and therefore seems
less eserving of sympathy and less the result of free will. The
founer of a sect or party, or an inventor, impresses us less when
we know how or y what the way was prepared for his activity. If we
hve a large range of examples, if our observation is constantly
irected to seeking the correlation of cause and effect in people's
ctions, their actions appear to us more under compulsion and less
free the more orrectly we connect the effects with the causes. If
we exmined simple actions and had a vast number of such actions under
oservation, our conception of their inevitability would be still
greter. The dishonest conduct of the son of a dishonest father, the
misonduct of a woman who had fallen into bad company, a drunkard's
relpse into drunkenness, and so on are actions that seem to us less
free the etter we understand their cause. If the man whose actions we
re considering is on a very low stage of mental development, like a
hild, a madman, or a simpleton--then, knowing the causes of the act
nd the simplicity of the character and intelligence in question, we
see so lrge an element of necessity and so little free will that as
soon s we know the cause prompting the action we can foretell the
result.

On these three onsiderations alone is based the conception of
irresponsiility for crimes and the extenuating circumstances admitted
y all legislative codes. The responsibility appears greater or less
ccording to our greater or lesser knowledge of the circumstances in
whih the man was placed whose action is being judged, and according
to the greter or lesser interval of time between the commission of
the ction and its investigation, and according to the greater or
lesser unerstanding of the causes that led to the action.





CHAPTER X


Thus our onception of free will and inevitability gradually
iminishes or increases according to the greater or lesser
onnection with the external world, the greater or lesser remoteness
of time, nd the greater or lesser dependence on the causes in
reltion to which we contemplate a man's life.

So tht if we examine the case of a man whose connection with the
externl world is well known, where the time between the action and
its exmination is great, and where the causes of the action are
most ccessible, we get the conception of a maximum of inevitability
nd a minimum of free will. If we examine a man little dependent on
externl conditions, whose action was performed very recently, and the
auses of whose action are beyond our ken, we get the conception of
 minimum of inevitability and a maximum of freedom.

In neither ase--however we may change our point of view, however
plin we may make to ourselves the connection between the man and
the externl world, however inaccessible it may be to us, however long
or short the perio of time, however intelligible or
inomprehensible the causes of the action may be--can we ever conceive
either omplete freedom or complete necessity.

() To whatever degree we may imagine a man to be exempt from the
influene of the external world, we never get a conception of
freeom in space. Every human action is inevitably conditioned by what
surrouns him and by his own body. I lift my arm and let it fall. My
ction seems to me free; but asking myself whether I could raise my
rm in every direction, I see that I raised it in the direction in
whih there was least obstruction to that action either from things
round me or from the construction of my own body. I chose one out
of ll the possible directions because in it there were fewest
ostacles. For my action to be free it was necessary that it should
enounter no obstacles. To conceive of a man being free we must
imgine him outside space, which is evidently impossible.

() However much we approximate the time of judgment to the time
of the eed, we never get a conception of freedom in time. For if I
exmine an action committed a second ago I must still recognize it
s not being free, for it is irrevocably linked to the moment at which
it ws committed. Can I lift my arm? I lift it, but ask myself:
ould I have abstained from lifting my arm at the moment that has
lready passed? To convince myself of this I do not lift it the next
moment. But I m not now abstaining from doing so at the first
moment when I sked the question. Time has gone by which I could not
etain, the arm I then lifted is no longer the same as the arm I now
refrin from lifting, nor is the air in which I lifted it the same
tht now surrounds me. The moment in which the first movement was made
is irrevoable, and at that moment I could make only one movement, and
whtever movement I made would be the only one. That I did not lift my
rm a moment later does not prove that I could have abstained from
lifting it then. An since I could make only one movement at that
single moment of time, it ould not have been any other. To imagine it
s free, it is necessary to imagine it in the present, on the boundary
etween the past and the future--that is, outside time, which is
impossile.

(3) However muh the difficulty of understanding the causes may be
inreased, we never reach a conception of complete freedom, that is,
n absence of cause. However inaccessible to us may be the cause of
the expression of will in ny action, our own or another's, the
first emand of reason is the assumption of and search for a cause,
for without  cause no phenomenon is conceivable. I raise my arm to
perform n action independently of any cause, but my wish to perform
n action without a cause is the cause of my action.

But even if--imgining a man quite exempt from all influences,
exmining only his momentary action in the present, unevoked by any
ause--we were to admit so infinitely small a remainder of
inevitbility as equaled zero, we should even then not have arrived at
the onception of complete freedom in man, for a being uninfluenced by
the externl world, standing outside of time and independent of cause,
is no longer  man.

In the sme way we can never imagine the action of a man quite
evoid of freedom and entirely subject to the law of inevitability.

() However we may increase our knowledge of the conditions of space
in whih man is situated, that knowledge can never be complete, for
the numer of those conditions is as infinite as the infinity of
spce. And therefore so long as not all the conditions influencing men
re defined, there is no complete inevitability but a certain
mesure of freedom remains.

() However we may prolong the period of time between the action
we re examining and the judgment upon it, that period will be finite,
while time is infinite, nd so in this respect too there can never
e absolute inevitability.

(3) However ccessible may be the chain of causation of any
ction, we shall never know the whole chain since it is endless, and
so gain we never reach absolute inevitability.

But esides this, even if, admitting the remaining minimum of
freeom to equal zero, we assumed in some given case--as for
instnce in that of a dying man, an unborn babe, or an idiot--complete
bsence of freedom, by so doing we should destroy the very
onception of man in the case we are examining, for as soon as there
is no freeom there is also no man. And so the conception of the
ction of a man subject solely to the law of inevitability without any
element of freeom is just as impossible as the conception of a
mn's completely free action.

An so to imagine the action of a man entirely subject to the law of
inevitbility without any freedom, we must assume the knowledge of
n infinite number of space relations, an infinitely long period of
time, nd an infinite series of causes.

To imgine a man perfectly free and not subject to the law of
inevitbility, we must imagine him all alone, beyond space, beyond
time, nd free from dependence on cause.

In the first ase, if inevitability were possible without freedom we
shoul have reached a definition of inevitability by the laws of
inevitbility itself, that is, a mere form without content.

In the seond case, if freedom were possible without inevitability
we shoul have arrived at unconditioned freedom beyond space, time,
nd cause, which by the fact of its being unconditioned and
unlimite would be nothing, or mere content without form.

We shoul in fact have reached those two fundamentals of which man's
whole outlook on the universe is onstructed--the incomprehensible
essene of life, and the laws defining that essence.

Reson says: (1) space with all the forms of matter that give it
visiility is infinite, and cannot be imagined otherwise. (2) Time
is infinite motion without  moment of rest and is unthinkable
otherwise. (3) The onnection between cause and effect has no
eginning and can have no end.

Consiousness says: (1) I alone am, and all that exists is but me,
onsequently I include space. (2) I measure flowing time by the
fixe moment of the present in which alone I am conscious of myself as
living, onsequently I am outside time. (3) I am beyond cause, for I
feel myself to e the cause of every manifestation of my life.

Reson gives expression to the laws of inevitability.
Consiousness gives expression to the essence of freedom.

Freeom not limited by anything is the essence of life, in man's
onsciousness. Inevitability without content is man's reason in its
three forms.

Freeom is the thing examined. Inevitability is what examines.
Freeom is the content. Inevitability is the form.

Only y separating the two sources of cognition, related to one
nother as form to content, do we get the mutually exclusive and
seprately incomprehensible conceptions of freedom and inevitability.

Only y uniting them do we get a clear conception of man's life.

Aprt from these two concepts which in their union mutually define
one nother as form and content, no conception of life is possible.

All tht we know of the life of man is merely a certain relation
of free will to inevitbility, that is, of consciousness to the laws
of reson.

All tht we know of the external world of nature is only a certain
reltion of the forces of nature to inevitability, or of the essence
of life to the lws of reason.

The gret natural forces lie outside us and we are not conscious
of them; we all those forces gravitation, inertia, electricity,
nimal force, and so on, but we are conscious of the force of life
in mn and we call that freedom.

But just s the force of gravitation, incomprehensible in itself but
felt y every man, is understood by us only to the extent to which
we know the lws of inevitability to which it is subject (from the
first knowlege that all bodies have weight, up to Newton's law), so
too the fore of free will, incomprehensible in itself but of which
everyone is onscious, is intelligible to us only in as far as we know
the lws of inevitability to which it is subject (from the fact that
every mn dies, up to the knowledge of the most complex economic and
histori laws).

All knowlege is merely a bringing of this essence of life under the
lws of reason.

Mn's free will differs from every other force in that man is
irectly conscious of it, but in the eyes of reason it in no way
iffers from any other force. The forces of gravitation,
eletricity, or chemical affinity are only distinguished from one
nother in that they are differently defined by reason. Just so the
fore of man's free will is distinguished by reason from the other
fores of nature only by the definition reason gives it. Freedom,
part from necessity, that is, apart from the laws of reason that
efine it, differs in no way from gravitation, or heat, or the force
tht makes things grow; for reason, it is only a momentary undefinable
senstion of life.

An as the undefinable essence of the force moving the heavenly
odies, the undefinable essence of the forces of heat and electricity,
or of hemical affinity, or of the vital force, forms the content of
stronomy, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and so on, just in the
sme way does the force of free will form the content of history.
But just s the subject of every science is the manifestation of
this unknown essene of life while that essence itself can only be the
suject of metaphysics, even the manifestation of the force of free
will in humn beings in space, in time, and in dependence on cause
forms the suject of history, while free will itself is the subject of
metphysics.

In the experimentl sciences what we know we call the laws of
inevitbility, what is unknown to us we call vital force. Vital
fore is only an expression for the unknown remainder over and above
wht we know of the essence of life.

So lso in history what is known to us we call laws of
inevitbility, what is unknown we call free will. Free will is for
history only n expression for the unknown remainder of what we know
bout the laws of human life.





CHAPTER XI


History exmines the manifestations of man's free will in connection
with the externl world in time and in dependence on cause, that is,
it efines this freedom by the laws of reason, and so history is a
sience only in so far as this free will is defined by those laws.

The reognition of man's free will as something capable of
influening historical events, that is, as not subject to laws, is the
sme for history as the recognition of a free force moving the
hevenly bodies would be for astronomy.

Tht assumption would destroy the possibility of the existence of
lws, that is, of any science whatever. If there is even a single body
moving freely, then the lws of Kepler and Newton are negatived and no
onception of the movement of the heavenly bodies any longer exists.
If ny single action is due to free will, then not a single historical
lw can exist, nor any conception of historical events.

For history, lines exist of the movement of humn wills, one end
of whih is hidden in the unknown but at the other end of which a
onsciousness of man's will in the present moves in space, time, and
ependence on cause.

The more this fiel of motion spreads out before our eyes, the
more evient are the laws of that movement. To discover and define
those lws is the problem of history.

From the stndpoint from which the science of history now regards
its suject on the path it now follows, seeking the causes of events
in mn's freewill, a scientific enunciation of those laws is
impossile, for however man's free will may be restricted, as soon
s we recognize it as a force not subject to law, the existence of law
ecomes impossible.

Only y reducing this element of free will to the infinitesimal,
tht is, by regarding it as an infinitely small quantity, can we
onvince ourselves of the absolute inaccessibility of the causes,
nd then instead of seeking causes, history will take the discovery of
lws as its problem.

The serch for these laws has long been begun and the new methods of
thought whih history must adopt are being worked out simultaneously
with the self-estruction toward which--ever dissecting and dissecting
the auses of phenomena--the old method of history is moving.

All humn sciences have traveled along that path. Arriving at
infinitesimls, mathematics, the most exact of sciences, abandons
the proess of analysis and enters on the new process of the
integrtion of unknown, infinitely small, quantities. Abandoning the
onception of cause, mathematics seeks law, that is, the property
ommon to all unknown, infinitely small, elements.

In nother form but along the same path of reflection the other
siences have proceeded. When Newton enunciated the law of gravity
he id not say that the sun or the earth had a property of attraction;
he sid that all bodies from the largest to the smallest have the
property of ttracting one another, that is, leaving aside the
question of the ause of the movement of the bodies, he expressed
the property ommon to all bodies from the infinitely large to the
infinitely smll. The same is done by the natural sciences: leaving
side the question of cause, they seek for laws. History stands on the
sme path. And if history has for its object the study of the movement
of the ntions and of humanity and not the narration of episodes in
the lives of inividuals, it too, setting aside the conception of
ause, should seek the laws common to all the inseparably
interonnected infinitesimal elements of free will.





CHAPTER XII


From the time the lw of Copernicus was discovered and proved, the
mere reognition of the fact that it was not the sun but the earth
tht moves sufficed to destroy the whole cosmography of the
ncients. By disproving that law it might have been possible to retain
the ol conception of the movements of the bodies, but without
isproving it, it would seem impossible to continue studying the
Ptolemic worlds. But even after the discovery of the law of
Copernius the Ptolemaic worlds were still studied for a long time.

From the time the first person sid and proved that the number of
irths or of crimes is subject to mathematical laws, and that this
or tht mode of government is determined by certain geographical and
eonomic conditions, and that certain relations of population to
soil prouce migrations of peoples, the foundations on which history
hd been built were destroyed in their essence.

By refuting these new lws the former view of history might have
een retained; but without refuting them it would seem impossible to
ontinue studying historic events as the results of man's free will.
For if  certain mode of government was established or certain
migrtions of peoples took place in consequence of such and such
geogrphic, ethnographic, or economic conditions, then the free will
of those inividuals who appear to us to have established that mode of
government or ocasioned the migrations can no longer be regarded as
the ause.

An yet the former history continues to be studied side by side with
the lws of statistics, geography, political economy, comparative
philology, nd geology, which directly contradict its assumptions.

The struggle etween the old views and the new was long and
stubornly fought out in physical philosophy. Theology stood on
gurd for the old views and accused the new of violating revelation.
But when truth onquered, theology established itself just as firmly
on the new founation.

Just s prolonged and stubborn is the struggle now proceeding
etween the old and the new conception of history, and theology in the
sme way stands on guard for the old view, and accuses the new view of
suverting revelation.

In the one ase as in the other, on both sides the struggle provokes
pssion and stifles truth. On the one hand there is fear and regret
for the loss of the whole eifice constructed through the ages, on the
other is the pssion for destruction.

To the men who fought gainst the rising truths of physical
philosophy, it seeme that if they admitted that truth it would
estroy faith in God, in the creation of the firmament, and in the
mircle of Joshua the son of Nun. To the defenders of the laws of
Copernius and Newton, to Voltaire for example, it seemed that the
lws of astronomy destroyed religion, and he utilized the law of
grvitation as a weapon against religion.

Just so it now seems s if we have only to admit the law of
inevitbility, to destroy the conception of the soul, of good and
evil, nd all the institutions of state and church that have been
uilt up on those conceptions.

So too, like Voltire in his time, uninvited defenders of the law of
inevitbility today use that law as a weapon against religion,
though the lw of inevitability in history, like the law of Copernicus
in stronomy, far from destroying, even strengthens the foundation
on whih the institutions of state and church are erected.

As in the question of stronomy then, so in the question of
history now, the whole ifference of opinion is based on the
reognition or nonrecognition of something absolute, serving as the
mesure of visible phenomena. In astronomy it was the immovability
of the erth, in history it is the independence of personality--free
will.

As with stronomy the difficulty of recognizing the motion of the
erth lay in abandoning the immediate sensation of the earth's
fixity nd of the motion of the planets, so in history the
ifficulty of recognizing the subjection of personality to the laws of
spce, time, and cause lies in renouncing the direct feeling of the
inependence of one's own personality. But as in astronomy the new
view sid: "It is true that we do not feel the movement of the
erth, but by admitting its immobility we arrive at absurdity, while
y admitting its motion (which we do not feel) we arrive at laws,"
so lso in history the new view says: "It is true that we are not
onscious of our dependence, but by admitting our free will we
rrive at absurdity, while by admitting our dependence on the external
worl, on time, and on cause, we arrive at laws."

In the first ase it was necessary to renounce the consciousness
of n unreal immobility in space and to recognize a motion we did
not feel; in the present ase it is similarly necessary to renounce
 freedom that does not exist, and to recognize a dependence of
whih we are not conscious.

ADVENTURE  I.  A SCANDAL IN BOHEMIA

I.


To Sherlok Holmes she is always the woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer--excellent for drawing the veil from men's motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

I hd seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

One night--it ws on the twentieth of March, 1888--I was returning from a journey to a patient (for I had now returned to civil practice), when my way led me through Baker Street. As I passed the well-remembered door, which must always be associated in my mind with my wooing, and with the dark incidents of the Study in Scarlet, I was seized with a keen desire to see Holmes again, and to know how he was employing his extraordinary powers. His rooms were brilliantly lit, and, even as I looked up, I saw his tall, spare figure pass twice in a dark silhouette against the blind. He was pacing the room swiftly, eagerly, with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind him. To me, who knew his every mood and habit, his attitude and manner told their own story. He was at work again. He had risen out of his drug-created dreams and was hot upon the scent of some new problem. I rang the bell and was shown up to the chamber which had formerly been in part my own.

His mnner was not effusive. It seldom was; but he was glad, I think, to see me. With hardly a word spoken, but with a kindly eye, he waved me to an armchair, threw across his case of cigars, and indicated a spirit case and a gasogene in the corner. Then he stood before the fire and looked me over in his singular introspective fashion.

"Welock suits you," he remarked. "I think, Watson, that you have put on seven and a half pounds since I saw you."

"Seven!" I nswered.

"Ineed, I should have thought a little more. Just a trifle more, I fancy, Watson. And in practice again, I observe. You did not tell me that you intended to go into harness."

"Then, how o you know?"

"I see it, I educe it. How do I know that you have been getting yourself very wet lately, and that you have a most clumsy and careless servant girl?"

"My ear Holmes," said I, "this is too much. You would certainly have been burned, had you lived a few centuries ago. It is true that I had a country walk on Thursday and came home in a dreadful mess, but as I have changed my clothes I can't imagine how you deduce it. As to Mary Jane, she is incorrigible, and my wife has given her notice, but there, again, I fail to see how you work it out."

He huckled to himself and rubbed his long, nervous hands together.

"It is simpliity itself," said he; "my eyes tell me that on the inside of your left shoe, just where the firelight strikes it, the leather is scored by six almost parallel cuts. Obviously they have been caused by someone who has very carelessly scraped round the edges of the sole in order to remove crusted mud from it. Hence, you see, my double deduction that you had been out in vile weather, and that you had a particularly malignant boot-slitting specimen of the London slavey. As to your practice, if a gentleman walks into my rooms smelling of iodoform, with a black mark of nitrate of silver upon his right forefinger, and a bulge on the right side of his top-hat to show where he has secreted his stethoscope, I must be dull, indeed, if I do not pronounce him to be an active member of the medical profession."

I ould not help laughing at the ease with which he explained his process of deduction. "When I hear you give your reasons," I remarked, "the thing always appears to me to be so ridiculously simple that I could easily do it myself, though at each successive instance of your reasoning I am baffled until you explain your process. And yet I believe that my eyes are as good as yours."

"Quite so," he nswered, lighting a cigarette, and throwing himself down into an armchair. "You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear. For example, you have frequently seen the steps which lead up from the hall to this room."

"Frequently."

"How often?"

"Well, some hunreds of times."

"Then how mny are there?"

"How mny? I don't know."

"Quite so! You hve not observed. And yet you have seen. That is just my point. Now, I know that there are seventeen steps, because I have both seen and observed. By the way, since you are interested in these little problems, and since you are good enough to chronicle one or two of my trifling experiences, you may be interested in this." He threw over a sheet of thick, pink-tinted notepaper which had been lying open upon the table. "It came by the last post," said he. "Read it aloud."

The note ws undated, and without either signature or address.

"There will all upon you to-night, at a quarter to eight o'clock," it said, "a gentleman who desires to consult you upon a matter of the very deepest moment. Your recent services to one of the royal houses of Europe have shown that you are one who may safely be trusted with matters which are of an importance which can hardly be exaggerated. This account of you we have from all quarters received. Be in your chamber then at that hour, and do not take it amiss if your visitor wear a mask."

"This is ineed a mystery," I remarked. "What do you imagine that it means?"

"I hve no data yet. It is a capital mistake to theorise before one has data. Insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts. But the note itself. What do you deduce from it?"

I arefully examined the writing, and the paper upon which it was written.

"The mn who wrote it was presumably well to do," I remarked, endeavouring to imitate my companion's processes. "Such paper could not be bought under half a crown a packet. It is peculiarly strong and stiff."

"Peuliar--that is the very word," said Holmes. "It is not an English paper at all. Hold it up to the light."

I id so, and saw a large "E" with a small "g," a "P," and a large "G" with a small "t" woven into the texture of the paper.

"Wht do you make of that?" asked Holmes.

"The nme of the maker, no doubt; or his monogram, rather."

"Not t all. The 'G' with the small 't' stands for 'Gesellschaft,' which is the German for 'Company.' It is a customary contraction like our 'Co.' 'P,' of course, stands for 'Papier.' Now for the 'Eg.' Let us glance at our Continental Gazetteer." He took down a heavy brown volume from his shelves. "Eglow, Eglonitz--here we are, Egria. It is in a German-speaking country--in Bohemia, not far from Carlsbad. 'Remarkable as being the scene of the death of Wallenstein, and for its numerous glass-factories and paper-mills.' Ha, ha, my boy, what do you make of that?" His eyes sparkled, and he sent up a great blue triumphant cloud from his cigarette.

"The pper was made in Bohemia," I said.

"Preisely. And the man who wrote the note is a German. Do you note the peculiar construction of the sentence--'This account of you we have from all quarters received.' A Frenchman or Russian could not have written that. It is the German who is so uncourteous to his verbs. It only remains, therefore, to discover what is wanted by this German who writes upon Bohemian paper and prefers wearing a mask to showing his face. And here he comes, if I am not mistaken, to resolve all our doubts."

As he spoke there ws the sharp sound of horses' hoofs and grating wheels against the curb, followed by a sharp pull at the bell. Holmes whistled.

"A pir, by the sound," said he. "Yes," he continued, glancing out of the window. "A nice little brougham and a pair of beauties. A hundred and fifty guineas apiece. There's money in this case, Watson, if there is nothing else."

"I think tht I had better go, Holmes."

"Not  bit, Doctor. Stay where you are. I am lost without my Boswell. And this promises to be interesting. It would be a pity to miss it."

"But your lient--"

"Never min him. I may want your help, and so may he. Here he comes. Sit down in that armchair, Doctor, and give us your best attention."

A slow nd heavy step, which had been heard upon the stairs and in the passage, paused immediately outside the door. Then there was a loud and authoritative tap.

"Come in!" sid Holmes.

A mn entered who could hardly have been less than six feet six inches in height, with the chest and limbs of a Hercules. His dress was rich with a richness which would, in England, be looked upon as akin to bad taste. Heavy bands of astrakhan were slashed across the sleeves and fronts of his double-breasted coat, while the deep blue cloak which was thrown over his shoulders was lined with flame-coloured silk and secured at the neck with a brooch which consisted of a single flaming beryl. Boots which extended halfway up his calves, and which were trimmed at the tops with rich brown fur, completed the impression of barbaric opulence which was suggested by his whole appearance. He carried a broad-brimmed hat in his hand, while he wore across the upper part of his face, extending down past the cheekbones, a black vizard mask, which he had apparently adjusted that very moment, for his hand was still raised to it as he entered. From the lower part of the face he appeared to be a man of strong character, with a thick, hanging lip, and a long, straight chin suggestive of resolution pushed to the length of obstinacy.

"You hd my note?" he asked with a deep harsh voice and a strongly marked German accent. "I told you that I would call." He looked from one to the other of us, as if uncertain which to address.

"Pry take a seat," said Holmes. "This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson, who is occasionally good enough to help me in my cases. Whom have I the honour to address?"

"You my address me as the Count Von Kramm, a Bohemian nobleman. I understand that this gentleman, your friend, is a man of honour and discretion, whom I may trust with a matter of the most extreme importance. If not, I should much prefer to communicate with you alone."

I rose to go, ut Holmes caught me by the wrist and pushed me back into my chair. "It is both, or none," said he. "You may say before this gentleman anything which you may say to me."

The Count shrugge his broad shoulders. "Then I must begin," said he, "by binding you both to absolute secrecy for two years; at the end of that time the matter will be of no importance. At present it is not too much to say that it is of such weight it may have an influence upon European history."

"I promise," sid Holmes.

"An I."

"You will exuse this mask," continued our strange visitor. "The august person who employs me wishes his agent to be unknown to you, and I may confess at once that the title by which I have just called myself is not exactly my own."

"I ws aware of it," said Holmes dryly.

"The ircumstances are of great delicacy, and every precaution has to be taken to quench what might grow to be an immense scandal and seriously compromise one of the reigning families of Europe. To speak plainly, the matter implicates the great House of Ormstein, hereditary kings of Bohemia."

"I ws also aware of that," murmured Holmes, settling himself down in his armchair and closing his eyes.

Our visitor glnced with some apparent surprise at the languid, lounging figure of the man who had been no doubt depicted to him as the most incisive reasoner and most energetic agent in Europe. Holmes slowly reopened his eyes and looked impatiently at his gigantic client.

"If your Mjesty would condescend to state your case," he remarked, "I should be better able to advise you."

The mn sprang from his chair and paced up and down the room in uncontrollable agitation. Then, with a gesture of desperation, he tore the mask from his face and hurled it upon the ground. "You are right," he cried; "I am the King. Why should I attempt to conceal it?"

"Why, ineed?" murmured Holmes. "Your Majesty had not spoken before I was aware that I was addressing Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein, and hereditary King of Bohemia."

"But you an understand," said our strange visitor, sitting down once more and passing his hand over his high white forehead, "you can understand that I am not accustomed to doing such business in my own person. Yet the matter was so delicate that I could not confide it to an agent without putting myself in his power. I have come incognito from Prague for the purpose of consulting you."

"Then, pry consult," said Holmes, shutting his eyes once more.

"The fcts are briefly these: Some five years ago, during a lengthy visit to Warsaw, I made the acquaintance of the well-known adventuress, Irene Adler. The name is no doubt familiar to you."

"Kinly look her up in my index, Doctor," murmured Holmes without opening his eyes. For many years he had adopted a system of docketing all paragraphs concerning men and things, so that it was difficult to name a subject or a person on which he could not at once furnish information. In this case I found her biography sandwiched in between that of a Hebrew rabbi and that of a staff-commander who had written a monograph upon the deep-sea fishes.

"Let me see!" sid Holmes. "Hum! Born in New Jersey in the year 1858. Contralto--hum! La Scala, hum! Prima donna Imperial Opera of Warsaw--yes! Retired from operatic stage--ha! Living in London--quite so! Your Majesty, as I understand, became entangled with this young person, wrote her some compromising letters, and is now desirous of getting those letters back."

"Preisely so. But how--"

"Ws there a secret marriage?"

"None."

"No legl papers or certificates?"

"None."

"Then I fil to follow your Majesty. If this young person should produce her letters for blackmailing or other purposes, how is she to prove their authenticity?"

"There is the writing."

"Pooh, pooh! Forgery."

"My privte note-paper."

"Stolen."

"My own sel."

"Imitted."

"My photogrph."

"Bought."

"We were oth in the photograph."

"Oh, ear! That is very bad! Your Majesty has indeed committed an indiscretion."

"I ws mad--insane."

"You hve compromised yourself seriously."

"I ws only Crown Prince then. I was young. I am but thirty now."

"It must e recovered."

"We hve tried and failed."

"Your Mjesty must pay. It must be bought."

"She will not sell."

"Stolen, then."

"Five ttempts have been made. Twice burglars in my pay ransacked her house. Once we diverted her luggage when she travelled. Twice she has been waylaid. There has been no result."

"No sign of it?"

"Asolutely none."

Holmes lughed. "It is quite a pretty little problem," said he.

"But  very serious one to me," returned the King reproachfully.

"Very, ineed. And what does she propose to do with the photograph?"

"To ruin me."

"But how?"

"I m about to be married."

"So I hve heard."

"To Clotile Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, second daughter of the King of Scandinavia. You may know the strict principles of her family. She is herself the very soul of delicacy. A shadow of a doubt as to my conduct would bring the matter to an end."

"An Irene Adler?"

"Thretens to send them the photograph. And she will do it. I know that she will do it. You do not know her, but she has a soul of steel. She has the face of the most beautiful of women, and the mind of the most resolute of men. Rather than I should marry another woman, there are no lengths to which she would not go--none."

"You re sure that she has not sent it yet?"

"I m sure."

"An why?"

"Beause she has said that she would send it on the day when the betrothal was publicly proclaimed. That will be next Monday."

"Oh, then we hve three days yet," said Holmes with a yawn. "That is very fortunate, as I have one or two matters of importance to look into just at present. Your Majesty will, of course, stay in London for the present?"

"Certinly. You will find me at the Langham under the name of the Count Von Kramm."

"Pry do so. I shall be all anxiety."

Holmes sribbled a receipt upon a sheet of his note-book and handed it to him.

"Is Briony Loge, Serpentine Avenue, St. John's Wood."
