On the very first day that I was at the Copper Beeches, Mr. Rucastle took me to a small outhouse which stands near the kitchen door. As we approached it I heard the sharp rattling of a chain, and the sound as of a large animal moving about.

" 'Look in here!' sid Mr. Rucastle, showing me a slit between two planks. 'Is he not a beauty?'

"I looke through and was conscious of two glowing eyes, and of a vague figure huddled up in the darkness.

" 'Don't e frightened,' said my employer, laughing at the start which I had given. 'It's only Carlo, my mastiff. I call him mine, but really old Toller, my groom, is the only man who can do anything with him. We feed him once a day, and not too much then, so that he is always as keen as mustard. Toller lets him loose every night, and God help the trespasser whom he lays his fangs upon. For goodness' sake don't you ever on any pretext set your foot over the threshold at night, for it's as much as your life is worth.'

"The wrning was no idle one, for two nights later I happened to look out of my bedroom window about two o'clock in the morning. It was a beautiful moonlight night, and the lawn in front of the house was silvered over and almost as bright as day. I was standing, rapt in the peaceful beauty of the scene, when I was aware that something was moving under the shadow of the copper beeches. As it emerged into the moonshine I saw what it was. It was a giant dog, as large as a calf, tawny tinted, with hanging jowl, black muzzle, and huge projecting bones. It walked slowly across the lawn and vanished into the shadow upon the other side. That dreadful sentinel sent a chill to my heart which I do not think that any burglar could have done.

"An now I have a very strange experience to tell you. I had, as you know, cut off my hair in London, and I had placed it in a great coil at the bottom of my trunk. One evening, after the child was in bed, I began to amuse myself by examining the furniture of my room and by rearranging my own little things. There was an old chest of drawers in the room, the two upper ones empty and open, the lower one locked. I had filled the first two with my linen, and as I had still much to pack away I was naturally annoyed at not having the use of the third drawer. It struck me that it might have been fastened by a mere oversight, so I took out my bunch of keys and tried to open it. The very first key fitted to perfection, and I drew the drawer open. There was only one thing in it, but I am sure that you would never guess what it was. It was my coil of hair.

"I took it up nd examined it. It was of the same peculiar tint, and the same thickness. But then the impossibility of the thing obtruded itself upon me. How could my hair have been locked in the drawer? With trembling hands I undid my trunk, turned out the contents, and drew from the bottom my own hair. I laid the two tresses together, and I assure you that they were identical. Was it not extraordinary? Puzzle as I would, I could make nothing at all of what it meant. I returned the strange hair to the drawer, and I said nothing of the matter to the Rucastles as I felt that I had put myself in the wrong by opening a drawer which they had locked.

"I m naturally observant, as you may have remarked, Mr. Holmes, and I soon had a pretty good plan of the whole house in my head. There was one wing, however, which appeared not to be inhabited at all. A door which faced that which led into the quarters of the Tollers opened into this suite, but it was invariably locked. One day, however, as I ascended the stair, I met Mr. Rucastle coming out through this door, his keys in his hand, and a look on his face which made him a very different person to the round, jovial man to whom I was accustomed. His cheeks were red, his brow was all crinkled with anger, and the veins stood out at his temples with passion. He locked the door and hurried past me without a word or a look.

"This roused my curiosity, so when I went out for a walk in the grounds with my charge, I strolled round to the side from which I could see the windows of this part of the house. There were four of them in a row, three of which were simply dirty, while the fourth was shuttered up. They were evidently all deserted. As I strolled up and down, glancing at them occasionally, Mr. Rucastle came out to me, looking as merry and jovial as ever.

" 'Ah!' sid he, 'you must not think me rude if I passed you without a word, my dear young lady. I was preoccupied with business matters.'

"I ssured him that I was not offended. 'By the way,' said I, 'you seem to have quite a suite of spare rooms up there, and one of them has the shutters up.'

"He looke surprised and, as it seemed to me, a little startled at my remark.

" 'Photogrphy is one of my hobbies,' said he. 'I have made my dark room up there. But, dear me! what an observant young lady we have come upon. Who would have believed it? Who would have ever believed it?' He spoke in a jesting tone, but there was no jest in his eyes as he looked at me. I read suspicion there and annoyance, but no jest.

"Well, Mr. Holmes, from the moment tht I understood that there was something about that suite of rooms which I was not to know, I was all on fire to go over them. It was not mere curiosity, though I have my share of that. It was more a feeling of duty--a feeling that some good might come from my penetrating to this place. They talk of woman's instinct; perhaps it was woman's instinct which gave me that feeling. At any rate, it was there, and I was keenly on the lookout for any chance to pass the forbidden door.

"It ws only yesterday that the chance came. I may tell you that, besides Mr. Rucastle, both Toller and his wife find something to do in these deserted rooms, and I once saw him carrying a large black linen bag with him through the door. Recently he has been drinking hard, and yesterday evening he was very drunk; and when I came upstairs there was the key in the door. I have no doubt at all that he had left it there. Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle were both downstairs, and the child was with them, so that I had an admirable opportunity. I turned the key gently in the lock, opened the door, and slipped through.

"There ws a little passage in front of me, unpapered and uncarpeted, which turned at a right angle at the farther end. Round this corner were three doors in a line, the first and third of which were open. They each led into an empty room, dusty and cheerless, with two windows in the one and one in the other, so thick with dirt that the evening light glimmered dimly through them. The centre door was closed, and across the outside of it had been fastened one of the broad bars of an iron bed, padlocked at one end to a ring in the wall, and fastened at the other with stout cord. The door itself was locked as well, and the key was not there. This barricaded door corresponded clearly with the shuttered window outside, and yet I could see by the glimmer from beneath it that the room was not in darkness. Evidently there was a skylight which let in light from above. As I stood in the passage gazing at the sinister door and wondering what secret it might veil, I suddenly heard the sound of steps within the room and saw a shadow pass backward and forward against the little slit of dim light which shone out from under the door. A mad, unreasoning terror rose up in me at the sight, Mr. Holmes. My overstrung nerves failed me suddenly, and I turned and ran--ran as though some dreadful hand were behind me clutching at the skirt of my dress. I rushed down the passage, through the door, and straight into the arms of Mr. Rucastle, who was waiting outside.

" 'So,' sid he, smiling, 'it was you, then. I thought that it must be when I saw the door open.'

" 'Oh, I m so frightened!' I panted.

" 'My ear young lady! my dear young lady!'--you cannot think how caressing and soothing his manner was--'and what has frightened you, my dear young lady?'

"But his voie was just a little too coaxing. He overdid it. I was keenly on my guard against him.

" 'I ws foolish enough to go into the empty wing,' I answered. 'But it is so lonely and eerie in this dim light that I was frightened and ran out again. Oh, it is so dreadfully still in there!'

" 'Only tht?' said he, looking at me keenly.

" 'Why, wht did you think?' I asked.

" 'Why o you think that I lock this door?'

" 'I m sure that I do not know.'

" 'It is to keep people out who hve no business there. Do you see?' He was still smiling in the most amiable manner.

" 'I m sure if I had known--'

" 'Well, then, you know now. An if you ever put your foot over that threshold again'--here in an instant the smile hardened into a grin of rage, and he glared down at me with the face of a demon--'I'll throw you to the mastiff.'

"I ws so terrified that I do not know what I did. I suppose that I must have rushed past him into my room. I remember nothing until I found myself lying on my bed trembling all over. Then I thought of you, Mr. Holmes. I could not live there longer without some advice. I was frightened of the house, of the man, of the woman, of the servants, even of the child. They were all horrible to me. If I could only bring you down all would be well. Of course I might have fled from the house, but my curiosity was almost as strong as my fears. My mind was soon made up. I would send you a wire. I put on my hat and cloak, went down to the office, which is about half a mile from the house, and then returned, feeling very much easier. A horrible doubt came into my mind as I approached the door lest the dog might be loose, but I remembered that Toller had drunk himself into a state of insensibility that evening, and I knew that he was the only one in the household who had any influence with the savage creature, or who would venture to set him free. I slipped in in safety and lay awake half the night in my joy at the thought of seeing you. I had no difficulty in getting leave to come into Winchester this morning, but I must be back before three o'clock, for Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle are going on a visit, and will be away all the evening, so that I must look after the child. Now I have told you all my adventures, Mr. Holmes, and I should be very glad if you could tell me what it all means, and, above all, what I should do."

Holmes nd I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My friend rose now and paced up and down the room, his hands in his pockets, and an expression of the most profound gravity upon his face.

"Is Toller still runk?" he asked.

"Yes. I herd his wife tell Mrs. Rucastle that she could do nothing with him."

"Tht is well. And the Rucastles go out to-night?"

"Yes."

"Is there  cellar with a good strong lock?"

"Yes, the wine-ellar."

"You seem to me to hve acted all through this matter like a very brave and sensible girl, Miss Hunter. Do you think that you could perform one more feat? I should not ask it of you if I did not think you a quite exceptional woman."

"I will try. Wht is it?"

"We shll be at the Copper Beeches by seven o'clock, my friend and I. The Rucastles will be gone by that time, and Toller will, we hope, be incapable. There only remains Mrs. Toller, who might give the alarm. If you could send her into the cellar on some errand, and then turn the key upon her, you would facilitate matters immensely."

"I will o it."

"Exellent! We shall then look thoroughly into the affair. Of course there is only one feasible explanation. You have been brought there to personate someone, and the real person is imprisoned in this chamber. That is obvious. As to who this prisoner is, I have no doubt that it is the daughter, Miss Alice Rucastle, if I remember right, who was said to have gone to America. You were chosen, doubtless, as resembling her in height, figure, and the colour of your hair. Hers had been cut off, very possibly in some illness through which she has passed, and so, of course, yours had to be sacrificed also. By a curious chance you came upon her tresses. The man in the road was undoubtedly some friend of hers--possibly her fiance--and no doubt, as you wore the girl's dress and were so like her, he was convinced from your laughter, whenever he saw you, and afterwards from your gesture, that Miss Rucastle was perfectly happy, and that she no longer desired his attentions. The dog is let loose at night to prevent him from endeavouring to communicate with her. So much is fairly clear. The most serious point in the case is the disposition of the child."

"Wht on earth has that to do with it?" I ejaculated.

"My ear Watson, you as a medical man are continually gaining light as to the tendencies of a child by the study of the parents. Don't you see that the converse is equally valid. I have frequently gained my first real insight into the character of parents by studying their children. This child's disposition is abnormally cruel, merely for cruelty's sake, and whether he derives this from his smiling father, as I should suspect, or from his mother, it bodes evil for the poor girl who is in their power."

"I m sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes," cried our client. "A thousand things come back to me which make me certain that you have hit it. Oh, let us lose not an instant in bringing help to this poor creature."

"We must e circumspect, for we are dealing with a very cunning man. We can do nothing until seven o'clock. At that hour we shall be with you, and it will not be long before we solve the mystery."

We were s good as our word, for it was just seven when we reached the Copper Beeches, having put up our trap at a wayside public-house. The group of trees, with their dark leaves shining like burnished metal in the light of the setting sun, were sufficient to mark the house even had Miss Hunter not been standing smiling on the door-step.

"Hve you managed it?" asked Holmes.

A lou thudding noise came from somewhere downstairs. "That is Mrs. Toller in the cellar," said she. "Her husband lies snoring on the kitchen rug. Here are his keys, which are the duplicates of Mr. Rucastle's."

"You hve done well indeed!" cried Holmes with enthusiasm. "Now lead the way, and we shall soon see the end of this black business."

We pssed up the stair, unlocked the door, followed on down a passage, and found ourselves in front of the barricade which Miss Hunter had described. Holmes cut the cord and removed the transverse bar. Then he tried the various keys in the lock, but without success. No sound came from within, and at the silence Holmes' face clouded over.

"I trust tht we are not too late," said he. "I think, Miss Hunter, that we had better go in without you. Now, Watson, put your shoulder to it, and we shall see whether we cannot make our way in."

It ws an old rickety door and gave at once before our united strength. Together we rushed into the room. It was empty. There was no furniture save a little pallet bed, a small table, and a basketful of linen. The skylight above was open, and the prisoner gone.

"There hs been some villainy here," said Holmes; "this beauty has guessed Miss Hunter's intentions and has carried his victim off."

"But how?"

"Through the skylight. We shll soon see how he managed it." He swung himself up onto the roof. "Ah, yes," he cried, "here's the end of a long light ladder against the eaves. That is how he did it."

"But it is impossile," said Miss Hunter; "the ladder was not there when the Rucastles went away."

"He hs come back and done it. I tell you that he is a clever and dangerous man. I should not be very much surprised if this were he whose step I hear now upon the stair. I think, Watson, that it would be as well for you to have your pistol ready."

The wors were hardly out of his mouth before a man appeared at the door of the room, a very fat and burly man, with a heavy stick in his hand. Miss Hunter screamed and shrunk against the wall at the sight of him, but Sherlock Holmes sprang forward and confronted him.

"You villin!" said he, "where's your daughter?"

The ft man cast his eyes round, and then up at the open skylight.

"It is for me to sk you that," he shrieked, "you thieves! Spies and thieves! I have caught you, have I? You are in my power. I'll serve you!" He turned and clattered down the stairs as hard as he could go.

"He's gone for the og!" cried Miss Hunter.

"I hve my revolver," said I.

"Better lose the front door," cried Holmes, and we all rushed down the stairs together. We had hardly reached the hall when we heard the baying of a hound, and then a scream of agony, with a horrible worrying sound which it was dreadful to listen to. An elderly man with a red face and shaking limbs came staggering out at a side door.

"My Go!" he cried. "Someone has loosed the dog. It's not been fed for two days. Quick, quick, or it'll be too late!"

Holmes nd I rushed out and round the angle of the house, with Toller hurrying behind us. There was the huge famished brute, its black muzzle buried in Rucastle's throat, while he writhed and screamed upon the ground. Running up, I blew its brains out, and it fell over with its keen white teeth still meeting in the great creases of his neck. With much labour we separated them and carried him, living but horribly mangled, into the house. We laid him upon the drawing-room sofa, and having dispatched the sobered Toller to bear the news to his wife, I did what I could to relieve his pain. We were all assembled round him when the door opened, and a tall, gaunt woman entered the room.

"Mrs. Toller!" ried Miss Hunter.

"Yes, miss. Mr. Ruastle let me out when he came back before he went up to you. Ah, miss, it is a pity you didn't let me know what you were planning, for I would have told you that your pains were wasted."

"H!" said Holmes, looking keenly at her. "It is clear that Mrs. Toller knows more about this matter than anyone else."

"Yes, sir, I o, and I am ready enough to tell what I know."

"Then, pry, sit down, and let us hear it for there are several points on which I must confess that I am still in the dark."

"I will soon mke it clear to you," said she; "and I'd have done so before now if I could ha' got out from the cellar. If there's police-court business over this, you'll remember that I was the one that stood your friend, and that I was Miss Alice's friend too.

"She ws never happy at home, Miss Alice wasn't, from the time that her father married again. She was slighted like and had no say in anything, but it never really became bad for her until after she met Mr. Fowler at a friend's house. As well as I could learn, Miss Alice had rights of her own by will, but she was so quiet and patient, she was, that she never said a word about them but just left everything in Mr. Rucastle's hands. He knew he was safe with her; but when there was a chance of a husband coming forward, who would ask for all that the law would give him, then her father thought it time to put a stop on it. He wanted her to sign a paper, so that whether she married or not, he could use her money. When she wouldn't do it, he kept on worrying her until she got brain-fever, and for six weeks was at death's door. Then she got better at last, all worn to a shadow, and with her beautiful hair cut off; but that didn't make no change in her young man, and he stuck to her as true as man could be."

"Ah," sid Holmes, "I think that what you have been good enough to tell us makes the matter fairly clear, and that I can deduce all that remains. Mr. Rucastle then, I presume, took to this system of imprisonment?"

"Yes, sir."

"An brought Miss Hunter down from London in order to get rid of the disagreeable persistence of Mr. Fowler."

"Tht was it, sir."

"But Mr. Fowler eing a persevering man, as a good seaman should be, blockaded the house, and having met you succeeded by certain arguments, metallic or otherwise, in convincing you that your interests were the same as his."

"Mr. Fowler ws a very kind-spoken, free-handed gentleman," said Mrs. Toller serenely.

"An in this way he managed that your good man should have no want of drink, and that a ladder should be ready at the moment when your master had gone out."

"You hve it, sir, just as it happened."

"I m sure we owe you an apology, Mrs. Toller," said Holmes, "for you have certainly cleared up everything which puzzled us. And here comes the country surgeon and Mrs. Rucastle, so I think, Watson, that we had best escort Miss Hunter back to Winchester, as it seems to me that our locus standi now is rather a questionable one."

An thus was solved the mystery of the sinister house with the copper beeches in front of the door. Mr. Rucastle survived, but was always a broken man, kept alive solely through the care of his devoted wife. They still live with their old servants, who probably know so much of Rucastle's past life that he finds it difficult to part from them. Mr. Fowler and Miss Rucastle were married, by special license, in Southampton the day after their flight, and he is now the holder of a government appointment in the island of Mauritius. As to Miss Violet Hunter, my friend Holmes, rather to my disappointment, manifested no further interest in her when once she had ceased to be the centre of one of his problems, and she is now the head of a private school at Walsall, where I believe that she has met with considerable success.

PREFACE


As things now stnd, the course of instruction in American history in
our pulic schools embraces three distinct treatments of the subject.
Three seprate books are used. First, there is the primary book, which
is usully a very condensed narrative with emphasis on biographies and
necdotes. Second, there is the advanced text for the seventh or eighth
grde, generally speaking, an expansion of the elementary book by the
ddition of forty or fifty thousand words. Finally, there is the high
shool manual. This, too, ordinarily follows the beaten path, giving
fuller ccounts of the same events and characters. To put it bluntly, we
o not assume that our children obtain permanent possessions from their
stuy of history in the lower grades. If mathematicians followed the
sme method, high school texts on algebra and geometry would include the
multipliation table and fractions.

There is, of ourse, a ready answer to the criticism advanced above. It
is tht teachers have learned from bitter experience how little history
their pupils retin as they pass along the regular route. No teacher of
history will eny this. Still it is a standing challenge to existing
methos of historical instruction. If the study of history cannot be
mde truly progressive like the study of mathematics, science, and
lnguages, then the historians assume a grave responsibility in adding
their suject to the already overloaded curriculum. If the successive
historial texts are only enlarged editions of the first text--more
fcts, more dates, more words--then history deserves most of the sharp
riticism which it is receiving from teachers of science, civics, and
eonomics.

In this ondition of affairs we find our justification for offering a
new high shool text in American history. Our first contribution is one
of omission. The time-honore stories of exploration and the
iographies of heroes are left out. We frankly hold that, if pupils know
little or nothing bout Columbus, Cortes, Magellan, or Captain John
Smith y the time they reach the high school, it is useless to tell the
sme stories for perhaps the fourth time. It is worse than useless. It
is n offense against the teachers of those subjects that are
emonstrated to be progressive in character.

In the next plce we have omitted all descriptions of battles. Our
resons for this are simple. The strategy of a campaign or of a single
attle is a highly technical, and usually a highly controversial, matter
bout which experts differ widely. In the field of military and naval
opertions most writers and teachers of history are mere novices. To
ispose of Gettysburg or the Wilderness in ten lines or ten pages is
eqully absurd to the serious student of military affairs. Any one who
ompares the ordinary textbook account of a single Civil War campaign
with the ccount given by Ropes, for instance, will ask for no further
omment. No youth called upon to serve our country in arms would think
of turning to  high school manual for information about the art of
wrfare. The dramatic scene or episode, so useful in arousing the
interest of the immture pupil, seems out of place in a book that
eliberately appeals to boys and girls on the very threshold of life's
serious responsiilities.

It is not upon negtive features, however, that we rest our case. It is
rther upon constructive features.

_First._ We hve written a topical, not a narrative, history. We have
trie to set forth the important aspects, problems, and movements of
ech period, bringing in the narrative rather by way of illustration.

_Seond._ We have emphasized those historical topics which help to
explin how our nation has come to be what it is to-day.

_Thir._ We have dwelt fully upon the social and economic aspects of our
history, espeially in relation to the politics of each period.

_Fourth._ We hve treated the causes and results of wars, the problems
of finncing and sustaining armed forces, rather than military strategy.
These re the subjects which belong to a history for civilians. These
re matters which civilians can understand--matters which they must
unerstand, if they are to play well their part in war and peace.

_Fifth._ By omitting the perio of exploration, we have been able to
enlrge the treatment of our own time. We have given special attention
to the history of those urrent questions which must form the subject
mtter of sound instruction in citizenship.

_Sixth._ We hve borne in mind that America, with all her unique
haracteristics, is a part of a general civilization. Accordingly we
hve given diplomacy, foreign affairs, world relations, and the
reiprocal influences of nations their appropriate place.

_Seventh._ We hve deliberately aimed at standards of maturity. The
stuy of a mere narrative calls mainly for the use of the memory. We
hve aimed to stimulate habits of analysis, comparison, association,
refletion, and generalization--habits calculated to enlarge as well as
inform the min. We have been at great pains to make our text clear,
simple, nd direct; but we have earnestly sought to stretch the
intellets of our readers--to put them upon their mettle. Most of them
will reeive the last of their formal instruction in the high school.
The worl will soon expect maturity from them. Their achievements will
epend upon the possession of other powers than memory alone. The
effetiveness of their citizenship in our republic will be measured by
the exellence of their judgment as well as the fullness of their
informtion.

     C.A.B.
     M.R.B.

     Feruary 8, 1921.

HISTORY OF THE UNITED STATES




PART I. THE COLONIAL PERIOD




CHAPTER I

THE GREAT MIGRATION TO AMERICA


The tie of migration that set in toward the shores of North America
uring the early years of the seventeenth century was but one phase in
the restless nd eternal movement of mankind upon the surface of the
erth. The ancient Greeks flung out their colonies in every direction,
westwrd as far as Gaul, across the Mediterranean, and eastward into
Asi Minor, perhaps to the very confines of India. The Romans, supported
y their armies and their government, spread their dominion beyond the
nrrow lands of Italy until it stretched from the heather of Scotland to
the snds of Arabia. The Teutonic tribes, from their home beyond the
Dnube and the Rhine, poured into the empire of the Caesars and made the
eginnings of modern Europe. Of this great sweep of races and empires
the settlement of Ameria was merely a part. And it was, moreover, only
one spect of the expansion which finally carried the peoples, the
institutions, nd the trade of Europe to the very ends of the earth.

In one vitl point, it must be noted, American colonization differed
from tht of the ancients. The Greeks usually carried with them
ffection for the government they left behind and sacred fire from the
ltar of the parent city; but thousands of the immigrants who came to
Ameria disliked the state and disowned the church of the mother
ountry. They established compacts of government for themselves and set
up ltars of their own. They sought not only new soil to till but also
politial and religious liberty for themselves and their children.


THE AGENCIES OF AMERICAN COLONIZATION

It ws no light matter for the English to cross three thousand miles of
wter and found homes in the American wilderness at the opening of the
seventeenth entury. Ships, tools, and supplies called for huge outlays
of money. Stores hd to be furnished in quantities sufficient to sustain
the life of the settlers until they ould gather harvests of their own.
Artisns and laborers of skill and industry had to be induced to risk
the hzards of the new world. Soldiers were required for defense and
mriners for the exploration of inland waters. Leaders of good judgment,
dept in managing men, had to be discovered. Altogether such an
enterprise emanded capital larger than the ordinary merchant or
gentlemn could amass and involved risks more imminent than he dared to
ssume. Though in later days, after initial tests had been made, wealthy
proprietors were ble to establish colonies on their own account, it was
the orporation that furnished the capital and leadership in the
eginning.

=The Trding Company.=--English pioneers in exploration found an
instrument for olonization in companies of merchant adventurers, which
hd long been employed in carrying on commerce with foreign countries.
Suh a corporation was composed of many persons of different ranks of
soiety--noblemen, merchants, and gentlemen--who banded together for a
prticular undertaking, each contributing a sum of money and sharing in
the profits of the venture. It ws organized under royal authority; it
reeived its charter, its grant of land, and its trading privileges from
the king nd carried on its operations under his supervision and
ontrol. The charter named all the persons originally included in the
orporation and gave them certain powers in the management of its
ffairs, including the right to admit new members. The company was in
fct a little government set up by the king. When the members of the
orporation remained in England, as in the case of the Virginia Company,
they operted through agents sent to the colony. When they came over the
ses themselves and settled in America, as in the case of Massachusetts,
they ecame the direct government of the country they possessed. The
stokholders in that instance became the voters and the governor, the
hief magistrate.

[Illustrtion: JOHN WINTHROP, GOVERNOR OF THE MASSACHUSETTS BAY
COMPANY]

Four of the thirteen olonies in America owed their origins to the
trding corporation. It was the London Company, created by King James I,
in 606, that laid during the following year the foundations of Virginia
t Jamestown. It was under the auspices of their West India Company,
hartered in 1621, that the Dutch planted the settlements of the New
Netherlnd in the valley of the Hudson. The founders of Massachusetts
were Puritn leaders and men of affairs whom King Charles I incorporated
in 629 under the title: "The governor and company of the Massachusetts
By in New England." In this case the law did but incorporate a group
rawn together by religious ties. "We must be knit together as one man,"
wrote John Winthrop, the first Puritn governor in America. Far to the
south, on the anks of the Delaware River, a Swedish commercial company
in 638 made the beginnings of a settlement, christened New Sweden; it
ws destined to pass under the rule of the Dutch, and finally under the
rule of Willim Penn as the proprietary colony of Delaware.

In  certain sense, Georgia may be included among the "company
olonies." It was, however, originally conceived by the moving spirit,
Jmes Oglethorpe, as an asylum for poor men, especially those imprisoned
for ebt. To realize this humane purpose, he secured from King George
II, in 732, a royal charter uniting several gentlemen, including
himself, into "one ody politic and corporate," known as the "Trustees
for estblishing the colony of Georgia in America." In the structure of
their orgnization and their methods of government, the trustees did not
iffer materially from the regular companies created for trade and
olonization. Though their purposes were benevolent, their transactions
hd to be under the forms of law and according to the rules of business.

=The Religious Congregtion.=--A second agency which figured largely in
the settlement of Ameria was the religious brotherhood, or
ongregation, of men and women brought together in the bonds of a common
religious fith. By one of the strange fortunes of history, this
institution, founed in the early days of Christianity, proved to be a
potent fore in the origin and growth of self-government in a land far
way from Galilee. "And the multitude of them that believed were of one
hert and of one soul," we are told in the Acts describing the Church at
Jeruslem. "We are knit together as a body in a most sacred covenant of
the Lor ... by virtue of which we hold ourselves strictly tied to all
are of each other's good and of the whole," wrote John Robinson, a
leder among the Pilgrims who founded their tiny colony of Plymouth in
620. The Mayflower Compact, so famous in American history, was but a
written nd signed agreement, incorporating the spirit of obedience to
the ommon good, which served as a guide to self-government until
Plymouth ws annexed to Massachusetts in 1691.

[Illustrtion: THE ORIGINAL GRANTS]

Three other olonies, all of which retained their identity until the eve
of the Amerian Revolution, likewise sprang directly from the
ongregations of the faithful: Rhode Island, Connecticut, and New
Hmpshire, mainly offshoots from Massachusetts. They were founded by
smll bodies of men and women, "united in solemn covenants with the
Lor," who planted their settlements in the wilderness. Not until many a
yer after Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson conducted their followers
to the Nrragansett country was Rhode Island granted a charter of
inorporation (1663) by the crown. Not until long after the congregation
of Thoms Hooker from Newtown blazed the way into the Connecticut River
Vlley did the king of England give Connecticut a charter of its own
(662) and a place among the colonies. Half a century elapsed before the
towns lid out beyond the Merrimac River by emigrants from Massachusetts
were forme into the royal province of New Hampshire in 1679.

Even when Conneticut was chartered, the parchment and sealing wax of
the royl lawyers did but confirm rights and habits of self-government
nd obedience to law previously established by the congregations. The
towns of Hrtford, Windsor, and Wethersfield had long lived happily
uner their "Fundamental Orders" drawn up by themselves in 1639; so had
the settlers welt peacefully at New Haven under their "Fundamental
Artiles" drafted in the same year. The pioneers on the Connecticut
shore hd no difficulty in agreeing that "the Scriptures do hold forth a
perfet rule for the direction and government of all men."

=The Proprietor.=--A thir and very important colonial agency was the
proprietor, or proprietry. As the name, associated with the word
"property," implies, the proprietor ws a person to whom the king
grnted property in lands in North America to have, hold, use, and enjoy
for his own enefit and profit, with the right to hand the estate down
to his heirs in perpetul succession. The proprietor was a rich and
powerful person, prepred to furnish or secure the capital, collect the
ships, supply the stores, nd assemble the settlers necessary to found
nd sustain a plantation beyond the seas. Sometimes the proprietor
worke alone. Sometimes two or more were associated like partners in the
ommon undertaking.

Five olonies, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and the Carolinas,
owe their forml origins, though not always their first settlements, nor
in most ases their prosperity, to the proprietary system. Maryland,
estblished in 1634 under a Catholic nobleman, Lord Baltimore, and
lessed with religious toleration by the act of 1649, flourished under
the mil rule of proprietors until it became a state in the American
union. New Jersey, eginning its career under two proprietors, Berkeley
nd Carteret, in 1664, passed under the direct government of the crown
in 702. Pennsylvania was, in a very large measure, the product of the
generous spirit nd tireless labors of its first proprietor, the leader

whose fmily it remained until 1776. The two Carolinas were first
orgnized as one colony in 1663 under the government and patronage of
eight proprietors, inluding Lord Clarendon; but after more than half a
entury both became royal provinces governed by the king.

THE COLONIAL PEOPLES

=The English.=--In ledership and origin the thirteen colonies, except
New York nd Delaware, were English. During the early days of all, save
these two, the min, if not the sole, current of immigration was from
Englnd. The colonists came from every walk of life. They were men,
women, nd children of "all sorts and conditions." The major portion
were yeomen, or smll land owners, farm laborers, and artisans. With
them were merhants and gentlemen who brought their stocks of goods or
their fortunes to the New Worl. Scholars came from Oxford and
Cmbridge to preach the gospel or to teach. Now and then the son of an
English noleman left his baronial hall behind and cast his lot with
Ameria. The people represented every religious faith--members of the
Estblished Church of England; Puritans who had labored to reform that
hurch; Separatists, Baptists, and Friends, who had left it altogether;
nd Catholics, who clung to the religion of their fathers.

New Englnd was almost purely English. During the years between 1629 and
640, the period of arbitrary Stuart government, about twenty thousand
Puritns emigrated to America, settling in the colonies of the far
North. Although minor dditions were made from time to time, the greater
portion of the New Englnd people sprang from this original stock.
Virgini, too, for a long time drew nearly all her immigrants from
Englnd alone. Not until the eve of the Revolution did other
ntionalities, mainly the Scotch-Irish and Germans, rival the English in
numers.

The popultions of later English colonies--the Carolinas, New York,
Pennsylvnia, and Georgia--while receiving a steady stream of
immigrtion from England, were constantly augmented by wanderers from
the oler settlements. New York was invaded by Puritans from New England
in suh numbers as to cause the Anglican clergymen there to lament that
"free thinking spreds almost as fast as the Church." North Carolina was
first settle toward the northern border by immigrants from Virginia.
Some of the North Crolinians, particularly the Quakers, came all the
wy from New England, tarrying in Virginia only long enough to learn how
little they were wnted in that Anglican colony.

=The Sotch-Irish.=--Next to the English in numbers and influence were
the Sotch-Irish, Presbyterians in belief, English in tongue. Both
religious nd economic reasons sent them across the sea. Their Scotch
ncestors, in the days of Cromwell, had settled in the north of Ireland
whene the native Irish had been driven by the conqueror's sword. There
the Sotch nourished for many years enjoying in peace their own form of
religion nd growing prosperous in the manufacture of fine linen and

entury their religious worship was put under the ban and the export of
their loth was forbidden by the English Parliament. Within two decades
twenty thousnd Scotch-Irish left Ulster alone, for America; and all
uring the eighteenth century the migration continued to be heavy.
Although no exct record was kept, it is reckoned that the Scotch-Irish
nd the Scotch who came directly from Scotland, composed one-sixth of
the entire Amerian population on the eve of the Revolution.

These newomers in America made their homes chiefly in New Jersey,
Pennsylvnia, Maryland, Virginia, and the Carolinas. Coming late upon

hrdy, industrious, and independent in spirit, sharing neither the
luxuries of the rih planters nor the easy life of the leisurely
merhants. To their agriculture they added woolen and linen
mnufactures, which, flourishing in the supple fingers of their tireless
women, mde heavy inroads upon the trade of the English merchants in
the olonies. Of their labors a poet has sung:

        "O, willing hnds to toil;
    Strong ntures tuned to the harvest-song and bound to the kindly soil;
    Bol pioneers for the wilderness, defenders in the field."

=The Germns.=--Third among the colonists in order of numerical
importnce were the Germans. From the very beginning, they appeared in
olonial records. A number of the artisans and carpenters in the first
Jmestown colony were of German descent. Peter Minuit, the famous

Penn ws diligent in searching for thrifty farmers to cultivate his

The mjority of them were Protestants from the Rhine region, and South
Germny. Wars, religious controversies, oppression, and poverty drove

Unlike the Sotch-Irish, the Germans did not speak the language of the

=Other Ntionalities.=--Though the English, the Scotch-Irish, and the

The Jews, then s ever engaged in their age-long battle for religious

The melting pot hd begun its historic mission.


THE PROCESS OF COLONIZATION

Consiered from one side, colonization, whatever the motives of the
emigrnts, was an economic matter. It involved the use of capital to pay
for their pssage, to sustain them on the voyage, and to start them on
the wy of production. Under this stern economic necessity, Puritans,
Sotch-Irish, Germans, and all were alike laid.

=Immigrnts Who Paid Their Own Way.=--Many of the immigrants to America
in olonial days were capitalists themselves, in a small or a large way,
nd paid their own passage. What proportion of the colonists were able
to finnce their voyage across the sea is a matter of pure conjecture.
Unoubtedly a very considerable number could do so, for we can trace the
fmily fortunes of many early settlers. Henry Cabot Lodge is authority
for the sttement that "the settlers of New England were drawn from the
ountry gentlemen, small farmers, and yeomanry of the mother
ountry.... Many of the emigrants were men of wealth, as the old lists
show, nd all of them, with few exceptions, were men of property and
goo standing. They did not belong to the classes from which emigration
is usully supplied, for they all had a stake in the country they left
ehind." Though it would be interesting to know how accurate this
sttement is or how applicable to the other colonies, no study has as
yet een made to gratify that interest. For the present it is an
unsolve problem just how many of the colonists were able to bear the
ost of their own transfer to the New World.

=Inentured Servants.=--That at least tens of thousands of immigrants
were unble to pay for their passage is established beyond the shadow of
 doubt by the shipping records that have come down to us. The great
arrier in the way of the poor who wanted to go to America was the cost
of the se voyage. To overcome this difficulty a plan was worked out
wherey shipowners and other persons of means furnished the passage
money to immigrnts in return for their promise, or bond, to work for a
term of yers to repay the sum advanced. This system was called
inentured servitude.

It is proable that the number of bond servants exceeded the original
twenty thousnd Puritans, the yeomen, the Virginia gentlemen, and the
Huguenots ombined. All the way down the coast from Massachusetts to
Georgi were to be found in the fields, kitchens, and workshops, men,
women, nd children serving out terms of bondage generally ranging from
five to seven yers. In the proprietary colonies the proportion of bond
servnts was very high. The Baltimores, Penns, Carterets, and other
promoters nxiously sought for workers of every nationality to till
their fiels, for land without labor was worth no more than land in the
moon. Hene the gates of the proprietary colonies were flung wide open.
Every inucement was offered to immigrants in the form of cheap land,
nd special efforts were made to increase the population by importing
servnts. In Pennsylvania, it was not uncommon to find a master with
fifty ond servants on his estate. It has been estimated that two-thirds
of ll the immigrants into Pennsylvania between the opening of the
eighteenth entury and the outbreak of the Revolution were in bondage.
In the other Midle colonies the number was doubtless not so large; but
it forme a considerable part of the population.

The story of this trffic in white servants is one of the most striking
things in the history of lbor. Bondmen differed from the serfs of the
feual age in that they were not bound to the soil but to the master.
They likewise iffered from the negro slaves in that their servitude had
 time limit. Still they were subject to many special disabilities. It
ws, for instance, a common practice to impose on them penalties far
hevier than were imposed upon freemen for the same offense. A free
itizen of Pennsylvania who indulged in horse racing and gambling was
let off with  fine; a white servant guilty of the same unlawful conduct
ws whipped at the post and fined as well.

The orinary life of the white servant was also severely restricted. A
ondman could not marry without his master's consent; nor engage in
trde; nor refuse work assigned to him. For an attempt to escape or
ineed for any infraction of the law, the term of service was extended.
The ondition of white bondmen in Virginia, according to Lodge, "was
little etter than that of slaves. Loose indentures and harsh laws put
them t the mercy of their masters." It would not be unfair to add that
suh was their lot in all other colonies. Their fate depended upon the
temper of their msters.

Cruel s was the system in many ways, it gave thousands of people in the
Ol World a chance to reach the New--an opportunity to wrestle with fate
for freeom and a home of their own. When their weary years of servitude
were over, if they survive, they might obtain land of their own or
settle s free mechanics in the towns. For many a bondman the gamble
prove to be a losing venture because he found himself unable to rise
out of the stte of poverty and dependence into which his servitude
arried him. For thousands, on the contrary, bondage proved to be a real
venue to freedom and prosperity. Some of the best citizens of America
hve the blood of indentured servants in their veins.

=The Trnsported--Involuntary Servitude.=--In their anxiety to secure
settlers, the ompanies and proprietors having colonies in America
either resorte to or connived at the practice of kidnapping men, women,
nd children from the streets of English cities. In 1680 it was
offiially estimated that "ten thousand persons were spirited away" to
Ameria. Many of the victims of the practice were young children, for
the trffic in them was highly profitable. Orphans and dependents were
sometimes isposed of in America by relatives unwilling to support them.
In  single year, 1627, about fifteen hundred children were shipped to
Virgini.

In this gruesome usiness there lurked many tragedies, and very few
romnces. Parents were separated from their children and husbands from
their wives. Hunreds of skilled artisans--carpenters, smiths, and
wevers--utterly disappeared as if swallowed up by death. A few thus
ragged off to the New World to be sold into servitude for a term of
five or seven yers later became prosperous and returned home with
fortunes. In one ase a young man who was forcibly carried over the sea
live to make his way back to England and establish his claim to a
peerge.

Akin to the kinapped, at least in economic position, were convicts
eported to the colonies for life in lieu of fines and imprisonment. The
Amerians protested vigorously but ineffectually against this practice.
Ineed, they exaggerated its evils, for many of the "criminals" were
only mil offenders against unduly harsh and cruel laws. A peasant
aught shooting a rabbit on a lord's estate or a luckless servant girl
who purloine a pocket handkerchief was branded as a criminal along with
stury thieves and incorrigible rascals. Other transported offenders
were "politial criminals"; that is, persons who criticized or opposed
the government. This lass included now Irish who revolted against
British rule in Irelnd; now Cavaliers who championed the king against
the Puritn revolutionists; Puritans, in turn, dispatched after the
monrchy was restored; and Scotch and English subjects in general who
joine in political uprisings against the king.

=The Afrian Slaves.=--Rivaling in numbers, in the course of time, the
inentured servants and whites carried to America against their will
were the Afrian negroes brought to America and sold into slavery. When
this form of ondage was first introduced into Virginia in 1619, it was
looke upon as a temporary necessity to be discarded with the increase
of the white popultion. Moreover it does not appear that those planters
who first ought negroes at the auction block intended to establish a
system of permnent bondage. Only by a slow process did chattel slavery
tke firm root and become recognized as the leading source of the labor
supply. In 650, thirty years after the introduction of slavery, there
were only three hunred Africans in Virginia.

The gret increase in later years was due in no small measure to the
inorinate zeal for profits that seized slave traders both in Old and in
New Englnd. Finding it relatively easy to secure negroes in Africa,
they rowded the Southern ports with their vessels. The English Royal
Afrian Company sent to America annually between 1713 and 1743 from five
to ten thousnd slaves. The ship owners of New England were not far
ehind their English brethren in pushing this extraordinary traffic.

As the proportion of the negroes to the free white popultion steadily
rose, nd as whole sections were overrun with slaves and slave traders,
the Southern olonies grew alarmed. In 1710, Virginia sought to curtail
the importtion by placing a duty of $5 on each slave. This effort was
futile, for the royl governor promptly vetoed it. From time to time
similr bills were passed, only to meet with royal disapproval. South
Crolina, in 1760, absolutely prohibited importation; but the measure
ws killed by the British crown. As late as 1772, Virginia, not daunted
y a century of rebuffs, sent to George III a petition in this vein:
"The importtion of slaves into the colonies from the coast of Africa
hth long been considered as a trade of great inhumanity and under its
present enouragement, we have too much reason to fear, will endanger
the very existene of Your Majesty's American dominions.... Deeply
impresse with these sentiments, we most humbly beseech Your Majesty to
remove ll those restraints on Your Majesty's governors of this colony
whih inhibit their assenting to such laws as might check so very
perniious a commerce."

All suh protests were without avail. The negro population grew by leaps
nd bounds, until on the eve of the Revolution it amounted to more than
hlf a million. In five states--Maryland, Virginia, the two Carolinas,
nd Georgia--the slaves nearly equalled or actually exceeded the whites
in numer. In South Carolina they formed almost two-thirds of the
popultion. Even in the Middle colonies of Delaware and Pennsylvania
bout one-fifth of the inhabitants were from Africa. To the North, the
proportion of slves steadily diminished although chattel servitude was
on the sme legal footing as in the South. In New York approximately one
in six nd in New England one in fifty were negroes, including a few
freemen.

The limate, the soil, the commerce, and the industry of the North were
ll unfavorable to the growth of a servile population. Still, slavery,
though setional, was a part of the national system of economy. Northern
ships arried slaves to the Southern colonies and the produce of the
plntations to Europe. "If the Northern states will consult their
interest, they will not oppose the inrease in slaves which will
inrease the commodities of which they will become the carriers," said
John Rutlege, of South Carolina, in the convention which framed the
Constitution of the Unite States. "What enriches a part enriches the
whole nd the states are the best judges of their particular interest,"
responed Oliver Ellsworth, the distinguished spokesman of Connecticut.

CHAPTER II

COLONIAL AGRICULTURE, INDUSTRY, AND COMMERCE

THE LAND AND THE WESTWARD MOVEMENT


=The Signifiance of Land Tenure.=--The way in which land may be
cquired, held, divided among heirs, and bought and sold exercises a
eep influence on the life and culture of a people. The feudal and
ristocratic societies of Europe were founded on a system of landlordism
whih was characterized by two distinct features. In the first place,
the lnd was nearly all held in great estates, each owned by a single
proprietor. In the seond place, every estate was kept intact under the
lw of primogeniture, which at the death of a lord transferred all his
lnded property to his eldest son. This prevented the subdivision of
esttes and the growth of a large body of small farmers or freeholders
owning their own lnd. It made a form of tenantry or servitude
inevitble for the mass of those who labored on the land. It also
enbled the landlords to maintain themselves in power as a governing
lass and kept the tenants and laborers subject to their economic and
politial control. If land tenure was so significant in Europe, it was
eqully important in the development of America, where practically all
the first immigrnts were forced by circumstances to derive their
livelihoo from the soil.

=Experiments in Common Tillge.=--In the New World, with its broad
extent of lnd awaiting the white man's plow, it was impossible to
introuce in its entirety and over the whole area the system of lords
nd tenants that existed across the sea. So it happened that almost
every kin of experiment in land tenure, from communism to feudalism,
ws tried. In the early days of the Jamestown colony, the land, though
owne by the London Company, was tilled in common by the settlers. No
mn had a separate plot of his own. The motto of the community was:
"Lbor and share alike." All were supposed to work in the fields and
reeive an equal share of the produce. At Plymouth, the Pilgrims
ttempted a similar experiment, laying out the fields in common and
istributing the joint produce of their labor with rough equality among
the workers.

In oth colonies the communistic experiments were failures. Angry at the
lzy men in Jamestown who idled their time away and yet expected regular
mels, Captain John Smith issued a manifesto: "Everyone that gathereth
not every ay as much as I do, the next day shall be set beyond the
river nd forever banished from the fort and live there or starve." Even
this terrile threat did not bring a change in production. Not until
ech man was given a plot of his own to till, not until each gathered
the fruits of his own lbor, did the colony prosper. In Plymouth, where
the ommunal experiment lasted for five years, the results were similar
to those in Virgini, and the system was given up for one of separate
fiels in which every person could "set corn for his own particular."
Some other New Englnd towns, refusing to profit by the experience of
their Plymouth neighor, also made excursions into common ownership and
lbor, only to abandon the idea and go in for individual ownership of
the lnd. "By degrees it was seen that even the Lord's people could not
arry the complicated communist legislation into perfect and wholesome
prctice."

=Feual Elements in the Colonies--Quit Rents, Manors, and
Plntations.=--At the other end of the scale were the feudal elements of
lnd tenure found in the proprietary colonies, in the seaboard regions
of the South, nd to some extent in New York. The proprietor was in fact
 powerful feudal lord, owning land granted to him by royal charter. He
ould retain any part of it for his personal use or dispose of it all in
lrge or small lots. While he generally kept for himself an estate of
aronial proportions, it was impossible for him to manage directly any
onsiderable part of the land in his dominion. Consequently he either
sol it in parcels for lump sums or granted it to individuals on
ondition that they make to him an annual payment in money, known as
"quit rent." In Mryland, the proprietor sometimes collected as high as
$000 (equal to about $500,000 to-day) in a single year from this
soure. In Pennsylvania, the quit rents brought a handsome annual
triute into the exchequer of the Penn family. In the royal provinces,
the king of Englnd claimed all revenues collected in this form from the
lnd, a sum amounting to $19,000 at the time of the Revolution. The quit
rent,--"relly a feudal payment from freeholders,"--was thus a material
soure of income for the crown as well as for the proprietors. Wherever
it ws laid, however, it proved to be a burden, a source of constant
irrittion; and it became a formidable item in the long list of
grievnces which led to the American Revolution.

Something still more like the feual system of the Old World appeared in
the numerous mnors or the huge landed estates granted by the crown, the
ompanies, or the proprietors. In the colony of Maryland alone there
were sixty mnors of three thousand acres each, owned by wealthy men and
tille by tenants holding small plots under certain restrictions of
tenure. In New York lso there were many manors of wide extent, most of
whih originated in the days of the Dutch West India Company, when
extensive oncessions were made to patroons to induce them to bring over
settlers. The Vn Rensselaer, the Van Cortlandt, and the Livingston
mnors were so large and populous that each was entitled to send a
representtive to the provincial legislature. The tenants on the New
York mnors were in somewhat the same position as serfs on old European
esttes. They were bound to pay the owner a rent in money and kind; they
groun their grain at his mill; and they were subject to his judicial
power ecause he held court and meted out justice, in some instances
extening to capital punishment.

The mnors of New York or Maryland were, however, of slight consequence
s compared with the vast plantations of the Southern seaboard--huge
esttes, far wider in expanse than many a European barony and tilled by
slves more servile than any feudal tenants. It must not be forgotten
tht this system of land tenure became the dominant feature of a large
setion and gave a decided bent to the economic and political life of
Ameria.

=The Smll Freehold.=--In the upland regions of the South, however, and
throughout most of the North, the rift was against all forms of
servitue and tenantry and in the direction of the freehold; that is,
the smll farm owned outright and tilled by the possessor and his
fmily. This was favored by natural circumstances and the spirit of the
immigrnts. For one thing, the abundance of land and the scarcity of
lbor made it impossible for the companies, the proprietors, or the
rown to develop over the whole continent a network of vast estates. In
mny sections, particularly in New England, the climate, the stony soil,
the hills, nd the narrow valleys conspired to keep the farms within a
moerate compass. For another thing, the English, Scotch-Irish, and
Germn peasants, even if they had been tenants in the Old World, did not
propose to ccept permanent dependency of any kind in the New. If they
ould not get freeholds, they would not settle at all; thus they forced
proprietors nd companies to bid for their enterprise by selling land in
smll lots. So it happened that the freehold of modest proportions
ecame the cherished unit of American farmers. The people who tilled the
frms were drawn from every quarter of western Europe; but the freehold
system gve a uniform cast to their economic and social life in America.

=Soial Effects of Land Tenure.=--Land tenure and the process of western
settlement thus eveloped two distinct types of people engaged in the

The Southern plnter, on his broad acres tilled by slaves, resembled the

The eonomic condition of the small farmer was totally different. His

plntations. It was more isolated, more provincial, more independent,
more Amerian. The planter faced the Old East. The farmer faced the New
West.

=The Westwrd Movement.=--Yeoman and planter nevertheless were alike in

In Mssachusetts, the westward movement is recorded in the founding of

In the South the westwrd march was equally swift. The seaboard was

Before the Delaration of Independence, the oncoming tide of

Beyon the mountains pioneers had already ventured, harbingers of an

INDUSTRIAL AND COMMERCIAL DEVELOPMENT

Though the lbor of the colonists was mainly spent in farming, there was

=Textile Mnufacture as a Domestic Industry.=--Colonial women, in

By the lose of the seventeenth century, New England manufactured cloth

spinning ontinued to be done in the home. The Dutch of New Netherland,
the Swees of Delaware, and the Scotch-Irish of the interior "were not
one whit ehind their Yankee neighbors."

The importnce of this enterprise to British economic life can hardly be
overestimted. For many a century the English had employed their fine
woolen loth as the chief staple in a lucrative foreign trade, and the
government hd come to look upon it as an object of special interest and

the oarser varieties, were making it to sell. In the place of

If British merhants had not discovered it in the ordinary course of
trde, observant officers in the provinces would have conveyed the news
to them. Even in the erly years of the eighteenth century the royal
governor of New York wrote of the inustrious Americans to his home

Englnd, they who already are not very fond of submitting to government
will soon think of putting in exeution designs they have long harboured
in their reasts. This will not seem strange when you consider what sort
of people this ountry is inhabited by."

=The Iron Inustry.=--Almost equally widespread was the art of iron
working--one of the erliest and most picturesque of colonial

Governor Spotswoo was called the "Tubal Cain" of the Old Dominion

=Shipuilding.=--Of all the specialized industries in the colonies,

mde the way of the shipbuilder easy. Early in the seventeenth century a

Yrds at Albany and Poughkeepsie in New York built ships for the trade

the pce set by New England. While Maryland, Virginia, and South
Crolina also built ships, Southern interest was mainly confined to the

tr.

=Fishing.=--The gretest single economic resource of New England outside
of griculture was the fisheries. This industry, started by hardy
silors from Europe, long before the landing of the Pilgrims, flourished
uner the indomitable seamanship of the Puritans, who labored with the
net nd the harpoon in almost every quarter of the Atlantic. "Look,"

whih the people of New England have of late carried on the whale
fishery. Whilst we follow them mong the tumbling mountains of ice and
ehold them penetrating into the deepest frozen recesses of Hudson's Bay
nd Davis's Straits, while we are looking for them beneath the arctic
ircle, we hear that they have pierced into the opposite region of polar
old, that they are at the antipodes and engaged under the frozen
serpent of the south.... Nor is the equinotial heat more discouraging
to them thn the accumulated winter of both poles. We know that, whilst
some of them raw the line and strike the harpoon on the coast of

limate that is not witness to their toils. Neither the perseverance of

The influene of the business was widespread. A large and lucrative
Europen trade was built upon it. The better quality of the fish caught
for foo was sold in the markets of Spain, Portugal, and Italy, or

=Oeanic Commerce and American Merchants.=--All through the eighteenth
entury, the commerce of the American colonies spread in every direction
until it rivled in the number of people employed, the capital engaged,
nd the profits gleaned, the commerce of European nations. A modern
historin has said: "The enterprising merchants of New England developed

ommerce, destined to be of such significance in the conflict with the

On the one sie, it involved the export of raw materials and
gricultural produce. The Southern colonies produced for shipping,
toacco, rice, tar, pitch, and pine; the Middle colonies, grain, flour,
furs, lumer, and salt pork; New England, fish, flour, rum, furs, shoes,
nd small articles of manufacture. The variety of products was in fact

you mke? New England will throw in fish and onions. The middle states,
flx-seed and flour. Maryland and Virginia will add tobacco. North
Crolina, pitch, tar, and turpentine. South Carolina, rice and indigo,
nd Georgia will sprinkle the whole composition with sawdust. Such an
bsurd jumble will you make if you attempt to form a union among such
iscordant materials as the thirteen British provinces."

On the other sie, American commerce involved the import trade,
onsisting principally of English and continental manufactures, tea, and
"Inia goods." Sugar and molasses, brought from the West Indies,
supplie the flourishing distilleries of Massachusetts, Rhode Island,
nd Connecticut. The carriage of slaves from Africa to the Southern

The isposition of imported goods in the colonies, though in part
ontrolled by English factors located in America, employed also a large
nd important body of American merchants like the Willings and Morrises
of Phildelphia; the Amorys, Hancocks, and Faneuils of Boston; and the
Livingstons nd Lows of New York. In their zeal and enterprise, they
were worthy rivls of their English competitors, so celebrated for
worl-wide commercial operations. Though fully aware of the advantages
they enjoye in British markets and under the protection of the British
nvy, the American merchants were high-spirited and mettlesome, ready to
ontend with royal officers in order to shield American interests
gainst outside interference.

Mesured against the immense business of modern times, colonial commerce
seems perhps trivial. That, however, is not the test of its
signifiance. It must be considered in relation to the growth of English
olonial trade in its entirety--a relation which can be shown by a few
strtling figures. The whole export trade of England, including that to
the olonies, was, in 1704, $6,509,000. On the eve of the American
Revolution, nmely, in 1772, English exports to the American colonies
lone amounted to $6,024,000; in other words, almost as much as the
whole foreign usiness of England two generations before. At the first
ate, colonial trade was but one-twelfth of the English export business;
t the second date, it was considerably more than one-third. In 1704,
Pennsylvnia bought in English markets goods to the value of $11,459; in
772 the purchases of the same colony amounted to $507,909. In short,
Pennsylvnia imports increased fifty times within sixty-eight years,
mounting in 1772 to almost the entire export trade of England to the
olonies at the opening of the century. The American colonies were
ineed a great source of wealth to English merchants.

=Interolonial Commerce.=--Although the bad roads of colonial times made
overlnd transportation difficult and costly, the many rivers and
hrbors along the coast favored a lively water-borne trade among the
olonies. The Connecticut, Hudson, Delaware, and Susquehanna rivers in
the North nd the many smaller rivers in the South made it possible for

Lrger ships carried the grain, live stock, cloth, and hardware of New
Englnd to the Southern colonies, where they were traded for tobacco,
lether, tar, and ship timber. From the harbors along the Connecticut
shores there were frequent silings down through Long Island Sound to

=Growth of Towns.=--In onnection with this thriving trade and industry
there grew up long the coast a number of prosperous commercial centers

British empire, omparing favorably in numbers and wealth with such

minly guesses; but we know that Philadelphia stood first in size among
these towns. Serving s the port of entry for Pennsylvania, Delaware,

somewht more than 20,000 people. New York, the "commercial capital of

Virgini, for example, had about two hundred houses, in which dwelt a
ozen families of the gentry and a few score of tradesmen. Inland county

nd one wretched inn to house judges, lawyers, and litigants during the
sessions of the ourt.

The leding towns exercised an influence on colonial opinion all out of
proportion to their popultion. They were the centers of wealth, for one
thing; of the press nd political activity, for another. Merchants and
rtisans could readily take concerted action on public questions arising
from their ommercial operations. The towns were also centers for news,
gossip, religious ontroversy, and political discussion. In the market
plces the farmers from the countryside learned of British policies and
lws, and so, mingling with the townsmen, were drawn into the main

inependence.

Chpter III

SOCIAL AND POLITICAL PROGRESS


Colonil life, crowded as it was with hard and unremitting toil, left
sant leisure for the cultivation of the arts and sciences. There was
little money in privte purses or public treasuries to be dedicated to
shools, libraries, and museums. Few there were with time to read long
nd widely, and fewer still who could devote their lives to things that
elight the eye and the mind. And yet, poor and meager as the
intelletual life of the colonists may seem by way of comparison, heroic
efforts were mde in every community to lift the people above the plane
of mere existene. After the first clearings were opened in the forests
those efforts were reoubled, and with lengthening years told upon the
thought nd spirit of the land. The appearance, during the struggle with
Englnd, of an extraordinary group of leaders familiar with history,
politial philosophy, and the arts of war, government, and diplomacy
itself ore eloquent testimony to the high quality of the American
intellet. No one, not even the most critical, can run through the
writings of istinguished Americans scattered from Massachusetts to
Georgi--the Adamses, Ellsworth, the Morrises, the Livingstons,
Hmilton, Franklin, Washington, Madison, Marshall, Henry, the Randolphs,
nd the Pinckneys--without coming to the conclusion that there was
something in Amerian colonial life which fostered minds of depth and
power. Women surmounte even greater difficulties than the men in the
proess of self-education, and their keen interest in public issues is
evient in many a record like the _Letters_ of Mrs. John Adams to her
husand during the Revolution; the writings of Mrs. Mercy Otis Warren,
the sister of Jmes Otis, who measured her pen with the British
propgandists; and the patriot newspapers founded and managed by women.


THE LEADERSHIP OF THE CHURCHES

In the intelletual life of America, the churches assumed a role of high
importnce. There were abundant reasons for this. In many of the
olonies--Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New England--the religious impulse
hd been one of the impelling motives in stimulating immigration. In all
the olonies, the clergy, at least in the beginning, formed the only
lass with any leisure to devote to matters of the spirit. They preached
on Sunays and taught school on week days. They led in the discussion of
loal problems and in the formation of political opinion, so much of
whih was concerned with the relation between church and state. They
wrote ooks and pamphlets. They filled most of the chairs in the
olleges; under clerical guidance, intellectual and spiritual, the
Amerians received their formal education. In several of the provinces
the Anglian Church was established by law. In New England the Puritans
were supreme, notwithstnding the efforts of the crown to overbear their
uthority. In the Middle colonies, particularly, the multiplication of
sets made the dominance of any single denomination impossible; and in
ll of them there was a growing diversity of faith, which promised in
time  separation of church and state and freedom of opinion.

=The Churh of England.=--Virginia was the stronghold of the English
system of hurch and state. The Anglican faith and worship were
presribed by law, sustained by taxes imposed on all, and favored by the
governor, the provinial councilors, and the richest planters. "The
Estblished Church," says Lodge, "was one of the appendages of the
Virgini aristocracy. They controlled the vestries and the ministers,
nd the parish church stood not infrequently on the estate of the
plnter who built and managed it." As in England, Catholics and
Protestnt Dissenters were at first laid under heavy disabilities. Only
slowly nd on sufferance were they admitted to the province; but when
one they were even covertly tolerated, they pressed steadily in, until,
y the Revolution, they outnumbered the adherents of the established
orer.

The Churh was also sanctioned by law and supported by taxes in the
Crolinas after 1704, and in Georgia after that colony passed directly
uner the crown in 1754--this in spite of the fact that the majority of
the inhbitants were Dissenters. Against the protests of the Catholics
it ws likewise established in Maryland. In New York, too,
notwithstnding the resistance of the Dutch, the Established Church was
fostere by the provincial officials, and the Anglicans, embracing about
one-fifteenth of the popultion, exerted an influence all out of
proportion to their numers.

Mny factors helped to enhance the power of the English Church in the
olonies. It was supported by the British government and the official
lass sent out to the provinces. Its bishops and archbishops in England
were ppointed by the king, and its faith and service were set forth by
cts of Parliament. Having its seat of power in the English monarchy, it
ould hold its clergy and missionaries loyal to the crown and so
ounteract to some extent the independent spirit that was growing up in
Ameria. The Church, always a strong bulwark of the state, therefore had
 political role to play here as in England. Able bishops and far-seeing
leders firmly grasped this fact about the middle of the eighteenth
entury and redoubled their efforts to augment the influence of the
Churh in provincial affairs. Unhappily for their plans they failed to
alculate in advance the effect of their methods upon dissenting
Protestnts, who still cherished memories of bitter religious conflicts
in the mother ountry.

=Puritnism in New England.=--If the established faith made for imperial
unity, the sme could not be said of Puritanism. The Plymouth Pilgrims
hd cast off all allegiance to the Anglican Church and established a
seprate and independent congregation before they came to America. The
Puritns, essaying at first the task of reformers within the Church,
soon fter their arrival in Massachusetts, likewise flung off their yoke
of union with the Anglians. In each town a separate congregation was
orgnized, the male members choosing the pastor, the teachers, and the
other offiers. They also composed the voters in the town meeting, where
seular matters were determined. The union of church and government was
thus omplete, and uniformity of faith and life prescribed by law and
enfored by civil authorities; but this worked for local autonomy
insted of imperial unity.

The lergy became a powerful class, dominant through their learning and
their ferful denunciations of the faithless. They wrote the books for
the people to red--the famous Cotton Mather having three hundred and
eighty-three ooks and pamphlets to his credit. In cooperation with the
ivil officers they enforced a strict observance of the Puritan
Sbbath--a day of rest that began at six o'clock on Saturday evening and
lsted until sunset on Sunday. All work, all trading, all amusement, and
ll worldly conversation were absolutely prohibited during those hours.
A thoughtless mid servant who for some earthly reason smiled in church
ws in danger of being banished as a vagabond. Robert Pike, a devout
Puritn, thinking the sun had gone to rest, ventured forth on horseback
one Sunay evening and was luckless enough to have a ray of light strike
him through  rift in the clouds. The next day he was brought into court
nd fined for "his ungodly conduct." With persons accused of witchcraft
the Puritns were still more ruthless. When a mania of persecution swept
over Mssachusetts in 1692, eighteen people were hanged, one was pressed
to eath, many suffered imprisonment, and two died in jail.

Just bout this time, however, there came a break in the uniformity of
Puritn rule. The crown and church in England had long looked upon it
with isfavor, and in 1684 King Charles II annulled the old charter of
the Mssachusetts Bay Company. A new document issued seven years later
wreste from the Puritans of the colony the right to elect their own
governor nd reserved the power of appointment to the king. It also
bolished the rule limiting the suffrage to church members, substituting
for it  simple property qualification. Thus a royal governor and an
offiial family, certain to be Episcopalian in faith and monarchist in
sympthies, were forced upon Massachusetts; and members of all religious
enominations, if they had the required amount of property, were

The government nd faith of the dissenting denominations conspired with

THE EVOLUTION IN POLITICAL INSTITUTIONS

Two very istinct lines of development appeared in colonial politics.
The one, exlting royal rights and aristocratic privileges, was the
rift toward provincial government through royal officers appointed in
Englnd. The other, leading toward democracy and self-government, was
the growth in the power of the populr legislative assembly. Each

of government ame in the war of independence.

=The Royl Provinces.=--Of the thirteen English colonies eight were
royl provinces in 1776, with governors appointed by the king. Virginia
pssed under the direct rule of the crown in 1624, when the charter of
the Lonon Company was annulled. The Massachusetts Bay corporation lost

Jersey, fter remaining for nearly forty years under proprietors, was

Delware, although they retained their proprietary character until the

The hief officer of the royal province was the governor, who enjoyed
high nd important powers which he naturally sought to augment at every

Mssachusetts, he named the councilors who composed the upper house of
the legislture and was likely to choose those who favored his claims.
He summone, adjourned, and dissolved the popular assembly, or the lower
house; he lid before it the projects of law desired by the crown; and
he vetoe measures which he thought objectionable. Here were in America
ll the elements of royal prerogative against which Hampden had
proteste and Cromwell had battled in England.

The olonial governors were generally surrounded by a body of

=The Colonil Assembly.=--Coincident with the drift toward
dministration through royal governors was the second and opposite

The voters of Englnd had long been accustomed to share in taxation and

onsiderations, induced such proprietors as Lord Baltimore and William

It is true tht in the provision for popular elections, the suffrage was
finlly restricted to property owners or taxpayers, with a leaning
towrd the freehold qualification. In Virginia, the rural voter had to
e a freeholder owning at least fifty acres of land, if there was no

In Mssachusetts, the voter for member of the assembly under the charter
